**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper development trends (2023–2024) across the five methods point to a common direction: replace brittle, resource‑heavy components with principled, scalable designs that preserve (or improve) robustness and accuracy under practical constraints.
> 
> 1) Perception: anchor‑free, one‑stage association on COCO‑style whole‑body splits
> - Trend: From anchor‑based, multi‑stage association (e.g., BPJDet) to anchor‑free, end‑to‑end decoding (PBADet, ICLR 2024). The method compresses representation from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2 and uses a single part‑to‑body center offset, scaling to many parts without degrading detection.
> - Why it matters: Better scalability to larger part sets, simpler post‑processing, and robustness when parts are occluded. Uses standard detectors and optimizers (e.g., YOLO backbones, SGD), and evaluates on COCO‑HumanParts/WholeBody.
> 
> 2) Sequence modeling: enforcing E/I constraints via spectral thinking
> - Trend: From attributing poor learning under Dale’s Law to sign constraints alone (ColEI) to a spectral view (DANN RNNs; NeurIPS 2023). The singular‑value spectrum—not just signs—governs stability/learnability.
> - Practical pattern: Normalize spectra (e.g., via normalized SVD entropy) to predict performance; larger networks and balanced E/I ratios yield unimodal, clustered spectra and better learning on sequential MNIST and Penn Treebank. Small or I‑scarce networks are harder to train—highlighting scaling laws tied to spectrum, not only architecture.
> 
> 3) Self‑supervised learning: latent prediction (JEPA) over pixel reconstruction (MAE)
> - Trend: Analytical deep‑linear results (NeurIPS 2024) show JEPA’s depth‑dependent implicit bias toward high‑influence (high‑regression‑coefficient) features, whereas MAE prioritizes highly covarying (often noisy) features.
> - Implication: With deeper encoders, JEPA learns predictive, low‑variance, semantic features faster; MAE remains tied to reconstruction of high‑variance pixels. Evidence spans static/temporal linear models and ImageNet experiments; complements practical SSL trends favoring joint‑embedding objectives.
> 
> 4) Optimization at scale: from 8‑bit to 4‑bit Adam/AdamW states
> - Trend: Push optimizer‑state precision from 8‑bit to 4‑bit (NeurIPS 2023) by (a) solving the zero‑point issue for the second moment (use linear mapping excluding zero), and (b) rank‑1 normalization to handle heterogeneous outliers. A factorized second moment further reduces memory.
> - Outcome: Near‑lossless fine‑tuning of Transformers (RoBERTa‑Large on GLUE/SQuAD, Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1K, GPT‑2 M on E2E‑NLG) and instruction‑tuning of LLaMA (Alpaca) with AdamW; improves throughput with optimizer offloading and enables larger models under fixed GPU memory. This shifts the efficiency frontier without changing model architectures.
> 
> 5) Hybrid RL: mixing offline data with on‑policy NPG, with guarantees
> - Trend: From hybrid methods that only do off‑policy bootstrapping to combining on‑policy NPG with fitted policy evaluation on offline data (HAC/HNPG, ICLR 2024). Provides best‑of‑both‑worlds guarantees: offline‑RL‑style bounds when Bellman completeness/coverage hold, and on‑policy NPG guarantees when they do not.
> - Practice: HNPG outperforms off‑policy hybrid baselines on rich‑observation Comblock and an image‑based variant using CLIP features from CIFAR‑100, remaining stable when off‑policy TD training is brittle. Supports continuous action spaces and parameterized policies.
> 
> Cross‑cutting themes
> - Scalability and stability: Methods replace brittle heuristics (anchors, uniform sign constraints, pure TD bootstrapping, 8‑bit limit) with principled constructs: anchor‑free offsets; spectral diagnostics (normalized SVD entropy); latent‑space predictive losses; zero‑free 4‑bit quantization with rank‑1 normalization; on‑policy updates layered with offline evaluation.
> - Resource efficiency without accuracy loss: 4‑bit AdamW states preserve fine‑tuning quality on large Transformers; anchor‑free association reduces output size and post‑processing; hybrid on‑policy RL reduces instability from off‑policy TD.
> - Measurable robustness: New metrics and assumptions (Bellman error transfer coefficient; normalized SVD entropy) explain when methods scale (e.g., larger networks, balanced E/I, coverage conditions) and when they fail (small I populations, zero‑point quantization, off‑policy TD under misspecification).
> 
> Where this is heading
> - Perception stacks trend toward end‑to‑end, anchor‑free, split‑agnostic designs (COCO variants) that scale in K (parts) and simplify decoding.
> - Sequence learners with biological constraints are moving from constraint‑enforcement to spectrum‑shaping for predictable training across sizes/tasks (MNIST→PTB).
> - SSL continues its pivot from reconstruction to joint‑embedding prediction, with depth‑amplified bias toward predictive (high‑influence) features—consistent with better downstream transfer on ImageNet‑style data.
> - System‑level training shifts to memory‑minimal, accuracy‑preserving optimizers (4‑bit AdamW), enabling larger Transformer fine‑tuning and faster pipelines.
> - Hybrid RL increasingly couples provable on‑policy improvements with offline data reuse, showing stability and generalization on vision‑centric tasks (CIFAR‑100/CLIP), beyond classic control.
> 
> Touchpoints with common entities
> - COCO/COCO‑HumanParts (PBADet); MNIST and Penn Treebank (E/I RNNs); CIFAR‑100 and CLIP features (Hybrid RL); Transformers and Adam/AdamW with fine‑tuning (4‑bit optimizers, JEPA experiments); SGD is used in detection training. Together, they illustrate a 2023–2024 move toward scalable, robust, and resource‑aware learning across perception, sequence modeling, SSL, optimization, and RL.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, here is the concise set of papers matching your five topics, followed by a summary of the trend.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection (ICLR 2024)** — Introduces a one-stage, anchor-free detector for part–body association. Using anchor-free detection across multi-scale feature maps plus a single part-to-body center offset (instead of BPJDet-style body-to-part offsets), it associates hands/feet/face to the correct person. Evaluated on COCO-WholeBody/COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman, outperforming SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN). Ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning all help.
> 
> 2. **Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — Studies RNNs obeying E/I sign constraints (Dale's Law) via a singular-value/spectral viewpoint. Shows the poor learning of simple sign-constrained (ColEI) recurrent nets is due mainly to the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed) rather than sign constraints, and introduces normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a performance diagnostic. Validated on the adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and object recognition.
> 
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — Analyzes why joint-embedding predictive pretraining (JEPA/self-distillation) beats pixel reconstruction (MAE). In deep linear nets it shows JEPA is implicitly biased to prioritize high-influence features (high regression coefficients) and suppress noise, with critical-time analysis and ImageNet-1K CCA experiments confirming I-JEPA aligns faster with perceptual low-variance subspace than MAE.
> 
> 4. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — Pushes Adam/AdamW optimizer states from 32-bit (and prior 8-bit) down to ~4 bits via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantization, and second-moment factorization. Matches 32-bit accuracy on GLUE (RoBERTa-L), ImageNet (Swin-T), SQuAD, E2E-NLG (GPT-2/LoRA), WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca/MMLU), with up to ~57.7% memory savings.
> 
> 5. **Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees (ICLR 2024)** — Hybrid RL (HAC/HNPG) that integrates off-policy Fitted Policy Evaluation into an on-policy Natural Policy Gradient framework. Achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantees: state-of-the-art offline rates when offline assumptions (e.g., Bellman completeness) hold, and standard on-policy NPG guarantees otherwise. Demonstrated on continuous and image-based Comblock, including a CIFAR-100 augmented combination lock, outperforming PPO/TRPO and the off-policy hybrid RLPD.
> 
> ## Development trend of these methods
> 
> - **(1) Part–body association:** From multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines (Mask R-CNN, HierR-CNN, BPJDet on YOLO anchors) toward a single-stage, anchor-free design with a unified, scalable part-to-body representation — simpler, more efficient, and more accurate, with task-alignment supervision.
> - **(2) E/I-constrained RNNs:** From simply imposing biological sign constraints (which hurt learning) to identifying via spectral/SVD analysis that the initial singular-value spectrum, not the sign constraint, is the dominant factor — enabling diagnostics (NSE), better initialization/architecture (DANN), and gradient-clipping fixes.
> - **(3) SSL pretraining:** From input-space reconstruction (MAE) to joint-embedding predictive pretraining, now explained by theory (deep linear analysis) revealing an implicit bias toward high-influence features and noise suppression, validated at scale on ImageNet/CIFAR — i.e., moving from empirical SSL recipes to principled understanding of representation dynamics.
> - **(4) Optimizers:** From full 32-bit Adam/AdamW to 8-bit then ~4-bit states, using progressively more sophisticated quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization, stochastic rounding) that preserves accuracy across Transformers (LLaMA, RoBERTa, Swin-T) and fine-tuning/instruction tuning, enabling larger models under fixed memory budgets.
> - **(5) RL:** From pure on-policy PG (sample-hungry) or pure offline/off-policy methods (fragile, assumption-heavy) toward hybrid RL that mixes offline batches into an on-policy NPG framework, yielding provable best-of-both-worlds guarantees and being tested on increasingly challenging, image-based (CIFAR-100 Comblock) rich-observation tasks.
> 
> Overall, the shared trend is **integration and simplification under principled analysis**: unifying detection into single-stage anchor-free models, replacing ad-hoc biological/architectural constraints with spectral/theoretical understanding, replacing reconstruction with latent predictive objectives justified by implicit-bias theory, compressing optimization states to the lowest precision that keeps accuracy, and combining on-policy robustness with offline data efficiency backed by provable guarantees.

**community 最终答案**

> ## The five papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — One-stage, anchor-free part-body association. Extends anchor-free detectors (YOLOv5/YOLOv7) with a single part-to-body center offset, so hands/feet/face associate to the correct person with a compact representation. Outperforms BPJDet, HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts (COCO-style whole-body splits), CrowdHuman; also extends to quadruped part-body association.
> 
> 2. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — Studies RNNs obeying E/I sign constraints (Dale's law). Using singular-value decompositions, spectrum "transplant" experiments, and normalised SVD entropy, it shows the initial singular-value spectrum of the recurrent weights (multimodal/dispersed for ColEI networks) matters more than the sign constraints themselves. Evaluated on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — Analyzes why joint-embedding predictive pretraining (JEPA self-distillation) beats pixel reconstruction (MAE) in deep linear networks. Proves JEPA greedily prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficients ρ), whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance/λ features regardless of informativeness. ImageNet-1K CCA experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance perceptual subspace faster than MAE.
> 
> 4. **4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States (NeurIPS 2023)** — Memory-efficient optimizers storing Adam/AdamW first/second moments in 4 bits. Uses smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, and a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment (optionally factorized). Matches 32-bit AdamW on RoBERTa-L/GLUE, Swin-T/ImageNet-1k, GPT-2/E2E-NLG, Transformer/WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca), saving up to 57.7% memory.
> 
> 5. **Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees (HAC/HNPG, ICLR 2024)** — Hybrid RL that integrates fitted off-policy evaluation on offline batches into an on-policy natural-policy-gradient (NPG) actor-critic. Achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantees: offline-RL rates when Bellman completeness/coverage hold, otherwise degrades gracefully to on-policy NPG rates. Outperforms PPO/TRPO/RLPD on rich-observation Comblock, including a variant with CIFAR-100 images as states.
> 
> ## Development trend
> 
> - **Unification and simplification of pipelines**: multi-stage/anchor-based detectors give way to one-stage anchor-free designs with minimal representations (PBADet), and pure on-policy or pure offline RL converge toward hybrid "best-of-both-worlds" algorithms (HAC/HNPG).
> - **Theory-guided understanding of learning dynamics**: both RNN (Dale's law) and SSL (JEPA vs MAE) works move from empirical observation to spectral/dynamical analysis (singular values, deep linear networks, implicit bias), using theory to explain *why* certain constraints/objectives help or hurt.
> - **Efficiency at scale**: optimizer state compression advances from 8-bit to 4-bit with dedicated quantization schemes, explicitly targeting large Transformers/LLMs and fine-tuning (LLaMA, LoRA-style settings, GLUE/ImageNet).
> - **Provable guarantees alongside strong empirics**: the RL and SSL papers couple new methods with formal guarantees, while the detection and optimizer papers emphasize scalability and accuracy retention under reduced complexity — a collective trend toward simpler, more efficient, theoretically justified, and scale-aware methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper development trend across the five methods shows a coherent shift toward scalability, robustness, and resource efficiency, with complementary advances that together meet the five components of the query.
> 
> 1) Scalable, robust part–person association at COCO scale (PBADet, ICLR’24)
> - Trend: from multi‑stage, anchor‑based or body‑to‑part representations to one‑stage, anchor‑free, part‑to‑body association.
>   • Representation length and complexity shrink (single 2D center offset per part → scalable to many parts without growing the output head), improving throughput and post‑processing simplicity.
>   • Multi‑scale dense prediction and task‑aligned learning (TOOD) replace hand‑crafted anchors; decoding becomes a simple nearest‑center match.
> - Scale/field change: validated on COCO‑HumanParts and CrowdHuman, plus BodyHands, showing the approach handles crowded scenes and multiple part types with competitive AP/mMR. The formulation generalizes to other domains (e.g., animal feet/head) without changing the head.
> - Direction of travel: anchor‑free, universal association heads that do not degrade when the number of parts grows; strong COCO‑class results under real crowding and occlusion.
> 
> 2) Label‑free pretraining that predicts representations (JEPA, NeurIPS’24)
> - Trend: from reconstruction (MAE) toward joint embedding prediction (JEPA) to avoid over‑fitting to pixel variance and emphasize semantics.
>   • Deep linear analysis: JEPA implicitly prioritizes high‑influence features (large regression coefficients ρ), especially as encoder depth increases; MAE mainly follows covariance (λ).
>   • Temporal and masked‑view models ground this in practice: JEPA avoids noisy/low‑predictive features by operating in latent space, improving data efficiency for perception.
> - Scale/field change: analysis and controlled experiments connect to realistic signals (e.g., video‑like temporal models, comparisons to CLIP‑style feature subspaces). This pinpoints why recent I‑/V‑JEPA variants pretrain faster and transfer better for perception tasks.
> - Direction of travel: deeper JEPA encoders that predict one view’s representation from another to emphasize semantically predictive, low‑variance features (vs. pixel reconstruction).
> 
> 3) Recurrent controllers under Dale’s Law that still train well (NeurIPS’23)
> - Trend: from sign‑constrained E/I columns (ColEI) that learn poorly to architectures and initializations that fix the spectrum (DANN‑style E/I) and train like standard RNNs.
>   • Core finding: spectral pathologies—not the sign constraint per se—explain failures; ColEI produces multimodal, dispersed singular values with large modes; DANN and standard RNNs have unimodal, clustered spectra.
>   • Normalized SVD entropy becomes a predictive metric for trainability; learning improves with higher NSE, balanced E/I ratios, and larger networks—even with strict E/I separation.
> - Scale/field change: verified across adding task, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank (PTB), and a naturalistic object recognition task—bridging neuroscience constraints with practical RNN training.
> - Direction of travel: spectral‑aware E/I RNN designs and initializations that preserve Dale’s Law yet match standard RNN stability and performance.
> 
> 4) Policy learners that start offline and improve on‑policy with stability (ICLR’24)
> - Trend: from hybrid RL that is purely off‑policy to best‑of‑both‑worlds actor–critic: Hybrid NPG (HNPG) embeds off‑policy fitted policy evaluation into an on‑policy NPG loop.
>   • Theory: when offline assumptions (e.g., Bellman completeness/coverage) hold, rates match state‑of‑the‑art offline RL; when they fail, the method retains on‑policy NPG guarantees.
>   • Practice: on rich‑observation combination locks, including a harder image‑based variant using CIFAR‑100 features, HNPG outperforms off‑policy only hybrid baselines and remains stable (on‑policy supervised advantages vs. off‑policy TD bootstrapping).
> - Scale/field change: moves hybrid RL from “rely on TD bootstrapping” to “off‑policy evaluation + on‑policy policy improvement,” improving stability and generalization.
> - Direction of travel: theoretically grounded hybrid actor–critic that can safely warm‑start from logs and keep improving on‑policy.
> 
> 5) Fine‑tuning Transformers/LLMs under tight VRAM with ~4‑bit AdamW states (NeurIPS’23)
> - Trend: from 8‑bit optimizers to 4‑bit states with careful quantization of first/second moments.
>   • Key advances: smaller block sizes for M1; rank‑1 (row+column) normalization and linear mapping for M2 to avoid the zero‑point failure; optional factorization for further memory cuts.
>   • Results: lossless or near‑lossless fine‑tuning across RoBERTa‑L/GLUE & SQuAD, WMT14 Transformer, Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k, GPT‑2 on E2E‑NLG, and LLaMA instruction tuning—while reducing optimizer memory and improving offloaded throughput.
> - Scale/field change: enables end‑to‑end AdamW fine‑tuning of large Transformers/LLMs under tight VRAM without switching to task‑specific adapters.
> - Direction of travel: practical, general 4‑bit optimizer stacks (with AdamW) that cut memory while preserving accuracy and stability, making broader fine‑tuning economically feasible.
> 
> Cross‑cutting characteristics and timeline
> - 2023→2024 shift emphasizes: (i) anchor‑free, representation‑efficient detection at COCO scale (ICLR’24); (ii) JEPA‑style SSL that learns predictive, semantic features (NeurIPS’24); (iii) spectrum‑aware biologically constrained RNNs (NeurIPS’23); (iv) hybrid on‑/off‑policy RL with provable “best‑of‑both‑worlds” (ICLR’24); (v) memory‑centric training stacks via 4‑bit AdamW for Transformers/LLMs (NeurIPS’23).
> - Scalability: detection heads scale with parts; JEPA scales with encoder depth and emphasizes influential features; E/I RNNs scale with size and E/I balance; hybrid RL scales by reusing logs while safeguarding on‑policy stability; 4‑bit optimizers scale fine‑tuning to larger backbones under the same VRAM.
> - Dataset/benchmark coverage: COCO‑HumanParts/CrowdHuman/BodyHands (detection), CIFAR‑100 in image‑based RL, sequential MNIST & PTB (E/I RNNs), ImageNet‑1k/GLUE/SQuAD/WMT14/LLaMA (4‑bit fine‑tuning).
> 
> Net effect for the target system
> - (a) PBADet supplies a one‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑body association that scales to COCO crowds.
> - (b) JEPA theory clarifies why representation‑prediction pretraining focuses on influential/semantic features and avoids pixel noise.
> - (c) Dale‑compatible recurrent controllers are now trainable and stable when designed/initialized for proper spectra.
> - (d) HNPG safely combines offline logs with on‑policy updates and keeps theoretical stability even when offline assumptions break.
> - (e) 4‑bit AdamW state optimizers enable full‑parameter Transformer/LLM fine‑tuning under tight VRAM, with reported parity to 32‑bit/8‑bit baselines.
> 
> Overall development trend: methods are converging on minimal representations (anchor‑free offsets, predictive embeddings), spectrum‑aware stability (E/I RNNs), hybrid learning guarantees (offline→on‑policy), and aggressive optimizer compression (4‑bit states), enabling scalable, robust, and memory‑efficient systems across vision, RL, and language.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes. Five recent papers in the collection collectively address the five components:
> 
> **(a) PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part–body association. A single part-to-body center offset links hands/face to their parent persons, evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, and CrowdHuman (face–body association), outperforming BPJDet and Hier-R-CNN.
> 
> **(b) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — analyzes JEPA self-distillation, which predicts one view's latent representation from another (g(f(x))→f(y)) instead of reconstructing pixels like MAE. It proves JEPAs are biased toward "influential" features and avoid noise; validated with I-JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet-1K.
> 
> **(c) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) — recurrent controllers with separate excitatory/inhibitory units. Naive sign-constrained "ColEI" RNNs train poorly, but the DANN reparameterization respects E/I separation yet trains as well as standard RNNs, explained by recurrent-weight spectral properties (normalized SVD entropy). Benchmarks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> **(d) "Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees"** (ICLR 2024) — hybrid RL (HAC/HNPG) that starts from a static offline dataset and keeps performing on-policy NPG updates; it provably achieves the better of offline-RL and on-policy rates ("best-of-both-worlds"), degrading gracefully to on-policy guarantees if offline assumptions fail. Tested on rich-observation Comblock.
> 
> **(e) "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit AdamW optimizer states (smaller block size, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, optional factorization) enable lossless fine-tuning of RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Swin-T, Transformer-Base, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B with up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU).
> 
> **Dataset coverage:** COCO scale ✓ (PBADet); MNIST/PTB ✓ (Dale's Law RNN paper); common fine-tuning setups ✓ (4-bit optimizer: GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT14, ImageNet-1K, Alpaca/MMLU; JEPA: ImageNet-1K). **Not established:** none of these five papers reports CIFAR-100 experiments — CIFAR-100 appears in the collection only in unrelated works (e.g., binary spiking online optimization and Hessian-spectrum papers).
> 
> **Development trend across methods:**
> 1. **Detection/association:** multi-stage heuristic or anchor-based part–body association → single-stage anchor-free, end-to-end (scalable, more efficient).
> 2. **Self-supervised learning:** pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) → latent-space prediction (JEPA), with theory explaining why latent prediction learns more informative, noise-robust features.
> 3. **Recurrent/constrained networks:** hard structural constraints (E/I, Dale's Law) historically hurt learning → reparameterized architectures plus spectral-aware initialization make constrained networks train as well as unconstrained ones.
> 4. **RL:** offline-only or online-only → hybrid methods combining static logs with on-policy updates, with provable (doubly-robust) stability guarantees.
> 5. **Optimization:** optimizer states pushed 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit via quantization/factorization, enabling large-model fine-tuning under tight VRAM.
> 
> Overall trajectory: **constraint-aware, memory-efficient, and theoretically grounded methods** — respecting biological/architectural and resource constraints while retaining (or even proving) training performance and stability.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection contains papers covering all five components:
> 
> **(a) Hand/face→person association (COCO scale):** *PBADet* (ICLR 2024) is a one-stage, anchor-free detector that links parts (hands, face, feet) to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset. It is evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, and COCO, outperforming BPJDet/HierR-CNN and DETR-style pose estimators.
> 
> **(b) Label-free pretraining (predicting representations, not pixels):** The JEPA analysis paper (NeurIPS 2024) studies self-distillation that predicts one view's representation from another and shows it suppresses noisy features better than pixel-reconstructing MAE (ImageNet-1K). *LDReg* (ICLR 2024) regularizes SSL against dimensional collapse and reports CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and COCO detection; the contrastive-embedding-similarities paper covers CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.
> 
> **(c) E/I-separated recurrent controller that trains well:** *Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023) shows sign-constrained ColEI RNNs train poorly, while recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) with separate E-to-E/E-to-I/I-to-E projections train as well as standard RNNs—evaluated on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition.
> 
> **(d) Policy learner from a static log with on-policy updates and stability:** *HNPG/HAC* (ICLR 2024) integrates off-policy fitting on offline data into an on-policy NPG framework, achieving best-of-both-worlds guarantees (offline rates when assumptions hold, on-policy NPG rates otherwise). *PPO-Clip convergence* (ICLR 2024) proves stationary-point convergence, justifying off-policy sample reuse.
> 
> **(e) ~4-bit AdamW fine-tuning under tight VRAM:** *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023) quantizes AdamW moments with small blocks, zero-point exclusion, and rank-1 normalization/factorization; it matches 32-bit accuracy on RoBERTa (GLUE/SQuAD), Swin-T (ImageNet), GPT-2 (E2E), Transformer (WMT), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B (Alpaca/MMLU) with up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> - **(a)** Two-stage heuristic/learned part–body association → one-stage anchor-free, single-offset part-to-body association, making representations simpler and association scalable at COCO scale.
> - **(b)** Pixel-reconstruction pretraining (MAE) → representation-prediction/self-distillation (JEPA), with theory showing why it avoids noisy features, plus theory-driven regularization (LDReg) and variance-reduction against collapse.
> - **(c)** Naive E/I sign-constrained RNNs (ColEI, poor learning) → reparameterized E/I architectures (DANN), with diagnosis shifting from sign constraints to spectral properties (unimodal singular-value spectra, SVD entropy) as the key to trainability.
> - **(d)** Pure offline (strong assumptions) or pure online RL → hybrid RL that reuses a static log inside on-policy NPG with provable guarantees, alongside convergence theory for PPO-Clip enabling stable off-policy reuse.
> - **(e)** 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit optimizer states, moving from block-wise quantization to smaller blocks, zero-point exclusion, rank-1 normalization and factorization—lossless accuracy with drastically reduced memory for Transformer/LLM fine-tuning.

I’m interested in links to regularization under cross-entropy, practical optimizer choices, and how to keep GPU memory low during training.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development trend across the requested themes
> 
> 1) Geometry of contrastive embeddings (cosine similarity, temperature, batch size)
> - Earlier full‑batch analyses established a geometric “simplex ETF” optimum: positive pairs align (cosine ≈ 1) while all negatives sit at uniform cosine −1/(n−1) when temperature‑based InfoNCE/Sigmoid losses are optimized.
> - Recent work generalizes this picture and shows a key mini‑batch effect: smaller batches increase the variance of negative‑pair similarities even when their mean stays near −1/(n−1). This variance is now recognized as a distinctive mini‑batch artifact that degrades downstream accuracy; the proposed trend is to explicitly reduce it (e.g., an auxiliary variance‑reduction term that drives negative similarities toward −1/(n−1)).
> - A complementary design insight is to include within‑view negatives in the loss: doing so mitigates excessive separation of negatives (which otherwise forces imperfect positive alignment). Together, these advances move the field from “mean geometry” (uniform negatives) to “distributional geometry” (controlling variance under small batches), with practical recipes: tune temperature t jointly with a variance penalty and consider within‑view negatives.
> 
> 2) Implicit bias in JEPA/self‑distillation (JEPA → influential features)
> - The implicit bias of joint‑embedding self‑distillation has been sharpened: in deep linear models, JEPA prioritizes “influential features” (large regression coefficients), not merely high‑variance directions. Depth amplifies this bias; shallow encoders behave more like reconstruction/MAE. This reframes why predictive, latent‑space objectives often learn semantic, low‑noise directions faster, and formalizes the tradeoff relative to reconstruction objectives.
> - Trend: principled, depth‑dependent analyses now guide practice (e.g., choosing deeper encoders for stronger JEPA bias toward informative features; using temporal/simple linear generative models to predict when JEPA down‑weights noisy features).
> 
> 3) Memory‑efficient optimizers (sub‑8‑bit states) for vision/transformers and LoRA fine‑tuning
> - Optimizer state precision has progressed from 8‑bit to 4‑bit while matching full‑precision accuracy across vision (e.g., Swin), language (RoBERTa/GPT‑2), and instruction‑tuned LLaMA. Key breakthroughs:
>   • Outlier‑aware quantization for first moments (smaller blocks; row/column patterns),
>   • A zero‑point fix for the second moment (exclude zero in the mapping; simple linear mapping works best),
>   • Rank‑1 normalization to handle heterogeneous outlier patterns,
>   • Optional factorization of the second moment (Adafactor‑style) for further memory cuts.
> - Practical outcome: 4‑bit AdamW states (with optional factorization) reduce total training memory 30–58% and pair well with optimizer offloading; fused kernels recover or exceed 8‑bit speed. This enables larger per‑GPU batch sizes—synergizing with the contrastive trend above by lowering negative‑pair variance. LoRA‑style instruction tuning is supported end‑to‑end under these 4‑bit states.
> - Trend: memory savings move from parameter quantization to optimizer‑state quantization/factorization, focusing on robust per‑tensor/row/column schemes and zero‑point handling; this is now a general recipe for both CNN and Transformer training.
> 
> 4) One‑stage, anchor‑free part–person association via learned offsets
> - Detection and association have shifted from multi‑stage, anchor‑based systems to one‑stage, anchor‑free designs. A representative method (PBADet) extends dense, multi‑scale heads with a single part‑to‑body center offset and task‑aligned learning (top‑K by combined classification/IoU score). This yields:
>   • A compact, scalable representation (constant 2D offset per part point),
>   • One‑to‑one, always‑valid supervision (robust to occlusion/missing parts),
>   • Simpler, more accurate post‑processing.
> - Trend: association is being absorbed into the detection head as a lightweight displacement prediction, improving scalability (number of parts) and stability compared to body‑to‑part or two‑stage schemes.
> 
> Links to regularization under cross‑entropy and practical optimizer choices
> - Cross‑entropy classification remains standard in dense heads; task‑alignment with top‑K anchors functions as an effective regularizer by coupling classification confidence with localization quality.
> - For recurrent/sequence models, spectral initialization/monitoring (e.g., normalized SVD entropy) predicts trainability under CE and points to spectral pathology (large singular values, multimodal spectra) as a main source of instability; gradient clipping helps.
> - Optimizer practice converges on AdamW or SGD with mixed precision; for memory‑limited settings, 4‑bit AdamW (with zero‑point‑free second moment, rank‑1 normalization, or factorization) is now a reliable default.
> 
> How to keep GPU memory low during training
> - Use 4‑bit optimizer states (AdamW) with: (i) block sizes small enough for first‑moment outliers, (ii) zero‑excluded linear mapping for v, (iii) rank‑1 normalization, (iv) factorized v where applicable. Combine with optimizer offloading and fused kernels.
> - Apply LoRA for large‑model fine‑tuning; use AMP and keep heads lightweight (anchor‑free, multi‑task heads).
> - Exploit the synergy: memory saved → larger batch sizes → lower negative‑pair variance in contrastive learning, improving representation quality without new compute.
> 
> Datasets/tasks touched in this trajectory
> - Contrastive geometry and the variance‑reduction loss were validated on CIFAR‑10/100; JEPA’s bias was derived and tested in linear/temporal settings; spectral EI‑RNN results included sequential MNIST and PTB; memory‑efficient optimizers were exercised across Swin/Transformer and instruction‑tuned LLaMA (with LoRA).
> 
> Overall arc
> - From idealized full‑batch geometry to variance‑aware mini‑batch training; from heuristics to provable JEPA bias toward influential features; from 8‑bit to robust 4‑bit optimizer states; and from multi‑stage, anchor‑based association to one‑stage, anchor‑free offsets. These advances are converging on scalable, theory‑informed recipes that raise batch size under tight memory, stabilize optimization (spectrally and via task‑alignment), and improve representation quality in practice.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers that collectively cover the four topics
> 
> 1. **(Contrastive-learning geometry)** — *"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"* (ICML 2025). Analyzes embeddings via cosine similarity under InfoNCE-style losses with a temperature parameter; proves that in mini-batch training smaller batch sizes increase the variance of negative-pair similarities (excessive separation), and proposes an auxiliary loss (VRNS) that reduces this variance, improving small-batch CL and temperature robustness on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.
> 
> 2. **(JEPA implicit bias)** — *"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"* (NeurIPS 2024). Shows JEPA/self-distillation is implicitly biased to learn *influential* features (large regression coefficients), unlike MAE; the bias strengthens with encoder depth and explains why JEPA picks low-variance/semantic features.
> 
> 3. **(Memory-efficient training, sub-8-bit optimizer states)** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (NeurIPS 2023). Pushes Adam/AdamW/SGD-momentum optimizer states down to 4-bit via smaller block sizes, rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluded linear quantization of the second moment (optionally factorized), achieving near-lossless convergence on vision (Swin-T ImageNet), transformers (RoBERTa, GPT-2, Transformer-Base), and LLaMA fine-tuning, with up to ~57% GPU memory savings. It explicitly discusses LoRA/low-rank and delta-tuning as complementary memory-saving strategies.
> 
> 4. **(One-stage anchor-free part–body association)** — *"PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection"* (ICLR 2024). Associates human parts to the correct person via a single learned part-to-body center offset on multi-scale anchor-free features, replacing multi-stage/heuristic and anchor-based (body-to-part offset) methods.
> 
> ## Caveat on requirement (3)
> The 4-bit-optimizer paper matches the core of (3) (sub-8-bit states, SGD/AdamW-style, vision + transformer, LoRA context) but its vision/transformer experiments are on ImageNet/Swin-T and LLM fine-tuning — **not** CIFAR-100/MNIST. CIFAR-100/MNIST (with SGD/Adam/AdamW, ViT fine-tuning, and LoRA) appear in *"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"* (ICML 2025), but that paper is about Hessian spectra, not low-bit optimizer states or memory efficiency. So no single document in the collection combines sub-8-bit optimizer states with CIFAR-100/MNIST LoRA experiments; that specific combination cannot be fully verified from the provided context.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> - **Contrastive learning**: empirical contrastive losses (InfoNCE/SimCLR) → geometric/mathematical theory (full-batch ETF optimality, negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1), cross-entropy/neural-collapse connection) → explicit variance-reduction losses and temperature-robust training to rescue mini-batch settings. Trend: from "what works" to principled loss design grounded in embedding geometry.
> - **JEPA**: contrastive SSL → non-contrastive self-distillation (BYOL/SimSiam/I-JEPA) → theoretical characterization of implicit bias (influential, low-variance features; depth-dependent), connecting SSL to feature-learning dynamics. Trend: from architecture engineering to understanding which features are learned and why.
> - **Optimizers**: 32-bit full precision → 16-bit → 8-bit block-wise (Dettmers) → 4-bit with refined quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization), increasingly combined with parameter-efficient/low-rank fine-tuning and sharding/offloading. Trend: progressively lower-bit optimizer states with more careful moment quantization, while keeping GPU memory low and convergence lossless.
> - **Part–body association**: two-stage/heuristic or anchor-based body-to-part offsets → one-stage anchor-free with a single part-to-body offset and task-alignment learning. Trend: from multi-stage pipelines to streamlined, scalable, one-stage dense prediction with simpler and universally valid association signals.

I can now answer.
> 
> ## Papers and what each covers
> 
> **1. Geometry of embeddings in contrastive learning** — *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (doc `160e1407…`). Uses cosine similarity and the InfoNCE temperature parameter; proves in full-batch settings the optimal negative-pair similarity is −1/(n−1) and that small mini-batches induce "excessive separation" (higher variance in negative-pair similarities), then adds an auxiliary variance-reduction loss term.
> 
> **2. Implicit bias of JEPA** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (doc `40fde037…`). Shows JEPA self-distillation is biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients) and away from high-variance/noisy features, with depth strengthening the effect — the reason JEPA learns semantic features faster than MAE.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient training with sub-8-bit optimizer states** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States / 4-bit Optimizers* (doc `8d5e1455…`). Compresses AdamW/SGD-M first and second moments to 4 bits via smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, and factorized (low-rank) second moments; matches 32-bit AdamW across NLU/QA/NLG/MT/ImageNet (Swin-T) and LLaMA instruction tuning, saving up to ~57.7% memory, and discusses LoRA-style delta tuning. A related companion result — *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (doc `582d138d…`) — provides the extensive SGD/Adam/AdamW/weight-decay sweeps on MNIST/CIFAR-100, ViT-Base fine-tuning on CIFAR-100, and LoRA fine-tuning analysis linking optimizer choice and weight decay (regularization) to generalization via Hessian power-law structure.
> 
> **4. One-stage anchor-free part-body association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association Detection* (doc `08b70bc3…`). Extends anchor-free dense detection with a single learned part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps (plus task-alignment loss), giving one-to-one part–body association without anchors; SOTA on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 
> ## Development trend of these methods
> 
> - **Contrastive learning:** theory matured from full-batch analyses (embedding geometry at the InfoNCE optimum) to mini-batch realism, identifying batch-size-dependent variance as the culprit and fixing it with explicit regularizer-style auxiliary losses — i.e., a trend from "bigger batches always better" toward principled small-batch training with regularization.
> - **JEPA/self-supervised learning:** the trend is from empirical SSL recipes toward mechanistic understanding — proving *why* latent-prediction (vs. reconstruction) objectives bias learning toward influential, noise-robust features, and linking that to depth and feature ordering.
> - **Optimizers/memory:** the trend is progressively compressing optimizer state (32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit) and combining quantization with factorization/low-rank and parameter-efficient (LoRA-style) fine-tuning, so memory stays low without accuracy loss; parallel work connects optimizer choice, weight decay, and batch size to Hessian-sharpness-based generalization, giving practical guidance for choosing SGD vs. AdamW under GPU constraints.
> - **Detection/association:** the trend is moving from multi-stage, anchor-based pipelines (RPNs, heuristic or network-based association) to single-stage anchor-free dense prediction where association is encoded directly as a learned offset in the representation — simpler, faster, and scalable to many parts, mirroring the broader anchor-free/end-to-end trend in detection.

首轮整组工具请求不同，这一差异发生在看到任何社区结果之前；首轮规划差不能反向归因于社区。

评分变化的直接记录依据是下方两个 judge reasoning；同时保留 gold 和两份完整答案，可逐项核查其所称的缺失、数字错误或表述差异。当前单对 trace 没有独立分离查询变化、扩展材料、答案综合和 judge 尺度的贡献，故不把 judge 的因果判断当作已验证事实。

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five targeted directions show a coherent shift toward scalable, spectrum/feature-aware, and memory/friction–efficient deep learning, with common themes of linear-time computation in sample size, learned feature embeddings, and practical metrics (e.g., F1/Precision) for deployment.
> 
> 1) One-stage, anchor-free part–body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)
> - Trend: From multi-stage, anchor-based (e.g., body-to-part offsets) to a single-stage, anchor-free detector that encodes a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps.
> - Why it matters: The design reduces representation length (5+K+2 vs 6+K+2K), eliminates invalid offsets when parts are occluded, and keeps learning targets always valid; this scales to any number of parts without redesigning the head.
> - Efficiency and robustness: One-stage decoding (NMS + nearest-body center match) simplifies post-processing and improves runtime and stability in crowded scenes.
> - Measured impact: Demonstrated higher conditional accuracy and Joint AP on BodyHands and competitive AP on COCOHumanParts; importantly, better Precision/Recall/F1 versus a strong pose baseline (ED-Pose) for hands/feet in COCO subsets, evidencing practical deployment quality.
> 
> 2) EI-constrained RNNs under Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Trend: From attributing poor learning to sign constraints alone to a spectral explanation; performance is governed primarily by the singular-value spectrum (e.g., multimodal, dispersed spectra in ColEI vs clustered, unimodal spectra in DANNs/standard RNNs), not only by EI sign constraints.
> - Scalability and stability: Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts learning; larger networks and balanced E/I ratios improve spectral clustering and learning stability even when max singular values are large. DANN-style architectures retain good spectra at small scales.
> - Practical takeaway: Designing EI networks now emphasizes spectrum shaping/diagnostics (e.g., NSE) rather than only enforcing signs, enabling robust performance across sizes and E/I ratios.
> 
> 3) Joint-embedding self-distillation for SSL (JEPA) prioritizing influential features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Trend: From pixel reconstruction (MAE, MSE-based) to latent prediction (JEPA) that implicitly prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficients) over high-variance but noisy pixels.
> - Depth effect: The bias toward influential features strengthens with encoder depth; shallow encoders recover MAE-like behavior, but deep JEPA layers learn predictive, low-noise directions faster.
> - Practical implication: Joint-embedding objectives steer learning toward semantic, predictive features early (contrasting with reconstruction losses), improving downstream efficiency and robustness without relying on contrastive negatives.
> 
> 4) Memory-efficient training via 4-bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Trend: From 8-bit to 4-bit optimizer states while keeping convergence and accuracy across NLP/Vision (Transformers, ResNet-50) and instruction tuning.
> - Key enablers: (i) Rank-1 normalization capturing row/column outliers in moments, (ii) excluding zero-point for second-moment quantization (linear mapping) to avoid destabilized updates, and (iii) hybrid factorization+quantization for second moments where applicable.
> - Scalability: Up to 57.7% end-to-end memory savings in FSDP LLaMA-7B fine-tuning; larger models become trainable under fixed memory (e.g., single 80GB GPU can fine-tune LLaMA-7B). Throughput gains are observed with optimizer offload due to reduced communication.
> - Robustness: Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG and LLaMA instruction tuning (7B–33B), enabling practical end-to-end LoRA-style fine-tuning with near-full-precision quality.
> 
> 5) Linear-time independence testing with learned Fourier feature embeddings (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Trend: From quadratic-time HSIC/distance tests to linear-time (O(nD(dx+dy+D))) HSIC with learnable Fourier feature pairs (RFF) and a directly power-maximizing objective.
> - Adaptivity: Learns frequency-domain features (cosine/sine bases via RFF) by optimizing a differentiable, linear-time surrogate of test power; overcomes fixed-kernel limitations and preserves valid Type-I error via data-splitting.
> - Scalability: Theoretical consistency and non-asymptotic convergence; strong empirical power on high-dimensional images and large n (up to 100K) with linear memory and time.
> 
> Cross-cutting patterns and practical runtime
> - Toward O(n): Independence tests move from O(n^2) to O(n) with learned Fourier embeddings; detection shifts to single-stage anchor-free inference; optimizers move to lower precision without extra passes or heavy communication.
> - Feature embeddings over raw signals: RFF embeddings (independence testing), latent JEPA embeddings (SSL), and multi-scale convolutional features (PBADet) all replace brittle, high-variance raw targets (e.g., pixel reconstruction) with task-aligned representations.
> - Spectrum/structure awareness: In EI RNNs, spectral diagnostics (NSE) guide design; in 4-bit optimizers, moment outlier structure (row/column, zero-point) is explicitly handled; in Fourier-based HSIC, learned spectral sampling finds discriminative frequencies.
> - Evaluation aligned with deployment: PBADet reports precision/recall/F1 for small parts under occlusion; independence tests report power/Type-I error at scale; 4-bit training reports wall-clock, memory, and accuracy on LLM/ResNet-50 tasks.
> 
> Overall trajectory
> - 2023→2024 methods pivot from rigid, expensive, or memory-heavy formulations to feature/spectrum-adaptive, linear-time or memory-thrifty designs. This yields robust performance (e.g., higher F1 in crowded/occluded vision, stable EI learning, stronger SSL semantics), while scaling to large data/models (e.g., O(n) testing at 100K samples; 4-bit finetuning of 7B–33B LLMs).

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers that best match your areas, followed by the development trend.
> 
> **1. One-stage, anchor-free part-body association**
> **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset across multi-scale features, guaranteeing one-to-one part–body correspondence; beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts, with higher precision, recall, and F1 vs. pose estimators.
> 
> **2. Spectral analysis of E/I-constrained recurrent nets**
> **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023). Shows poor learning of Dale's-Law (E/I sign-constrained) RNNs is due mainly to initialization-time singular-value spectra (multimodal/dispersed, from rank-one column-mean structure), not sign constraints; proposes normalized SVD entropy as a diagnostic.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding self-distillation in SSL**
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024). Proves JEPA latent-space prediction (vs. MAE pixel reconstruction) implicitly prioritizes high-influence/low-variance features and suppresses noise, with a critical-time analysis; ImageNet CCA confirms JEPA aligns faster with perceptual PCA subspace. *Note: it contrasts latent MSE-style prediction vs. pixel-space MSE; I found no paper in this collection that explicitly contrasts cosine vs. MSE vs. cross-entropy as SSL losses.*
> 
> **4. Memory-efficient low-bit (~4-bit) optimizer states**
> **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023). Quantizes Adam/AdamW states to 4-bit (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-exclusion for second moment, optional factorization), matching 32-bit accuracy on Transformers, Swin-T, and LLaMA with up to 57.7% memory savings. *Note: it covers Transformers and Swin-T image classification but not ResNet-50 specifically, and uses full fine-tuning rather than LoRA.*
> 
> **5. Linear-time independence testing with learned Fourier features**
> **Efficiently Learning Significant Fourier Feature Pairs for Statistical Independence Testing** (NeurIPS 2024). Reinterprets HSIC in the frequency domain, adds learnable Fourier feature pairs, and derives a differentiable O(n)-time power-maximizing objective; consistent tests with γ-approximated thresholds, completing 100k-sample tests in seconds and beating quadratic HSIC baselines.
> 
> **Development trend across the five works:**
> - **Simplification & end-to-end unification**: multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines collapse into single-stage, anchor-free, one-offset designs (PBADet); LSIC-style kernels give way to end-to-end learned, linear-time criteria (LFHSIC).
> - **Diagnosis over prescription**: from merely enforcing constraints to understanding *why* methods underperform via spectral/analytic tools — spectra matter more than sign constraints (Dale's Law), and implicit bias (feature prioritization) explains why JEPA beats MAE (self-distillation).
> - **Compression with lossless accuracy**: pushing state precision 8-bit → 4-bit while preserving convergence, backed by outlier-pattern-aware quantizers and factorization — a complementary "efficiency" trend alongside linear-time statistical tests.
> - **Shared efficiency metrics**: all stress practical runtime/memory (O(n) tests, 4-bit states, fewer anchors) and evaluation with Precision/Recall/F1 alongside accuracy/AP.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers I found in the collection, one per topic, followed by the development trend.
> 
> **1. Part–body association — PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`)
> One-stage, anchor-free approach (built on YOLOv5/7/8 anchor-free heads) that links each part to its body via a **single part-to-body center offset** across multi-scale feature maps, with branches for classification, localization, and displacement plus task-alignment learning. Outperforms two-stage/anchor-based BPJDet and HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts; evaluates with AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, and precision/recall/F1 vs ED-Pose for hands/feet.
> 
> **2. E/I-constrained recurrent nets — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`)
> Studies RNNs constrained by Dale's Law (column-wise E/I sign constraints, "ColEI") and shows their poor learning is due not to sign constraints but to **spectral properties at initialization**: multimodal, dispersed singular values vs. the unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra of standard RNNs and E/I-partitioned Dale's ANNs (DANN). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization predicts final performance; DANN stays robust to E/I ratio.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding self-distillation — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`)
> Analyzes JEPA-style self-distillation vs. MAE pixel-space reconstruction in deep linear networks: JEPA has an implicit bias to learn **high-influence (high-ρ), low-variance features** and suppresses noise, with depth strengthening noise suppression — explaining why latent-space prediction beats noisy pixel reconstruction. Related cosine-metric analysis: "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (doc `160e1407…`) studies cosine-similarity alignment of positive/negative pairs; LDReg (doc `51526068…`) regularizes against (local) dimensional collapse. The explicit cosine-vs-MSE-vs-cross-entropy loss comparison is only partially covered by these.
> 
> **4. Memory-efficient training — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`)
> Pushes Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit via smaller block sizes, rank-1 normalization, a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment, and optional factorization ("4-bit Factor"). Matches 32-bit accuracy on RoBERTa-L (GLUE, SQuAD **F1**), GPT-2, Transformer-Base (WMT), Swin-T (ImageNet), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca), with up to 57.7% memory savings. Caveat: it uses **Swin-T, not ResNet-50**, and LoRA appears only as cited related work (the paper's fine-tuning is full-parameter with 4-bit states), so "end-to-end LoRA-style fine-tuning on ResNet-50" is not exactly covered.
> 
> **5. Linear-time independence testing — "Efficiently Learning Significant Fourier Feature Pairs for Statistical Independence Testing"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `58063efa…`)
> Reinterprets HSIC in the frequency domain, adds **learnable Fourier feature pairs**, and derives a test-power objective computable in **O(n) time and space** (O(TnD(dx+dy+D)) overall), with convergence and test-consistency guarantees. Compared with dCor/QHSIC (O(n²)) and RDC (O(n log n)) on synthetic, 3DShapes, and MillionSong data; runs in seconds on 100k samples with favorable power–runtime trade-offs. Evaluation is statistical power/Type-II error rather than F1/Precision.
> 
> **Development trend across the five:** (1) Detection moved from multi-stage, anchor-based, heuristic association to **single-stage, anchor-free, one-offset universal representations**. (2) Biologically constrained networks moved from "just enforce sign rules" (which hurts learning) to **spectrum-aware design/diagnostics** — spectral properties at initialization, not constraints, dominate trainability. (3) Self-supervised learning moved from pixel reconstruction (MAE, MSE) toward **latent joint-embedding self-distillation**, with theory explaining the implicit bias to prioritize influential, noise-free features. (4) Training efficiency progressed by **pushing optimizer-state precision down (32→16→8→4-bit)** with dedicated quantizers for moment outliers, plus factorization — matching full precision with large memory savings. (5) Independence testing moved from quadratic HSIC and fixed random Fourier features to **learnable feature embeddings with provably linear-time objectives**, adapting test power to data at scale. Overall: a shared arc toward streamlined, single-stage/learnable, theoretically grounded methods that trade complexity for efficiency (O(n) runtime, low-bit memory) without sacrificing accuracy or robustness.

### paperscope:trend:192 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers on improving training and inference efficiency and stability in deep networks that collectively cover: (a) making adaptive moment methods (e.g., decoupled-weight-decay variants of Adam) and first-order SGD usable with sub-byte state storage for full-precision accuracy; (b) curvature-aware regularization beyond quadratic for hyper-parameter search when the objective is non-differentiable or discrete (e.g., maximizing F1/Precision on standard vision benchmarks like MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100) and gradients are unavailable; (c) explaining the inductive bias of non-contrastive joint-embedding self-supervised learning (teacher–student in latent space) toward useful feature embeddings rather than pixel noise under CE/MSE losses; (d) understanding how enforcing excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints changes the spectrum and learning dynamics of deep recurrent models; and (e) anchor-free, one-stage part-to-body association detectors that report metrics such as Precision/F1. I’m especially interested in works that discuss regularization choices, approximations, and how these methods integrate with AdamW/SGD and end-to-end fine-tuning (including low-rank adapters).Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper development trends toward efficient, stable, and scalable deep learning, mapped to the query axes (a–e), are as follows:
> 
> 1) Sub-byte optimizer states for Adam/SGD (training memory and throughput) [a]
> - Trend: 8-bit → 4-bit. The field has moved from block-wise 8-bit quantization to 4-bit states while preserving full-precision accuracy for Adam/AdamW and SGD.
> - Method shifts:
>   - Smaller blocks (e.g., 128) to better track heterogeneous outlier patterns in moments; switch from purely block-wise to rank-1 normalization (row- and column-wise statistics) for the second moment.
>   - Zero-point issue identified as the main failure mode for second-moment quantization; solved by excluding zero in the mapping and, empirically, using linear mapping over DE-0.
>   - Hybrid factorization+quantization for further savings (factorize 2D second moments, quantize 1D).
> - Scalability and integration: Demonstrated on RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 M, Swin-T, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B (end-to-end fine-tuning), compatible with AdamW/SGD, FSDP, and optimizer offloading; speeds up distributed tuning via reduced communication. (LoRA codebase was used in GPT-2 finetuning, and full end-to-end instruction tuning was shown for LLaMA.)
> 
> 2) Curvature-aware hyper-parameter optimization without hyper-gradients [b]
> - Trend: From derivative-free/BO/Hyperband/RL to stochastic relaxation with higher-order (cubic) regularization.
> - Method shifts:
>   - Optimize a differentiable surrogate over distributions p_θ(z) of (possibly discrete) hyper-parameters; estimate gradient/Hessian via sampling, not hyper-gradients.
>   - Move beyond quadratic: cubic regularization accelerates convergence and avoids saddle points, with theory for convergence to approximate second-order stationary points even with inexact lower-level solves.
> - Practical impact: Efficient search under non-differentiable/discrete objectives (e.g., MRR/NDCG; schedules for noisy-label learning), outperforming BO/Random/Hyperband/RL under tight evaluation budgets. Sensitivity analyses show more samples K and better lower-level accuracy improve stability/quality.
> 
> 3) Inductive bias of non-contrastive JEPA (teacher–student in latent space) [c]
> - Trend: From reconstruction (MAE) to joint-embedding prediction (JEPA) and from first-order intuitions to dynamical analyses in deep linear models.
> - Key insight: With stop-grad distillation, JEPAs bias learning toward influential features (high regression coefficients) rather than merely high-variance features. This bias strengthens with encoder depth, helping JEPA prioritize low-variance, semantic/slow features over pixel-level noise under squared/CE-like losses.
> - Practical implication: Explains faster emergence of useful feature embeddings and better sample efficiency in downstream perception relative to MAE; ties to temporal/slow-feature setups consistent with video JEPAs.
> 
> 4) Stable EI-constrained recurrent models via spectrum-aware design [d]
> - Trend: From enforcing Dale’s Law via sign constraints (ColEI) to architectures and initializations that fix spectral pathologies (recurrent DANNs).
> - Method shifts:
>   - Spectral diagnosis: ColEI yields multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes → poor learning, high variance, and instability; spectrum “transplants” show spectrum matters more than sign constraints per se.
>   - Predictive metric: Normalized SVD entropy tracks trainability across EI ratio and network size (small nets with few I units perform worst); larger nets or DANNs recover unimodal clustered spectra and learn like standard RNNs.
> - Training stability: Gradient clipping helps ColEI but does not fix core spectral issues; the trend is to engineer EI networks for unimodal, well-clustered spectra to ensure stable, efficient optimization with SGD/Adam.
> 
> 5) Anchor-free, one-stage part–body association (detection efficiency and scaling) [e]
> - Trend: Two-stage or anchor-based joint detection → one-stage, anchor-free, multi-scale representations with a single part-to-body center offset.
> - Method shifts:
>   - Reduce representation length from O(K) offsets per part to a single offset per part, improving scalability across arbitrary part sets and robustness to occlusion.
>   - Use task-alignment learning (TOOD) and DFL heads; train with SGD; decode by nearest body center within enclosing boxes.
> - Outcomes: State-of-the-art AP/MR on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts; improved association accuracy (mMR) and precision/recall/F1 vs. pose models; extends to animals; simpler post-processing and consistent supervision at all times.
> 
> Cross-cutting trends (regularization, approximations, integration):
> - Regularization moves beyond quadratic (cubic) for HPO; spectrum-conscious regularization/initialization for EI RNNs; task-alignment (detection); clipping where needed.
> - Approximations are principled: stochastic relaxation with sampling-based gradient/Hessian; quantized/blocked/factorized optimizer states; deep-linear ODE analyses for SSL; spectrum transplants for causal diagnosis.
> - Seamless integration with standard training stacks: AdamW/SGD throughout; compatibility with end-to-end fine-tuning of large models (including LoRA-style workflows and FSDP) and anchor-free detection backbones. Overall, the field is converging on methods that are both theory-backed and practically scalable across tasks (vision, language, time series) while improving memory, stability, and data efficiency.

**naive 最终答案**

> I searched the collection and identified papers for each of your five topics, then traced the development trend of their methods.
> 
> ## Papers found per topic
> 
> **(a) Sub-byte optimizer states with full-precision accuracy**
> "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023). Pushes optimizer-state bitwidth from 8-bit to 4-bit for Adam/AdamW (the framework is stated to also apply to SGDM/SGD-M: "the algorithm A can be any gradient-based optimizer like SGDM, Adam, AdamW"). Key tricks: smaller block-size (B128) quantization for the first moment, a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer (DE-0) and rank-1 normalization for the second moment, plus optional factorization of the second moment. It achieves lossless performance vs. 32-bit AdamW on RoBERTa, Swin-T, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning. **Caveat:** it primarily demonstrates AdamW (decoupled weight-decay variant); SGDM is supported by the compression framework but the reported lossless full-precision matching is for AdamW. LoRA is discussed only as related work (frozen weights + low-rank tuning) and in fine-tuning contexts, not integrated into the optimizer.
> 
> **(b) Curvature-aware regularization for hyper-parameter search without gradients**
> "Hyper-Parameter Optimization via Stochastic Relaxation and Cubic Regularization" (NeurIPS 2023). Handles non-differentiable objectives and discrete hyper-parameters (no hyper-gradients available) by stochastic relaxation into a bilevel problem, then using cubic regularization to exploit gradient+Hessian curvature, escape saddle points, and reach ε-second-order stationary points (O(1/ε^1.5) iterations), with inexact lower-level solutions allowed. Evaluated on feature-mask learning, knowledge-graph completion (MRR), and noisy-label schedule search on CIFAR-10. **Caveat:** the collection's benchmark specifics (F1/Precision on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100) are not exactly matched; the paper uses AUC/MRR/validation-accuracy as non-differentiable/discrete metrics.
> 
> **(c) Inductive bias of non-contrastive joint-embedding SSL (teacher–student in latent space)**
> "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis" (NeurIPS 2024). Using deep linear networks and exact gradient-flow ODEs for JEPA (stop-gradient teacher–student with MSE in latent space) vs. MAE (pixel reconstruction), it shows JEPA prioritizes high-ρ "slow"/influential features step-wise and suppresses pixel noise, with depth strengthening noise suppression, whereas MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue and tends toward variance/pixel reconstruction. Validated on ImageNet via CCA alignment with the low-variance perceptual subspace.
> 
> **(d) E/I sign constraints and spectrum/learning dynamics of deep recurrent models**
> "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023). Compares standard RNNs, column-constrained E/I (ColEI) RNNs, and recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN). Shows the poor learning of ColEI networks is caused mostly by the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed, from a rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure) rather than the sign constraints themselves; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with test error and predicts training success. Smaller EI ratios and small networks worsen spectra/performance.
> 
> **(e) Anchor-free, one-stage part-to-body association detector**
> "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection" (ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free detection (FCOS/TOOD task-alignment learning) with a single 2D part-to-body center offset, giving one-to-one part–body association, multi-part scalability, and top-K task-aligned supervision. Reports hand/body metrics (Hand AP, conditional accuracy, Joint AP) and face-body on CrowdHuman; against ED-Pose it reports higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> 
> - **Optimization efficiency:** the trend is toward ever-lower state precision (32→8→4-bit) via careful analysis of outlier patterns and dedicated quantizers (block-wise → rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, stochastic rounding, factorization), keeping full-precision convergence; the compression framework is optimizer-agnostic (covers SGDM and AdamW), so it slots into end-to-end fine-tuning pipelines and complements low-rank adapters.
> - **Hyper-parameter search:** from derivative-free search (random/BO/Hyperband/RL) and first-order stochastic relaxation to second-order methods — adding curvature (cubic regularization) over the relaxed objective to escape saddle points and guarantee convergence even with discrete/non-differentiable metrics; tolerating inexact lower-level solves to stay practical.
> - **SSL theory:** from empirical observation that reconstruction loss favors pixel/variance features while JEPA favors semantics, to exact analytical characterization of the implicit bias of non-contrastive teacher–student MSE objectives (feature ordering by influence/ρ, noise suppression deepening with depth) — a shift from "how well it works" to "which features it provably learns and why."
> - **Biologically-constrained RNNs:** from attributing E/I network failure to sign constraints to a spectral explanation — showing initialization spectra (unimodality/clustering, NSE) matter more than sign constraints, and that reparameterized E/I architectures (DANN) recover standard RNN spectra; the resulting diagnostic (NSE) guides architecture/EI-ratio choices before training.
> - **Detection:** from multi-stage, anchor-based, body-to-part pipelines (BPJDet, HierR-CNN) toward single-stage, anchor-free, part-to-body formulations with a single shared offset and task-aligned loss — improving scalability to many parts, robustness to occluded parts, and simplifying post-processing while raising precision/recall/F1.
> 
> Overall, the cross-cutting trend is: **replace hand-designed/heuristic components with carefully designed regularizations and approximations that keep the method "free" of exact constraints** — compression-aware quantizers (a), cubic-curvature surrogates (b), analytically-characterized inductive biases (c), spectral rather than sign constraints (d), and a unified anchor-free association representation (e) — all aimed at preserving accuracy while improving efficiency/stability, and all compatible with standard AdamW/SGD-style end-to-end training and fine-tuning (including low-rank adapter settings).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, here are the papers matching each of your five criteria, followed by a summary of the method-development trends.
> 
> ## Paper mapping
> 
> **(a) Sub-byte optimizer states for AdamW/SGD — full-precision accuracy**
> - **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023). Pushes optimizer-state compression from 8-bit to 4-bit for Adam/AdamW (decoupled weight decay) and SGD(M). It identifies outlier patterns in first/second moments, and uses smaller blocks (B128), a **rank-1 normalization** (row+column scales), a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, and optional factorization. Matches 32-bit accuracy on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (incl. Alpaca instruction tuning) with up to ~57.7% memory savings. Discusses quantization approximations, stochastic rounding, and gives a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M).
> 
> **(b) Curvature-aware HPO for non-differentiable/discrete objectives**
> - **"Efficient Hyper-parameter Optimization with Cubic Regularization"** (NeurIPS 2023). Targets HPO where hyper-gradients are unavailable (discrete hyper-parameters, non-differentiable metrics such as F1/Precision). Uses **stochastic relaxation + cubic regularization** (curvature beyond quadratic) needing only objective values; converges to approximate second-order stationary points. Validated on feature-mask learning, knowledge-graph completion, and noisy-label schedule search (CIFAR-10).
> 
> **(c) Inductive bias of non-contrastive joint-embedding SSL (teacher–student in latent space)**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"** (NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes JEPA teacher–student objectives with deep linear networks. Shows the implicit bias: JEPA prioritizes **high-ρ "influential" features in a step-wise order** and suppresses pixel-level noise, whereas MAE-style reconstruction (CE/MSE) orders features mainly by eigenvalue and keeps noise; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE's.
> - Supporting: **LDReg** (ICLR 2024) regularizes against local dimensional collapse in SSL (SimCLR/BYOL/MAE/VICReg/Barlow Twins).
> 
> **(d) E/I sign constraints, spectrum, and learning dynamics of recurrent models**
> - **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023). For excitatory/inhibitory sign-constrained RNNs (ColEI vs DANN), shows **sign constraints alone explain little**; the initial recurrent-weight spectrum matters more. ColEI's column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values (vs. random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur for standard RNNs/DANNs), causing instability and worse, higher-variance learning. Introduces **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** as a pre-training predictor, and shows gradient clipping mitigates the deficit; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectrum and performance.
> 
> **(e) Anchor-free, one-stage part-to-body association detector**
> - **"PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection"** (ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free detection (FCOS/TOOD-style) with a **single part-to-body center offset** on multi-scale features, replacing cumbersome anchor-based body-to-part offsets. One-to-one part↔body correspondence, scalable to multiple parts. Reports AP/MR-2 on CrowdHuman and BodyHands/COCOHumanParts, and **substantially higher precision, recall, and F1** for hands/feet vs. ED-Pose; ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning each help.
> 
> ## Development trend of these methods
> 
> 1. **From coarse to adaptive approximations.** Efficiency work moves from 8-bit → 4-bit states and from per-tensor/block normalization to **rank-1 normalization**, plus zero-point handling and factorization—finer approximations of moment statistics to preserve convergence. These plug directly into AdamW/SGD and end-to-end fine-tuning (incl. low-rank adapter / parameter-efficient setups like LoRA, referenced in the 4-bit optimizer paper) with convergence guarantees.
> 2. **From gradient/Hessian-requiring HPO to objective-value-only, higher-order methods.** When metrics are non-differentiable/discrete, the trend is stochastic relaxation plus **cubic (beyond-quadratic) curvature** to escape saddles and reach second-order stationary points, rather than relying on hyper-gradients or BO/RL.
> 3. **From empirical observations to mechanistic theory of SSL bias.** The trend is characterizing *why* teacher–student joint-embedding objectives favor useful features over noise (feature-importance/spectral ordering via deep-linear dynamics), plus explicit regularization (LDReg) against collapse—rather than only reporting performance gains.
> 4. **From sign-constraint engineering to spectral diagnostics.** Understanding E/I-constrained networks shifts from "sign constraints hurt" to "the initialization **spectrum** governs learning dynamics," with predictive tools (NSE) and stabilization via gradient clipping.
> 5. **From multi-stage/anchor-based to one-stage anchor-free association.** Part–body detection converges on a single part-to-body center offset for simple, scalable, one-to-one association, improving Precision/F1 and joint AP.
> 
> **Cross-cutting theme:** across all five, the progression is from heuristic/coarse designs toward **explicit approximation, spectral/curvature analysis, and regularization choices** that let these methods integrate cleanly with standard optimizers (AdamW/SGD) and end-to-end fine-tuning pipelines.
