Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper development trend across the five works
> 
> 1) Vision: From anchor‑based, multi‑stage association to one‑stage, anchor‑free, scalable detection
> - Earlier hand/face–body association relied on multi‑stage or anchor‑based detectors (e.g., YOLO variants, BPJDet), with growing representation size as the number of parts increased and brittle post‑processing.
> - PBADet (ICLR 2024) advances to a one‑stage, anchor‑free design that adds a single 2D part‑to‑body center offset on multi‑scale feature maps with task‑aligned learning. This compresses the representation (fixed length independent of the number of parts), simplifies decoding, and scales to multiple parts and categories (even beyond humans), while improving robustness in multi‑person scenes.
> - Training remains standard and efficient (SGD, AMP), and evaluation broadens from AP to association‑specific metrics (mMR−2) and Precision/Recall/F1 (shown in comparisons to pose methods). Trend: anchor‑free, multi‑scale, task‑aligned, end‑to‑end association that scales without representation bloat.
> 
> 2) Code LLMs: From synthetic/closed data and single‑task evaluation to permissive instruction data and multi‑task, multi‑language assessment
> - Prior instruction‑tuned code models often depended on closed‑API outputs for synthetic data. OctoPack pivots to permissive, naturally occurring instruction signals from Git commits (COMMITPACK / COMMITPACKFT), avoiding licensing risks and instability of external APIs.
> - Instruction data is diversified (commit messages for edits/fixes, OASST for natural‑language targets) to teach models to both produce code and explain it. Mixing data with NL targets is necessary for strong explanation ability.
> - Evaluation expands from HumanEval (Python, code synthesis only) to HUMANEVALPACK: three tasks (Fix, Explain, Synthesize) across six languages (Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, C++, Rust) measured via execution‑based pass@1. Trend: broader, more realistic tasks and languages, with permissive data enabling deployable copilots; lightweight finetuning (LoRA was used in experiments for GPT‑2) fits resource‑constrained pipelines.
> 
> 3) Training efficiency: From 8‑bit to 4‑bit optimizer states via better quantization and factorization
> - Earlier low‑precision optimizers plateaued at 8‑bit. The 4‑bit Optimizers work (NeurIPS 2023) identifies why naïve 4‑bit fails (zero‑point collapsing second moments) and introduces: smaller block sizes, zero‑point‑free mappings (DE‑0/Linear), and rank‑1 normalization; optionally factorize second moments.
> - Result: Adam/AdamW with 4‑bit states matches 32‑bit accuracy across NLU, MT, vision pretraining, and instruction tuning, while cutting memory and improving throughput with offloading/FSDP. Trend: principled quantization (esp. for the second moment) and hybrid factorization push optimizer states from 8‑bit to 4‑bit without accuracy loss, enabling larger models or higher batch sizes on limited GPUs.
> 
> 4) Self‑supervision: From pixel‑space reconstruction (MAE) to latent‑space prediction (JEPA) with depth‑amplified bias to useful features
> - In deep linear analyses, JEPA/self‑distillation and MAE learn via different implicit biases. MAE prioritizes features with high covariance (even if noisy); JEPA prioritizes “influential” features (high regression coefficients), especially as encoder depth increases.
> - This explains empirical wins of latent‑space prediction for downstream perception and aligns with using cosine‑similarity probes and standard CE/MSE objectives. Trend: a shift toward latent‑space prediction that learns more predictive, less noisy features, with depth strengthening this bias.
> 
> 5) Neuromorphic constraints: From sign constraints to spectrum‑aware EI RNN design and diagnostics
> - Simply enforcing Dale’s Law via column sign constraints (ColEI) hurts learning. The spectral perspective shows performance is governed more by singular‑value spectra than by sign constraints per se.
> - Recurrent DANNs (EI but spectrally well‑behaved) learn as well as standard RNNs; spectrum transplantation confirms spectra matter most. Network size and E/I ratio shape spectra and stability; Normalized SVD Entropy predicts trainability. Trend: biologically constrained RNNs progress from naïve EI sign partitioning to spectrum‑aware architectures and metrics (NSE), improving stability and scaling.
> 
> Overall pipeline trajectory
> - Perception front‑end: anchor‑free, one‑stage, task‑aligned detectors (PBADet) deliver robust multi‑person part–body association, evaluated with Precision/F1 and association‑specific metrics, trained with SGD/CE‑style losses.
> - Language/code middle‑end: instruction‑tuned code LLMs trained on permissive, naturally structured data (COMMITPACKFT + NL data) generalize across tasks (fix/explain/synthesize) and languages, with LoRA‑style lightweight finetuning when needed.
> - Training stack: 4‑bit optimizer states with zero‑point‑aware quantization and rank‑1 normalization (plus optional factorization) reduce memory while preserving accuracy; standard CE/MSE objectives with SGD/AdamW remain effective.
> - Representation learning foundation: preference for latent‑space prediction (JEPA) to learn predictive features efficiently; for EI recurrent modules, prioritize spectral health over raw sign constraints, using NSE as a guide.
> 
> Time/scalability trends
> - Recent years show: (i) vision detectors moving from anchor‑based/two‑stage to anchor‑free/one‑stage with scalable association; (ii) code LLMs moving from single‑task, single‑language, and non‑permissive data to multi‑task, multi‑language, and permissive data; (iii) optimizers advancing from 8‑bit to 4‑bit via principled quantization; (iv) SSL shifting from reconstruction to latent prediction; (v) EI RNNs moving from sign‑only constraints to spectrum‑aware design. These shifts collectively favor scalability, deployability, and stability for end‑to‑end systems under resource constraints.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers fitting the end-to-end pipeline
> 
> 1. **Part–body detection (a)** → **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association; a single part-to-body center offset links hands/face to parent bodies in multi-person scenes. On BodyHands and COCOHumanParts it beats BPJDet, BodyHands, HierR-CNN, and ED-Pose on hand/feet Precision/Recall/F1 and joint AP.
> 
> 2. **Code copilot instruction tuning (b)** → **OctoPack** (ICLR 2024): CommitPack/CommitPackFT are ~4TB of *permissively licensed* Git commits (350 languages); instruction-tuning StarCoder yields OctoCoder/OctoGeeX, the best permissively licensed code LLMs on HumanEvalPack (synthesis, repair, explanation).
> 
> 3. **4-bit optimizer states (c)** → **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023): quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, optional factorization), matching 32-bit accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings — well-suited to limited GPUs and compatible with LoRA-style tuning.
> 
> 4. **Latent vs. pixel prediction in SSL** → **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): proves via deep-linear analysis that JEPA-style latent-space (self-distillation) prediction is biased toward high-influence, noise-free features, whereas MAE pixel reconstruction prioritizes features by eigenvalue, retaining noisy/uninformative pixels.
> 
> 5. **Dale/E-I constraints on RNN spectra & stability** → **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): column-constrained (ColEI) RNNs get multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra, worse learning, higher variance, and instability (requiring gradient clipping); DANN-style EI networks keep unimodal spectra like standard RNNs; normalized SVD entropy predicts trainability.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> 
> - **Detection:** multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines (Faster R-CNN-style, BodyHands' separate association network, BPJDet's body-to-part offsets) → a single-stage anchor-free detector with one compact part-to-body offset, giving lighter, faster, more scalable end-to-end part–body association.
> - **Code LLMs:** closed-source/synthetic instruction data (OpenAI-based WizardCoder, PanGu-Coder2) → fully permissive, naturally structured data (Git commits) with multi-task, multi-language evaluation, keeping open models commercially usable while approaching GPT-4.
> - **Optimizers:** full-precision Adam/AdamW → 8-bit block-wise optimizers → 4-bit states via finer quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-free linear mapping, factorization), enabling larger models on fewer GPUs without accuracy loss.
> - **SSL:** pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) → latent-space/joint-embedding prediction (JEPA/self-distillation), with theory showing latent prediction's implicit bias yields abstract, noise-robust features; complementary work (LDReg) counters dimensional collapse in such representations.
> - **E/I RNNs:** naive sign-constrained networks that underperform → spectral-aware designs (DANN, careful initialization) that keep random-matrix-like unimodal spectra and stable training while respecting Dale's Law.
> 
> These papers cover all five requested components; together they form a lightweight, end-to-end stack (anchor-free perception + permissive instruction-tuned copilot + 4-bit AdamW training + latent-space SSL + biologically constrained RNNs).

**community 最终答案**

> 
> | Need | Paper (doc) |

> | (b) Instruction-tuned code LLM on permissive data | **OctoPack: Instruction Tuning Code Large Language Models** — CommitPack/CommitPackFT (~4 TB permissively licensed Git commits), OctoCoder/OctoGeeX, HumanEvalPack benchmark; optionally **NEFTune** (noisy embeddings improve instruction finetuning, works with QLoRA) |
> | (c) 4-bit Adam-style optimizer states | **4-bit Optimizers (Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States**, NeurIPS 2023) — B128 blocks, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization, factorized second moment; lossless vs 32-bit AdamW, ~57.7% memory savings, LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU; combinable with LoRA/offloading/FSDP |
> | (d) Latent-space vs pixel prediction in SSL | **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** — JEPA latent prediction is biased to high-influence, noise-free features vs MAE pixel reconstruction (eigenvalue-driven); also **LDReg** (counters local dimensional collapse) and **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (cosine-similarity probes of embedding quality) |
> | (e) Dale/E-I constraints, RNN spectra & stability | **Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — ColEI sign-constrained RNNs get multimodal/dispersed singular spectra, instability (needs gradient clipping); DANN reparameterization restores standard-RNN spectra and stable learning; NSE predicts performance |
> 
> Also relevant for the lightweight end-to-end LoRA preference: **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure** analyzes LoRA adapter fine-tuning spectra/generalization (d_ks predicts generalization; power-law structure differs from full fine-tuning).
> 
> ## Development trend
> 
> - **Detection:** Two-stage heuristics/anchor-based detectors (BodyHands association networks, BPJDet body-to-part offsets) → one-stage **anchor-free dense prediction** (FCOS-style) with a *single* part-to-body offset and task-alignment, giving end-to-end, occlusion-robust, scalable part–body association with better Precision/F1.
> - **Code LLMs:** Comment-prompting → explicit **instruction tuning**; synthetic/borrowed data → large-scale *permissively licensed* structured data (Git commits) mixed with natural-language data; plus cheap augmentation (NEFTune) to boost instruction finetuning without extra compute.
> - **Optimization:** 32-bit → 8-bit → **4-bit optimizer states** (smaller blocks, zero-point exclusion, rank-1 normalization, factorization), achieving lossless convergence with major memory savings, and designed to compose with LoRA/QLoRA, FSDP, and offloading for limited-GPU training.
> - **Self-supervision:** Pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) → **latent-space prediction/self-distillation (JEPA)**, with theory showing latent prediction prioritizes high-influence, low-noise features; complemented by regularization against (local) dimensional collapse and cosine-similarity-based evaluation probes.
> - **E/I RNNs:** Naive column sign-constrained EI networks (ColEI) train poorly and unstably → realization that **initialization spectra matter more than sign constraints**; DANN-style reparameterization yields standard-RNN-like spectra, stability, and robust learning across E/I ratios, with spectrum-entropy diagnostics (NSE) predicting trainability.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper development trends for efficient training and interpretability across deep networks
> 
> (a) Memory‑efficient optimization for fine‑tuning Transformers (Adam/AdamW, 4‑bit states)
> - Trend: from 8‑bit to 4‑bit optimizer states with lossless convergence. The 4‑bit work compresses both first and second moments, fixing key failure modes (zero‑point in v, heterogeneous outliers) via smaller blocks (B128), rank‑1 normalization, and linear (zero‑free) mapping for second moments; it further combines 4‑bit quantization with factorization to cut memory even more. 
> - Scope and scalability: validated on vision (Swin‑T/ImageNet), NLU/GLUE, MT/WMT14, NLG (E2E‑NLG), and LLM instruction‑tuning (LLaMA), improving throughput under FSDP/offloading while matching 32‑bit accuracy. Compatible with full‑parameter fine‑tuning and PEFT (used LoRA codebase for GPT‑2; instruction tuning for LLaMA), enabling end‑to‑end Transformer fine‑tuning under tight memory.
> - Direction: practical fine‑tuning at scale by jointly optimizing quantizer design (block size, mapping, rank‑1 stats) and optimizer state layout; emphasis on real Transformer backbones (Adam/AdamW) and measured memory/latency gains without accuracy loss.
> 
> (b) Analyses of self‑distillation (JEPA) vs CE/MSE and reconstruction (MAE)
> - Trend: shift from reconstruction losses (MAE/MSE) toward joint‑embedding predictive objectives (JEPA/self‑distillation) to learn more semantic, less noisy representations. In deep linear models, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (predictive) features, whereas MAE favors highly covarying (potentially noisy) features; the JEPA bias strengthens with depth and reverses MAE’s learning order when covariance and influence diverge.
> - Implication: guidance for objective choice in representation learning pipelines (incl. Transformer encoders) when aiming for fast emergence of semantic feature embeddings and better downstream linear‑probe performance.
> 
> (c) Spectrum‑aware stability for Dale’s‑Law RNNs (SGD/Adam dynamics)
> - Trend: from hard sign constraints (ColEI) to spectrum‑aware design as the dominant determinant of learnability. The work shows sign constraints alone do not explain poor learning; instead, multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra and large max singular values hurt optimization. A spectrum transplant demonstrates spectra matter more than sign constraints.
> - Tools and scaling: Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) emerges as a predictive diagnostic; balanced E/I ratios and larger widths improve spectra and performance; gradient clipping aids stability. Demonstrated across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank—showing a move toward principled, spectrum‑aware initialization/analysis for stable training of biologically constrained deep networks.
> 
> (d) Anchor‑free, one‑stage part–body association detectors (F1/Precision reporting)
> - Trend: from two‑stage/anchor‑based (and body‑to‑part) designs to one‑stage, anchor‑free, part‑to‑body association with a single 2D center‑offset branch. PBADet reduces representation length (scales gracefully as parts K grow), uses task‑aligned learning instead of centerness, and simplifies decoding, improving robustness and scalability.
> - Generalization and metrics: SOTA or competitive detection/association on BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, CrowdHuman; better F1/Precision/Recall than strong multi‑person pose baselines on small parts (hands/feet); extends beyond humans (AP‑10K animals). This reflects a trend to compact association heads on multi‑scale feature maps for efficient, accurate one‑stage detectors.
> 
> (e) LLM‑assisted causal discovery with deep structural causal models (multi‑modal/time‑series)
> - Trend: from purely data‑driven or metadata‑only discovery to agentic, iterative hybrids. The CMA unifies LLMs (as priors/critics/post‑processors) with Deep Structural Causal Models (and DL‑parameterized chain graphs) as the data‑grounding engine. It iteratively proposes, fits (via likelihood), critiques, and amends graphs, with reasoning traces and counterfactuals for interpretability.
> - Breadth and evaluation: improves graph recovery (lower NHD/BHD ratios) over data‑only (NOTEARS/DAG‑GNN) and LLM‑only baselines on Arctic Sea Ice, Sangiovese, and an expert‑curated Alzheimer’s benchmark; handles time‑series settings (e.g., sea‑ice) and multi‑modal data (tabular+MRI) in ADNI; discovers plausible missing edges and external modulators, then validates via counterfactual inference.
> 
> Overarching trajectory
> - Efficiency at scale: Optimizer‑state quantization advances (4‑bit + factorization) make end‑to‑end Transformer/LLM fine‑tuning practical under constrained memory while preserving accuracy, complementing PEFT/LoRA and distributed strategies (FSDP/offload).
> - Objective and model design for semantics and stability: Theory favors JEPA‑style self‑distillation for semantic embeddings over reconstruction, and spectrum‑aware analysis over rigid constraints for stable RNN learning—both trends improve interpretability and downstream utility.
> - Unified, agentic interpretability: In perception, anchor‑free one‑stage association heads improve precision/F1 with simpler, scalable designs; in causality, LLM+DSCM agents provide human‑readable reasoning traces, testable hypotheses, and counterfactual explanations in multi‑modal/time‑series settings.
> - Benchmarks and signals: The corpus jointly spans sequential MNIST/PTB (RNN stability), COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman/AP‑10K (perception, F1/Precision), GLUE/ImageNet/WMT/E2E (Transformer fine‑tuning), and real scientific domains (Arctic sea‑ice, Alzheimer’s/ADNI), illustrating a broad move toward methods that are both scalable (memory/time) and interpretable (spectra, reasoning traces, counterfactuals).

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here are the matching papers and the trend they reveal.
> 
> ## Matching papers
> 
> **(a) Low-bit optimizer states for Transformer fine-tuning**
> - *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023). Pushes Adam/AdamW optimizer states from 8-bit to 4-bit using smaller block sizes (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantization, and factorization (4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor). Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L), SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG (GPT-2), WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (Alpaca), saving up to 57.7% memory; it also engages end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning (LoRA is cited for GPT-2 and LLaMA pipelines).
> 
> **(b) Self-distillation / JEPA vs CE-MSE and cosine-similarity objectives**
> - *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis* (NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes self-distillation JEPA (latent-space prediction, stop-grad) vs MAE/reconstruction (MSE-type) on deep linear networks, showing JEPA's implicit bias toward high-influence features and noise suppression; ImageNet CCA experiments confirm JEPA aligns faster with low-variance perceptual PCA features.
> - *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* — analyzes cosine-similarity-based InfoNCE-type losses (positive/negative pair similarity), proposes a variance-reduction auxiliary loss; evaluated on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet.
> 
> **(c) Spectrum-aware analysis for Dale's-Law RNNs**
> - *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). Shows sign constraints (ColEI) are less responsible for poor learning than the singular-value spectrum at initialization; DANN (reparameterized E/I) RNNs keep unimodal, clustered spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance, and gradient clipping substantially stabilizes the otherwise unstable ColEI SGD training; benchmarks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> 
> **(d) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association**
> - *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free dense detection (YOLOv5/v7) with a single part-to-body center offset; reports precision/recall/F1 (outperforming ED-Pose on hands/feet), state-of-the-art on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman face-body association, and generalizes to quadruped part-body association.
> 
> **(e) LLM-assisted causal discovery with deep structural causal models**
> - *Causal Modelling Agents (CMA): Causal Graph Discovery through Synergising Metadata- and Data-Driven Reasoning* (ICLR 2024). Iteratively combines LLMs (as prior, critic, post-processor) with Deep Structural Causal Models (DSCMs), including chain-graph parameterization for unmeasured confounding; handles multi-modal data (tabular + brain imaging, ADNI) and time-series benchmarks (Arctic sea ice), reported F1 = 0.57 (sea ice) and 0.81 (AD consensus graph), beating NOTEARS, DAG-GNN, and LLM-only baselines.
> - *G-Sim* (LLM-proposed simulators with gradient-free calibration) is a related LLM-assisted time-series causal-structure discovery work, reporting F1 scores (95.5% COVID-19, 93.3% supply chain, 100% hospital beds) and SHD.
> 
> Note: the context reports F1 (and SHD) for causal discovery; AUROC evaluation for these models is not evidenced in the retrieved material.
> 
> ## Development trend
> 
> 1. **Efficiency**: optimizer-state compression progressed 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit via moment-pattern-aware quantization and factorization, making full/fine-tuning of large Transformers (and LoRA-style pipelines) memory-feasible without accuracy loss.
> 2. **Representation learning theory**: the field moved from reconstruction (MAE, MSE/CE) and contrastive cosine losses toward latent-space predictive self-distillation (JEPA), with theoretical analyses of implicit bias (noise suppression, feature prioritization) now guiding embedding and loss design.
> 3. **Biologically constrained recurrent nets**: from merely enforcing sign constraints to understanding that the singular-value spectrum at initialization dominates trainability; diagnostics (NSE) and architecture/regularization (DANN, gradient clipping) replace ad-hoc fixes to stabilize SGD.
> 4. **Detection**: consolidation from multi-stage, anchor-based pipelines to unified one-stage anchor-free detectors with a single part-to-body offset, improving F1/Precision and scaling to arbitrary part sets (COCO/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman).
> 5. **Causal discovery**: from purely data-driven (NOTEARS, DAG-GNN) or purely metadata-driven (LLM-only) approaches to hybrid agentic frameworks (CMA) that loop LLM hypothesis generation ↔ deep causal model fitting ↔ post-processing, extending to multi-modal and time-series settings with F1-based evaluation.
> 
> Overall, the trend is toward **unified, efficient, and interpretable systems**: compressing optimization, single-objective/single-stage architectures, spectral- and bias-aware regularization, and LLM-grounded causal structure learning — all validated on common benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, COCO, GLUE, Alpaca).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, the matching papers are:
> 
> **(a)** "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW states from 8-bit to 4-bit via smaller blocks (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizers, and factorization; matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L), ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium with LoRA), WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca instruction tuning, saving up to 57.7% memory.
> **(b)** "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024) — deep-linear analysis of JEPA self-distillation vs MAE: JEPA prioritizes high-influence (low-variance) features and suppresses noise, with depth strengthening this bias; plus "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning," which analyzes cosine-similarity/InfoNCE objectives and adds a variance-reduction loss improving CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.
> **(c)** "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023) — spectrum-aware analysis: ColEI RNNs fail because of multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), not sign constraints; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance, and gradient clipping stabilizes SGD; related Hessian power-law work shows spectrum structure and LoRA-only fine-tuning behaves differently from full fine-tuning.
> **(d)** "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (ICLR 2024) — single part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5/v7 anchor-free heads; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts and reports higher Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., all parts F1 48.52 vs ED-Pose 31.51) on COCO validation.
> **(e)** "Causal Modelling Agents (CMA)" (ICLR 2024) — LLM-assisted causal discovery with Deep Structural Causal Models (DSCMs) and chain-graph parameterization for unmeasured confounding; best F1 on Arctic sea ice (0.57) and AD consensus graph (0.81), beating NOTEARS, DAG-GNN, and LLM-only; G-Sim (related) uses LLM-proposed simulators with causal-structure F1/SHD metrics on time-series environments.
> 
> **Development trend of methods:** Across all five, the direction is *efficiency and interpretability through compression, theory, and simplification*. (1) Optimizers move from full-precision to 4-bit states with data-adaptive quantization, making end-to-end/LoRA Transformer fine-tuning memory-cheap without accuracy loss. (2) Self-supervised representation learning shifts from empirical objectives to principled analysis of implicit bias (JEPA vs MAE/CE/MSE) and embedding-similarity statistics, guiding loss design. (3) Recurrent training stability is reinterpreted spectrally — initial singular-value/Hessian spectra, not hard constraints, determine SGD dynamics — yielding pre-training diagnostics (NSE, power laws). (4) Detection architectures simplify from multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines to one-stage anchor-free unified part–body association, improving F1/Precision. (5) Causal discovery moves from pure data-driven methods to hybrid LLM+DSCM agents where LLMs act as priors, critics, and post-processors, enabling multi-modal/time-series modeling evaluated by F1. Overall, the field trends toward fewer parameters/bits, simpler architectures, spectral/analytical grounding, and knowledge-data fusion, validated on standard benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR-100, COCO, GLUE).

### paperscope:trend:300 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) a one-stage, anchor-free approach for linking detected human parts (e.g., hands, face) to the correct person and reporting AP/F1 and Precision; (2) spectral stability analysis for recurrent deep networks that respect excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (Dale’s principle), going beyond simple sign clipping; (3) self-supervised joint-embedding prediction (non-contrastive self distillation) and its implicit bias toward high-influence features vs pixel reconstruction, with cosine-based similarity and log-loss used in downstream linear probes on a 100‑class image benchmark (e.g., CIFAR‑100); (4) training at scale with memory‑savvy optimizers that keep first/second moments in ~4‑bit while remaining compatible with Adam‑style decoupled weight decay and stochastic gradient descent fine‑tuning on attention/backbone models like a 50‑layer residual net or Transformers; and (5) learning‑augmented online algorithms that, with bandit access to multiple predictors, combine heuristics for metrical task systems and achieve sublinear regret. I’m specifically interested in work that mentions cross‑entropy, cosine similarity, F1/Precision, clean subset evaluation sets like D_k^c, and uses transformer‑based conditional guidance or similar, with near‑linear runtime in problem size.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Across the five areas in your query, the methods show a clear progression toward simpler, more scalable designs, explicit stability analyses, and practical training at larger scales with principled memory savings, while bandit-style learning-augmentation achieves regret guarantees that approach the best heuristic. Here is the development trend by topic, tied to the cited works and their reported metrics.\n\n(1) One-stage, anchor-free part–person association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)\n- Trend: from multi-stage and anchor-based linking (e.g., BPJDet/YOLO variants) to one-stage, anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset. This reduces representation length from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2 for K parts and makes decoding and supervision simpler.\n- Scalability: the single offset scales naturally to any number of parts without adding offsets per part, avoiding degradation as K grows; demonstrated across multiple datasets and even non-human quadrupeds.\n- Performance and evaluation: consistent AP improvements and association metrics (e.g., conditional accuracy and joint AP on BodyHands; AP.5:.95 and mMR−2 on COCOHumanParts). The method also reports Precision/Recall/F1 against ED-Pose (Appendix A.2), showing higher F1 and Precision for small parts (hands/feet).\n- Training and backbone: uses SGD and anchor-free heads on YOLOv5/YOLOv7; maintains strong performance while simplifying training and inference. \n\n(2) Dale’s Law in recurrent deep networks (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Trend: moving beyond “sign clipping” (simple EI column sign constraints) to spectrum-aware design and analysis. The recurrent DANN architecture (feedforward DANN extended to RNNs) performs as well as standard RNNs while respecting EI, unlike ColEI.\n- Stability mechanism: the singular value spectrum—not just sign constraints—drives learning stability. Unimodal, clustered spectra (quarter-circle-like) in DANN/standard RNNs contrast with multimodal, dispersed spectra in ColEI. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) quantifies this pathology and correlates with performance.\n- Scalability: performance and spectral quality improve with network size and are robust to EI ratio in DANNs (even with a single inhibitory neuron), whereas ColEI degrades for small networks or skewed EI ratios. Gradient clipping helps ColEI, but the decisive factor is spectral clustering.\n- Practical implication: design EI networks by controlling spectral properties at initialization, enabling better scaling while preserving Dale’s principle.\n\n(3) Self-supervised JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024)\n- Trend: from pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) to latent-space joint-embedding prediction (non-contrastive self-distillation, StopGrad), with an explicit theoretical mechanism explaining why JEPA avoids noisy features.\n- Implicit bias: in deep linear models, JEPA prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficients) and this bias strengthens with encoder depth; MAE prioritizes highly covarying (high-variance) features. This yields faster learning of semantic directions and reduced sensitivity to noisy pixels.\n- Time-series modeling: a simple temporal model shows JEPA favors “slow” (highly predictive, lower-variance) features; the learning order flips relative to MAE when feature covariance and regression coefficient trend in opposite directions.\n- Practical evidence: JEPA’s features align better with low-variance subspaces used for perception; empirical ImageNet experiments show greater similarity between full and bottom-variance subspaces for JEPA than MAE (CCA analysis), consistent with the theory.\n\n(4) Training at scale with ~4-bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Trend: from 8-bit state quantization to 4-bit optimizer states, while remaining compatible with Adam-style decoupled weight decay (AdamW) and SGDM, and usable with Transformer and CNN backbones.\n- Key advances: identify and fix the second moment “zero-point” problem (DE-0 mapping or linear mapping without zero), adopt smaller block sizes and rank-1 normalization to handle heterogeneous outlier patterns, and optionally factorize the second moment for further memory cuts.\n- Scalability and efficiency: comparable accuracy to full precision across NLU (RoBERTa-L), machine translation (Transformer-Base), image classification (Swin-T), and instruction tuning (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B); memory savings up to ~58% total training memory in certain setups and improved throughput under optimizer offloading.\n- Optimizer compatibility: direct drop-in for AdamW/SGDM; reduced communication cost makes large Transformer training more practical without sacrificing downstream accuracy.\n\n(5) Learning-augmented online MTS with bandit access to multiple predictors (ICML 2025)\n- Trend: combining heuristics moves from full-feedback to bandit-feedback with delayed access (m≥2), achieving sublinear regret O(OPT^{2/3}) relative to the best heuristic’s cost on the instance (competitive ratio tends to 1). This bridges learning-augmentation with bandit learning against memory-bounded adversaries.\n- Algorithmic pattern: alternation of exploitation and m-step exploration (to observe a heuristic’s cost), using HEDGE/SHARE-style updates; improper steps and spectrum-like stability ideas are used to make the regret depend on OPT rather than horizon T.\n- Robustness and scalability: extends to benchmarks that switch among heuristics at most k times, keeping regret sublinear in OPT and rising mildly in k; tight lower bounds show the dependence is near-optimal even with m=2.\n\nCross-cutting patterns\n- Simplification and scalability: anchor-free single-offset association (PBADet) scales in parts K; spectrum-aware EI architectures (DANN) scale in network size and EI ratio; 4-bit optimizers scale training across diverse Transformer/CNN tasks; bandit combination scales in number of predictors ℓ and delayed access m while keeping regret tied to instance difficulty (OPT).\n- Explicit stability diagnostics: spectral clustering/NSE in EI RNNs provides a measurable knob to ensure stable learning; JEPA’s ODE-based training dynamics explain feature prioritization, guiding depth choices.\n- Practical metrics and evaluations: part-body AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, mMR−2, and small-part F1/Precision in PBADet; CCA-based similarity for JEPA representation quality; accuracy retention on NLU/MT/CLS and instruction tuning for 4-bit optimizers; and regret/competitive-ratio guarantees for learning-augmented MTS.\n- Training regimes and models: SGD (PBADet) and AdamW/SGDM (4-bit optimizers) remain standard, with results reported on modern Transformer backbones and large language models.\n\nOverall, the trajectory is toward methods that (i) reduce structural burdens (anchors/stages, per-part offsets), (ii) replace brittle constraints with principled stability analyses (spectral properties under Dale’s Law), (iii) favor predictive latent targets over pixel reconstruction in self-supervision (JEPA), (iv) compress optimizer states to 4-bit without accuracy loss, and (v) bring learning-augmentation to bandit settings with instance-dependent sublinear regret. These changes jointly improve scalability, stability, and practicality across detection, representation learning, optimization, and online decision-making.'}

> 1. **Part-body association** – **PBADet (ICLR 2024)**: a one-stage, anchor-free detector linking human parts (hands, face, feet) to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated with AP on COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman and reports **Precision/Recall/F1** (Table 7 vs. ED-Pose).
> 
> 2. **Spectral stability under Dale's principle** – **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**: analyzes recurrent EI networks (ColEI vs. DANN), showing the **singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints/clipping**; introduces normalized SVD entropy as a performance predictor.
> 
> 3. **Non-contrastive self-distillation / JEPA** – **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**: shows JEPA (self-distillation) has an implicit bias toward **high-influence features vs. MAE pixel reconstruction**, using deep linear models and linear-probe/CCA evaluation. Closely related SSL work on CIFAR-100 with **cosine similarity and linear probing** is **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, top-1 linear probes) and **LDReg** (linear evaluation, transfer to CIFAR).
> 
> 4. **Memory-efficient optimizers** – **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)**: quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to ~4-bit, compatible with **decoupled weight decay (AdamW)**, evaluated on Swin-T, RoBERTa, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA; matches 32-bit accuracy with up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 
> 5. **Learning-augmented online algorithms** – **"Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors"**: combines multiple heuristics for **Metrical Task Systems with bandit feedback**, achieving **sublinear regret O(OPT^{2/3})** with matching lower bound.
> 
> **Not found in the corpus**: the specific notation "D_k^c" (clean subset evaluation set), explicit "near-linear runtime" claims, and a "transformer-based conditional guidance" paper matching the above. Cross-entropy does appear (e.g., Universal Guidance for diffusion uses cross-entropy-based guidance; RZ-NAS code), cosine similarity appears (contrastive-learning embeddings paper, AdvI2I), and F1/Precision appear (PBADet; GOT-D; Agreement-on-the-Line), but these are scattered across different papers, not one unifying work.
> 
> **Development trend across these methods**:
> - **From multi-stage to single-stage/end-to-end**: detection moved from two-stage anchor-based pipelines to one-stage anchor-free designs with lightweight association heads (PBADet), emphasizing scalability and simplicity.
> - **From sign constraints to spectral/initialization analysis**: the Dale's-law work shifts the explanation of EI-network failure from parameter sign clipping to spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values; NSE as diagnostic), guiding better architecture/initialization design.
> - **From contrastive to non-contrastive self-supervision with mechanistic understanding**: SSL moved from sample-contrastive losses to non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA), with theory explaining implicit bias (high-influence features over high-variance pixels) and practical fixes (variance reduction of negative-pair similarities, local dimensionality regularization).
> - **From full-precision to low-bit training at scale**: optimization evolved from 32-bit states to 8-bit then 4-bit quantized moments with smarter quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion), preserving AdamW behavior while cutting memory.
> - **From worst-case competitive analysis to learning-augmented algorithms**: online algorithms now combine classical worst-case guarantees with bandit-learned heuristics, achieving regret sublinear in the offline optimum and robustness via prediction portfolios.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, here are the papers that best cover your five topics, followed by the development trend.
> 
> ## Matching Papers
> 
> 1. **Part-body association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024; doc `08b70bc…c90`). One-stage, anchor-free detector linking hands/face to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset. Reports AP, Precision, Recall, and F1 (e.g., vs ED-Pose on COCO), and joint AP on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts.
> 
> 2. **Spectral stability of Dale's-law RNNs** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023; doc `e63a94c…0c8`). Shows that simple E/I sign partitioning (ColEI) yields multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra, and that spectral properties at initialization matter more than sign constraints; proposes DANN RNNs and normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a diagnostic — going beyond plain sign clipping.
> 
> 3. **Self-supervised joint-embedding prediction** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024; doc `40fde03…a8103`). Non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA vs MAE/pixel reconstruction) with an implicit bias toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) features; validated on ImageNet-1K with I-JEPA/MAE via CCA. *Note:* the cosine-similarity analysis with linear probes on CIFAR-100 appears in the related *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (doc `160e140…5c21a`); the JEPA paper itself does not use CIFAR-100/log-loss linear probes.
> 
> 4. **Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizers** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023; doc `8d5e145…37e1`). Compresses first/second moments to ~4-bit (small block size B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion), built on 32-bit AdamW with decoupled weight decay; evaluated on Swin-T, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Transformer-Base, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B (attention/Transformer backbones).
> 
> 5. **Learning-augmented online algorithms** — *Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors* (ICML 2025; doc `c97e745…f29e53e`). Combines ℓ heuristics for Metrical Task Systems with bandit (one query per step) access, achieving sublinear regret O(OPT_{≤0}^{2/3}) with a matching lower bound.
> 
> ## Gaps vs. your requested specifics
> - **D_k^c clean subset evaluation sets** and **near-linear runtime in problem size** could not be found in the collection.
> - **Cross-entropy** appears as classifier-guidance loss in the diffusion paper *Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models* (doc `9134ed6…7f668`), which uses transformer-based (Stable Diffusion) conditional guidance — but it is not among the five core topics.
> - **Log-loss/CIFAR-100 cosine-similarity linear probes** are in the contrastive-learning similarities paper, not the JEPA paper.
> 
> ## Development Trend
> - **Detection:** Multi-stage, anchor-based, body-to-part pipelines (BPJDet, Hier-R-CNN) → single-stage, anchor-free, part-to-body association (PBADet), emphasizing scalability, one-to-one correspondence, and task-alignment learning — simpler, more efficient, better AP/F1.
> - **Recurrent networks:** Naive sign clipping/constraint enforcement (ColEI) → spectral-aware architecture design (DANN) and spectrum-pathology metrics (NSE), showing *how* weights are initialized/structured matters more than *whether* signs are constrained.
> - **Self-supervised learning:** Pixel reconstruction (MAE) → joint-embedding prediction/self-distillation (JEPA), with theory (deep linear analysis) explaining why latent-space prediction biases toward influential, noise-free features; evaluation moves from accuracy-only to embedding-similarity/cosine-based analysis on CIFAR/ImageNet.
> - **Optimization:** 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit optimizer states, with dedicated quantization (rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization) preserving AdamW/SGD(M) convergence while enabling large-model (LLaMA-scale) training under tight memory.
> - **Online algorithms:** Full-feedback prediction → bandit access to multiple predictors, with MAB-style exploration/exploitation and MTS-style rounding yielding provably sublinear regret and near-1 competitive ratios robust to arbitrary heuristics.
> 
> Overall, the trend is **unification and efficiency**: replacing complex multi-stage/anchor-based or reconstruction-based designs with streamlined one-stage/latent-prediction formulations, compressing resources (memory, feedback, bits) while preserving or improving theoretical and empirical guarantees.

</details>

### paperscope:trend:303 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a real‑time, multi‑user gesture interface for a hospital setting that must associate each person’s hands/face to the right body while running under tight GPU memory. The pipeline pretrains with a joint‑embedding self‑supervised method, then fine‑tunes with AdamW/SGD on attention backbones (Transformers or a 50‑layer residual net), evaluates with F1/Precision and log‑loss, and uses cosine scoring on a 100‑class benchmark. I need: (a) an anchor‑free detector that links parts to bodies robustly, (b) a low‑memory optimizer (~4‑bit moments) to shrink training footprint, (c) guidance on designing recurrent modules that obey excitatory/inhibitory constraints yet remain spectrally stable for time‑series modeling, and (d) an online, bandit‑style way to pick among several predictors/heuristics with sublinear regret. Please point me to works that together address these needs and discuss transformer‑style conditional guidance, clean subset evaluation (D_k^c), and near‑linear time implementations.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five works map cleanly onto your four design needs and show a broader shift toward scalable, memory‑efficient, and theoretically grounded methods.
> 
> (a) Anchor‑free, scalable part‑to‑body association
> - Shift from anchor‑based/two‑stage to one‑stage, anchor‑free: PBADet (ICLR 2024) replaces body‑to‑part multi‑offset heads (e.g., BPJDet) with a single part‑to‑body center offset on dense, multi‑scale feature maps. This keeps the representation length independent of the number of parts, improving scalability when the part set grows and simplifying decoding.
> - Stability/robustness and metrics: PBADet uses task‑aligned learning atop anchor‑free heads, shows higher AP and lower miss/mismatch rates on BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, and CrowdHuman, and reports additional F1/Precision comparisons vs. multi‑person pose (ED‑Pose) in a controlled study.
> - Transformer context: While PBADet itself is built on YOLO‑style backbones, it situates the method among contemporary, attention‑based systems (e.g., HOTR for HOI via transformer encoder‑decoder), reflecting the field’s broader move toward attention models even when the final detector is convolutional.
> - Time trend: 2023 anchor‑based BPJDet → 2024 PBADet’s anchor‑free, part‑to‑body offset with simpler, more scalable decoding.
> 
> (b) Low‑memory optimization (~4‑bit states)
> - From 8‑bit to 4‑bit states: The NeurIPS 2023 4‑bit optimizer pushes beyond prior 8‑bit methods by analyzing moment outliers and the “zero‑point” failure in second‑moment quantization. The key advances are (i) smaller block sizes for first moment, (ii) rank‑1 row/column normalization, and (iii) a linear mapping that excludes zero for the second moment to avoid catastrophic update scaling.
> - Accuracy vs. memory: Across RoBERTa‑L, GPT‑2 Medium, Swin‑T, and a standard Transformer, 4‑bit states match 32‑bit AdamW convergence and accuracy while saving 34–58% total training memory (and further when combined with factorization of second moments). Fused implementations close or exceed 8‑bit runtime.
> - Practical trend: Optimizer design now targets the numerics of second moments (zero‑point avoidance) and structure‑aware normalization (rank‑1) to reach 4‑bit without accuracy loss.
> 
> (c) Recurrent modules with Dale’s Law and spectral stability for time‑series
> - From sign constraints to spectral design: The NeurIPS 2023 EI‑RNN study shows that simply enforcing column E/I signs (ColEI) hurts learning; the dominant factor is the singular‑value spectrum. Architectures like recurrent DANNs achieve unimodal, clustered spectra similar to standard RNNs, preserving performance while satisfying Dale’s Law.
> - Stability metric and scaling: Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance; higher NSE (more clustered spectra) correlates with better learning and lower variance. Larger networks and balanced E/I ratios improve spectra; intriguingly, large ColEI networks can learn well despite large maximum singular values due to rotational dynamics between singular directions.
> - Training practice: Gradient clipping notably stabilizes ColEI. Overall guidance shifts from “just obey Dale” to explicitly shaping spectral properties for stable time‑series modeling.
> 
> (d) Online, bandit‑style selection among predictors/heuristics with sublinear regret
> - Bandit feedback with delayed access: The ICML 2025 work addresses the realistic constraint that only one heuristic’s state can be queried at each step (with m‑step bootstrapping). It achieves regret O(OPT^{2/3}) against the best single heuristic, and O~(k^{1/3}·OPT^{2/3}) against a comparator that switches at most k times—both sublinear in OPT, with matching lower bounds (up to logs).
> - Design shift: Instead of full‑feedback expert mixing, the algorithm alternates exploitation and m‑step exploration and uses stability of a full‑information learner internally. This supports robust, on‑line model/policy selection under stringent query budgets.
> 
> Self‑supervised pretraining trend (for your joint‑embedding stage)
> - JEPA vs. MAE in deep linear models (NeurIPS 2024): The analysis explains why JEPA‑style self‑distillation prioritizes influential (high‑regression‑coefficient) features—especially with deeper encoders—while MAE prioritizes high‑variance/co‑varying features. In temporal models, JEPA focuses on slow, predictive features. This gives a principled rationale for joint‑embedding pretraining before fine‑tuning your attention backbones.
> 
> What is and isn’t covered relative to your pipeline add‑ons
> - Transformer‑style conditional guidance: The detector paper cites transformer‑based HOI (HOTR) as context, and JEPA papers commonly use transformer encoders, but none of the works here develop “conditional guidance” mechanisms per se.
> - Clean subset evaluation (D_k^c): Not discussed in these papers.
> - Near‑linear time implementations: The trend is toward efficiency (one‑stage anchor‑free detection; quantized optimizer states), but none of the works analyze or claim near‑linear O(n) or O(nD(⋅)) time bounds.
> 
> Putting it together for your hospital multi‑user, real‑time interface
> - Detection (a): Adopt PBADet’s one‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑body offset for robust hand/face‑to‑body linking in crowded scenes; its representation scales to many parts and simplifies decoding.
> - Memory (b): Train/fine‑tune with the 4‑bit optimizer: small blocks for first moment, rank‑1 normalization, and a zero‑free linear quantizer for the second moment; combine with factorized second moments where applicable to cut memory and communication.
> - Time‑series stability (c): If you enforce Dale’s Law in recurrent/temporal modules, design for unimodal, clustered singular‑value spectra (high NSE) rather than focusing only on sign constraints; balance E/I ratios, consider DANN‑style parametrizations, and use gradient clipping.
> - Online selection (d): Wrap multiple predictors/heuristics with the m‑delayed bandit selector to get regret O(OPT^{2/3}); the method is robustified further with a k‑switch comparator bound when scenarios change.
> - Pretraining: A JEPA‑style joint‑embedding stage (with deep encoders) aligns with the observed empirical benefit of learning influential, slow features before attention‑based fine‑tuning (AdamW/SGD) and evaluation with F1/Precision/log‑loss where appropriate.
> 
> Time‑ordered view of the trend
> - 2023: 4‑bit optimizer makes low‑memory training practical; EI‑RNNs shift from sign‑only constraints to spectral design for stability.
> - 2024: One‑stage, anchor‑free PBADet scales part‑to‑body association; JEPA theory clarifies why latent prediction pretraining avoids noisy features.
> - 2025: Bandit‑feedback model selection reaches sublinear regret in terms of OPT with tight lower bounds, enabling practical combination of specialized heuristics under query limits.
> 
> Overall pattern: methods move toward (i) scalable, one‑stage anchor‑free detection; (ii) quantization‑aware optimization that safely reaches 4‑bit states; (iii) biologically inspired recurrent models constrained by spectral, not just sign, criteria; and (iv) learning‑augmented, bandit‑style selection with regret guarantees tied to OPT rather than the horizon—all directly supporting your real‑time, multi‑user interface under memory and feedback constraints.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Works addressing your needs
> 
> **(a) Anchor-free part–body association** — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): a one-stage, anchor-free detector that links parts (hands, face, feet) to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset, guaranteeing one-to-one correspondence; evaluated with Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., vs. ED-Pose) on BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman.
> 
> **(b) Low-memory optimizer** — **"4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023): quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller blocks B128, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization, optional factorization), matching 32-bit accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings — directly applicable to your AdamW/SGD fine-tuning under tight GPU memory.
> 
> **(c) Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules, spectrally stable** — **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): shows simple sign-constrained EI RNNs (ColEI) learn poorly because of multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra, not the sign constraints themselves; recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) retain unimodal spectra and learn well; normalised SVD entropy predicts performance. Guidance: monitor/control the singular-value spectrum at initialization, use DANN-style reparameterization, and gradient clipping helps.
> 
> **(d) Online bandit-style predictor/heuristic selection with sublinear regret** — **"Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors"**: combines heuristics with bandit (delayed) feedback, alternates exploration/exploitation with MTS-style rounding, and attains sublinear regret (e.g., O((Dℓ lnℓ)^{1/3} m^{2/3} OPT^{2/3})); also the **BSO** paper gives online training with sublinear regret O(√T) and near-linear memory O(n²L/32).
> 
> ## Supporting pieces
> 
> - **Joint-embedding SSL pretraining**: **LDReg** (local dimensionality regularization for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE, ResNet-50 & ViT-B) and the **JEPA** analysis (joint-embedding predictive architecture; I-JEPA aligns faster with perceptual features than MAE) — relevant to your pretraining stage.
> - **Transformer-style conditional guidance**: **Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models** (ICLR 2024) — training-free guidance with arbitrary off-the-shelf functions (face/segmentation/object detection), extending classifier guidance; **CleanDiffuser** surveys classifier guidance vs. classifier-free guidance (CFG) as the two guided-sampling categories.
> - **Near-linear time implementations**: **"Accelerating ERM for data-driven algorithm design using output-sensitive techniques"** (output-sensitive, near-linear-in-output enumeration; also a parametric-DP paper with O(R·T_DP) ray search); Universal Guidance's time scales linearly with refinement steps k; BSO's memory is near-linear.
> - **Clean subset / evaluation**: closest matches are GOT-D's "clean" subset selection (toxicity, evaluated with F1/accuracy), DSL's gold-standard clean-label subsets with K-fold cross-fitting, and HASSOD's argument for AR over AP. **The exact "D_k^c clean subset evaluation" notation and a 100-class cosine-scored benchmark were not found in this collection** — I cannot confirm those specifics; the closest cosine-scoring protocols are Visual Data-Type Identification (cosine similarity matching against class prompts, log-likelihood scoring) and NFTS (prototypical/cosine-distance few-shot loss).
> 
> ## Development trend of these methods
> 
> 1. **Detection**: two-stage/anchor-based, heuristic or learned association (BodyHands, BPJDet body→part offsets) → **one-stage anchor-free with a single part→body offset** (PBADet), reducing complexity while improving robustness and scalability to many parts.
> 2. **Optimization memory**: full-precision 32-bit → 8-bit (block-wise, stable embeddings) → **4-bit states** with finer block sizes, zero-point-free linear quantization, rank-1 normalization, and factorization — pushing lossless compression of optimizer states.
> 3. **Recurrent EI design**: naive Dale's-Law constraint (ColEI) known to hurt learning → realization that **spectral properties matter more than sign constraints** → DANN-style reparameterization that respects E/I constraints while preserving a healthy (unimodal) singular-value spectrum.
> 4. **Online selection**: worst-case online algorithms → **learning-augmented + bandit feedback**, using exploration/exploitation with switching-cost-aware rounding and sublinear regret bounds (and, in BSO, online training with binary weights and O(√T) regret).
> 5. **Guidance/conditioning**: training task-specific conditional models → **training-free universal guidance** on frozen models; and **SSL** from contrastive losses toward joint-embedding/predictive architectures with local-dimensionality regularization to avoid collapse.
> 
> **Caveat**: the context does not contain a paper defining "D_k^c" clean-subset evaluation or a 100-class cosine benchmark, so those two specifics cannot be sourced from the available documents.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the works in this collection that together cover your needs:
> 
> **(a) Anchor-free part→body association detector**
> - **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (doc `08b70bc…`). A one-stage anchor-free detector linking hands/face/feet to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps; evaluated with F1/Precision and joint AP on BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman; robust one-to-one association, scalable to many parts, outperforms BPJDet, HierR-CNN, ED-Pose. Development trend: from two-stage heuristic/anchor-based association (DA-RNN, JointDet, BFJDet, HierR-CNN, BPJDet) to a single-stage anchor-free formulation with task-alignment learning (FCOS→TOOD→PBADet).
> 
> **(b) Low-memory 4-bit optimizer**
> - **4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States** (doc `8d5e145…`). Quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (small block B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, factorized second moment), matching 32-bit AdamW accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings; works with SGD/AdamW on Transformers (Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer-Base, LLaMA) — directly matches your fine-tuning setup. Related trend: Adafactor/SM3 factorization → 8-bit (Dettmers) → 4-bit states with better quantizers; also BSO (doc `4741ca1…`) pushes to binary spiking online training with sublinear O(√T) regret and O(n²L/32) memory.
> 
> **(c) Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules with spectral stability**
> - **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly** (doc `e63a94c…`). Shows sign (E/I) constraints alone aren't the problem — the initial recurrent-weight singular-value spectrum is: simple column-partitioned (ColEI) RNNs get multimodal, dispersed spectra and train poorly/unstably, while recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) keep standard RNN-like unimodal spectra and learn as well; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance, and gradient clipping mitigates instability. Development trend: sign-constrained RNNs → spectral analysis (random matrix theory, Marchenko–Pastur) → spectral-aware design/initialization as guidance for stable time-series EI networks.
> 
> **(d) Online bandit-style selection among predictors with sublinear regret**
> - **Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors** (doc `c97e745…`). Queries only one of ℓ heuristics per step, alternates exploration/exploitation (HEDGE/SHARE + MTS rounding), achieves O(OPT²ᐟ³) regret (sublinear in T and OPT) with matching lower bound, competitive ratio → 1 vs. best heuristic. Development trend: full-feedback combining heuristics (Blum & Burch) → bandit-feedback with block-based MAB (Arora et al.) → improper-step MTS-style rounding with tight T²ᐟ³ bounds.
> 
> **Additional topics you asked to discuss:**
> - **Transformer-style conditional guidance**: **Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models** (doc `9134ed60…`) covers the conditioning vs. guidance distinction, classifier guidance vs. classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans), and training-free guidance with off-the-shelf nets (segmentation, face, detection, CLIP) — forward+backward guidance with stepwise refinement whose time scales linearly with refinement steps k. **Beyond Induction Heads** (doc `3e35936…`) analyzes how attention-only Transformers acquire in-context (conditional) behavior via multi-phase circuits (bigram → label attention → full-context circuit), also in GPT2-XL.
> - **Clean subset evaluation (D_k^c)**: I could not find the exact "D_k^c" notation anywhere in this collection, so that specific protocol cannot be confirmed here. The closest matches are (i) **GOT-D** (doc `bb21f95…`), which selects subsets and evaluates utility on clean labeled target sets (e.g., 2.5K clean samples with toxicity ≤ 0.1 as selection target, 10K/20K subsets, downstream GLUE/zero-shot accuracy), and (ii) **Towards a Statistical Theory of Data Selection under Weak Supervision** (doc `826151f…`), which formalizes selecting a labeled subset G and training by regularized ERM. If D_k^c is essential, it is not evidenced in this corpus.
> - **Near-linear time implementations**: **Learning Kernels for Fast HSIC-Based Independence Testing** (doc `58063ef…`) gives linear-time (O(nD²)) differentiable estimators with O(n)/O(n log n) tests that finish in seconds on 100,000 samples (vs. quadratic baselines); **Accelerating ERM for Data-Driven Algorithm Design** (doc `9ea7329…`) gives output-sensitive, near-linear-time enumeration algorithms (Augmented Clarkson, execution DAGs) for ERM.
> 
> **Overall development trend**: multi-stage heuristic/anchor-based part-body detection → one-stage anchor-free detectors; full-precision → 8-bit → 4-bit (and binary/spiking) optimizer states; sign-constrained RNNs → spectral-aware EI design; full-feedback expert combining → bandit-feedback sublinear-regret selection; classifier guidance → classifier-free/universal training-free guidance; quadratic statistical tests → linear-time estimators; and SSL (contrastive/joint-embedding, e.g., LDReg/contrastive-similarity analyses on ResNet-50/ViT on ImageNet-100) increasingly coupled with such memory- and time-efficient components for deployment under tight GPU budgets.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Integrated development trend across the five lines of work (2019–2025):\n\n1) Part–body association in detection (PBADet, ICLR 2024)\n- Trend: from multi‑stage, anchor‑based association (e.g., Hier R‑CNN, BPJDet variants) to a one‑stage, anchor‑free design that encodes a single part‑to‑body center offset over multi‑scale feature maps.\n- Scalability: the single 2D offset scales to any number of parts without expanding the output head; decoding becomes simpler (one‑to‑one assignment). The same formulation transfers beyond humans (e.g., quadruped parts in AnimalPose/AP‑10K).\n- Optimization/metrics: trained with SGD and task‑alignment learning (classification CE/IoU/DFL plus an association L1 loss). On COCO/WholeBody and BodyHands the method reports AP and, where comparable to keypoint estimators, higher Precision/Recall/F1; qualitative and ablation results show better F1 than pose‑based grouping for small parts.\n- Overall shift: leaner anchor‑free heads and multi‑scale conditioning replace hand‑crafted anchors, improving throughput and robustness in crowded scenes (CrowdHuman) while maintaining precision.\n\n2) EI‑constrained deep networks (NeurIPS 2023): from sign constraints to spectral interpretability\n- Trend: the bottleneck in Dale’s‑Law RNNs is not the sign constraint per se, but spectrum pathologies. Performance correlates with unimodal, clustered singular‑value spectra—quantified by normalized SVD entropy—not just eigenvalue radius.\n- Architectural direction: recurrent Dale’s ANNs (DANNs) recover standard‑RNN‑like unimodal spectra and learn well; simple column E/I partitions (ColEI) yield dispersed, multimodal spectra and degrade. Larger networks and more balanced E/I ratios increase SVD entropy and stability.\n- Interpretability: spectrum/entropy becomes a predictive diagnostic before training, guiding scalable EI designs that obey biology yet match unconstrained models.\n\n3) Self‑supervised representation learning: JEPA vs reconstruction (NeurIPS 2024)\n- Trend: shift from reconstruction objectives (MAE) toward joint‑embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) driven by implicit bias. In deep linear analysis, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence features (large regression coefficients), while MAE prioritizes high covariance directions; JEPA’s bias strengthens with encoder depth.\n- Practical implication: predicting in latent space focuses learning on semantically informative, lower‑variance features earlier in training; fine‑tuning then benefits from stronger feature embeddings for downstream classification compared to reconstruction‑first pipelines.\n\n4) Memory‑efficient optimization at scale (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Trend: from 32‑bit/8‑bit states to 4‑bit AdamW with accuracy parity across Transformers, vision, MT, QA, and instruction tuning. Key advances include small‑block quantization, rank‑1 (row+column) normalization, and removing the zero‑point for second‑moment quantization; optionally factorize v for further savings.\n- Scalability: optimizer memory drops 2–4× vs 8‑bit while matching full precision on RoBERTa, Swin, Transformer‑Base and LLaMA fine‑tuning (with AdamW; LoRA used where applicable). This enables larger models per GPU and faster FSDP/offloaded training via reduced optimizer communication.\n- Methodological shift: careful second‑moment handling (zero‑point avoidance, linear mapping) replaces generic block quantization; hybrid quantization+factorization becomes a practical standard for large‑model training.\n\n5) World models on graphs and multi‑modal states (ICML 2025)\n- Trend: from video‑only, unstructured WMs to graph world models (GWM) that unify multi‑modal states as graphs, use similarity‑based retrieval links (top‑k by embedding similarity) and multi‑hop message passing, and interface with transformer‑guided decoders (LLMs, Stable Diffusion).\n- Generality and zero‑/few‑shot: a single GWM (token‑based and embedding‑based variants) matches or surpasses domain‑specific systems across recommendation, graph prediction, multi‑modal generation/matching, multi‑agent collaboration, RAG, and planning. Performance improves with 1–3 hop aggregation; excessive hops can over‑smooth.\n- Metrics/learning signals: tasks are cast as action nodes with targets selected by graph links or similarity retrieval; evaluation emphasizes Accuracy/Recall/F1 across tasks; multi‑modal decoders are instruction/projector‑tuned rather than trained end‑to‑end from scratch.\n\nCross‑cutting patterns over time\n- Structural simplification → scalability: anchor‑free detection heads (PBADet), spectrum‑aware EI designs (DANNs), and 4‑bit optimizers all simplify core machinery while scaling to larger part sets, wider networks, and bigger models.\n- Latent‑space operations: JEPA’s latent prediction and GWM’s embedding‑level message passing/projectors mirror diffusion in latent space and 4‑bit optimizer state compression—shifting computation from raw signals to structured latent representations for efficiency and stability.\n- Theory to practice: spectral entropy predicts EI network learnability; JEPA’s implicit bias explains faster emergence of semantic features; optimizer quantization theory (zero‑point handling, rank‑1 normalization) enables practical 4‑bit AdamW; graph message passing with retrieval formalizes multi‑hop reasoning in WMs.\n- Metrics and robustness: consistent gains in Precision/Recall/F1 for detection, matching, recommendation, and multi‑agent/RAG tasks; stability improves via spectrum regularity (EI), task‑alignment losses (detection), and quantization schemes (4‑bit AdamW).\n\nNet effect\nBetween 2023 and 2025, methods converge toward scalable, interpretable, and memory‑efficient pipelines that (i) replace anchors, handcrafted constraints, and pixel‑space reconstruction with anchor‑free heads, spectral/entropy diagnostics, and latent prediction; (ii) compress training states to 4‑bit without accuracy loss; and (iii) model multi‑modal worlds as graphs with similarity‑based retrieval and multi‑hop aggregation, achieving competitive F1/Accuracy with strong zero‑/few‑shot generalization.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, the five research lines map to these works:
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association; a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps; trained with **SGD** and task-alignment losses (IoU, DFL, classification + L1 association loss); evaluated on COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman with **Precision/Recall/F1** (e.g., vs ED-Pose) and AP.
> 2. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) — RNNs with excitatory–inhibitory (Dale's Law) constraints (ColEI vs DANN); shows **singular-value spectra** (multimodal/dispersed vs quarter-circle) drive learning more than sign constraints; uses **normalized SVD entropy (NSE)** as an interpretability/performance metric.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — implicit bias of latent-space prediction (self-distillation/JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) in deep linear networks: JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high ρ) low-noise features, with ordering by ρ vs λ; the fine-tuning angle is complemented by the Hessian power-law paper (ICML 2025), which shows **full fine-tuning induces the power-law spectrum while LoRA-only fine-tuning does not**.
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — **4-bit AdamW/Adam** via smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear quantizers; matches 32-bit AdamW on RoBERTa, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, saving up to ~57.7% memory.
> 5. **Graph World Model (GWM)** (ICML 2025) — world model representing multi-modal states as graphs (image/table/text nodes) with action nodes; **cosine/embedding-similarity retrieval** (Top-k, RAG-style), **multi-hop message passing** (GWM-T token-level, GWM-E embedding-level), and **transformer-guided generative decoders** (Llama-3-8B, Stable Diffusion); reports Recall/F1/Accuracy and benefits from multi-hop structures (with over-smoothing caveat).
> 
> **Development trend:**
> - **From multi-stage/anchor-based to one-stage, anchor-free, end-to-end** formulations that fold association into a single offset (BPJDet → PBADet), with denser evaluation (Precision/Recall/F1) beyond plain AP.
> - **From purely empirical training to spectral/theoretical analysis of learning dynamics** — singular-value spectra and entropy (Dale's Law) and power-law Hessian spectra are used both to explain why constraints impair learning and as predictors/interpretability tools for generalization and fine-tuning behavior.
> - **From understanding "what is learned" to understanding "why and when it is learned"** — exact ODE analysis of deep linear networks showing objective-dependent feature-ordering (JEPA vs MAE), tying latent-space prediction bias to noise suppression.
> - **From 32-bit/8-bit to 4-bit (sub-byte) optimizer states**, pushing memory efficiency while keeping full-precision accuracy and even improving throughput via reduced communication.
> - **From unstructured, single-modality world models to graph-structured, multi-modal world models** that unify prediction/generation/optimization, using similarity-based retrieval, multi-hop aggregation, and frozen transformer/stable-diffusion decoders with only projector tuning for scalability.
> 
> Caveat from context: AUROC and BPR/ranking-loss details are **not** present in the retrieved GWM material (metrics are Recall/F1/Accuracy; training uses Adam with LambdaLR), so those specific aspects cannot be confirmed.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here are the matching works and the development trend of their methods:
> 
> **Identified works (one per area):**
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** – one-stage, anchor-free part-body association; adds a single part-to-body center offset to anchor-free detectors (YOLOv5/v7) with task-alignment; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands with AP, mMR-2, and Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs ED-Pose 31.51). Note: training uses **SGD** with IoU/DFL/classification + association losses — the context does not confirm AdamW, CE, or MSE.
> 2. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** – excitatory–inhibitory RNNs; shows learning quality is governed by the singular-value spectrum at initialization, quantified by normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as an interpretability/predictive metric (anti-correlates with test error).
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** – latent-space prediction bias: JEPA/self-distillation implicitly prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (high-influence) features while MAE/reconstruction orders features by covariance; fine-tuning effects on embeddings are additionally covered by LDReg (local dimensional collapse, improved linear-eval/fine-tuning) and fine-tuning/linear-probing studies of CLIP.
> 4. **"4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)** – sub-byte optimizer states (4-bit AdamW/Adam, plus factorized variant) via smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, and factorization; matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Swin-T, Transformer, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B with up to ~57.7% memory savings.
> 5. **Graph World Model (GWM, ICML 2025)** – represents multi-modal states (image/table/text) as graphs with action nodes; uses cosine-similarity top-k retrieval (RAG) and multi-hop message passing (GWM-T token-level, GWM-E embedding-level), feeding LLM/Stable Diffusion decoders; reports F1/Recall/Accuracy. Note: AUROC and BPR are **not** found in GWM's context; BPR ranking with scalable approximations (Monte-Carlo ratio estimator, perturbed optimizers) and likelihood-vs-BPR regularization trade-offs appear in a separate decision-aware training paper (DAML, ICML 2025).
> 
> **Development trend:**
> - **Detection/association:** multi-stage heuristic or anchor-based pipelines → one-stage anchor-free dense prediction with a single universal offset (simpler, scalable, better F1).
> - **Network analysis:** explanations moved from parameter sign-constraints (Dale's law) to spectral/implicit dynamics — singular-value/Hessian spectra and entropy-based measures now predict performance and interpretability, also applied to SSL objectives.
> - **Self-supervised learning:** focus shifted from designing objectives to characterizing their implicit biases (latent-space prediction vs reconstruction) and to geometric/spatial regularization (local intrinsic dimensionality) to protect embeddings through fine-tuning.
> - **Optimization/efficiency:** optimizer-state precision compressed 32→8→4-bit with smarter quantization/factorization, achieving lossless Transformer training at far lower memory.
> - **World models:** unstructured sequence world models → graph-structured, multi-modal world states with action nodes, similarity-based retrieval, and multi-hop aggregation; token-based processing gave way to embedding-based message passing for 5–10× lower token cost while improving generalization, with decision-aware/ranking losses (BPR) and approximation techniques emerging for scalable, decision-oriented training.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-trend-312"></a>

### paperscope:trend:312 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers on efficient learning and transfer in deep networks (CNNs/Transformers and RNNs) that span: (1) one‑stage, anchor‑free part–to–body association for human parts on COCO with typical backbones (e.g., ResNet‑50) and standard CE/MSE training; (2) spectral analyses of biologically constrained recurrent models obeying excitatory/inhibitory sign rules, showing how singular value spectra affect optimization under SGD/AdamW; (3) theoretical work explaining the implicit bias of self‑distillation/JEPA objectives (e.g., via cosine similarity or MSE) on datasets like MNIST/CIFAR‑100; (4) memory‑efficient training via 4‑bit states for Adam/AdamW to cut footprint during fine‑tuning or End‑to‑end LoRA; and (5) self‑supervised RL that transfers across reward functions using random feature embeddings and planning. Ideally these works report common metrics (F1/Precision) and discuss practical approximations for deep networks.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

**score：2→3（Δ+1）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**
