Gold 1：

> Across the five works, a clear, time‑stamped trend emerges toward methods that make deep networks more transferable and efficient by simplifying architectures, controlling spectra, exploiting implicit objectives, compressing optimizer state, and planning with task‑agnostic representations.
> 
> 1) One‑stage, anchor‑free association (2024):
> - Shift from multi‑stage/anchor‑based to one‑stage, anchor‑free detection for part–body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024). Training uses standard classification/regression heads with task‑alignment learning, SGD, and COCO‑style protocols. The representation moves from body‑to‑part to a single part‑to‑body center offset, shrinking the output length and making the method scalable to many parts without expanding channels. This architectural simplification improves throughput and keeps accuracy (higher AP, lower MR−2; better Joint AP on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts). It also reports standard metrics (AP; and in head‑to‑toe comparisons, Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED‑Pose), reflecting a broader trend to unified, end‑to‑end heads that scale across datasets like COCO.
> 
> 2) Spectral perspectives on biologically constrained RNNs (2023):
> - The bottleneck in Dale’s‑law RNNs is now attributed less to sign constraints and more to singular‑value spectra at initialization (NeurIPS 2023). Networks with unimodal, clustered spectra (high normalized SVD entropy) train well with SGD/AdamW; pathological, multimodal spectra correlate with instability and the need for gradient clipping. Performance depends strongly on E/I ratio and width (small nets or too few inhibitory units worsen spectra/learning); architectures like recurrent DANNs preserve “standard RNN‑like” spectra and learn well. Net trend: spectral diagnostics (e.g., NSE) and spectrum‑aware initializations guide stable training under common optimizers.
> 
> 3) Implicit bias of JEPA/self‑distillation (2024):
> - Theory for deep linear networks explains why JEPA‑style (non‑contrastive, MSE‑type) objectives favor transfer‑useful features (NeurIPS 2024). Compared to MAE, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (large regression‑coefficient) features; depth amplifies this bias and can invert the learning order seen under reconstruction losses. Empirically (e.g., sequential MNIST and ImageNet‑scale probes), this aligns with JEPA’s faster focus on low‑variance, predictive structure rather than high‑variance pixels, clarifying why self‑distillation scales efficiently for downstream classifiers.
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient optimization via 4‑bit states (2023):
> - Optimizer state precision drops from 8‑bit to 4‑bit by tackling quantization details that matter in practice (NeurIPS 2023). Key advances: smaller block sizes for first moments; for second moments, removing the zero‑point (to avoid catastrophic 1/√v blow‑ups) and using rank‑1 (row/column) normalization or factorization. The result: Adam/AdamW with 4‑bit states matches 32‑bit accuracy across RoBERTa‑L (GLUE/SQuAD), Transformer‑Base (WMT14), Swin‑T (ImageNet), GPT‑2 Medium (E2E‑NLG), and LLaMA instruction tuning, while cutting memory (up to ~58%) and improving throughput with optimizer offloading/FSDP. This trend enables larger models and practical fine‑tuning pipelines (compatible with LoRA and end‑to‑end fine‑tuning) under standard losses (CE/MSE) and optimizers (Adam/AdamW).
> 
> 5) Transfer across rewards via self‑supervised RL with random features (2023):
> - To avoid compounding errors in model‑based RL, model‑free pretraining learns a “Q‑basis” over random feature embeddings of state–action, using offline data without rewards (NeurIPS 2023). At test‑time, a linear regression fits the new reward onto the random features; MPC/MPPI over the recombined Q‑basis yields rapid adaptation across tasks sharing dynamics (manipulation/locomotion, high‑D actions and pixels). Trend: planning on task‑agnostic, implicitly learned dynamics cumulants scales transfer better than explicit one‑step models, especially for long horizons.
> 
> Overall development pattern (2023→2024):
> - Architecture streamlining for scalability (one‑stage anchor‑free association) and spectrum‑aware initialization/diagnostics for constrained RNNs improve optimization under SGD/AdamW.
> - Theory tightens practice: self‑distillation/JEPA’s implicit bias (MSE‑based) explains rapid emergence of predictive features, complementing empirical successes on MNIST/ImageNet.
> - Systems efficiency advances from 8‑bit to 4‑bit optimizer states by addressing zero‑point and outlier patterns, enabling standard CE/MSE training and broad fine‑tuning (including instruction tuning and LoRA‑based workflows).
> - Transfer at scale shifts from explicit dynamics to self‑supervised, random‑feature Q‑bases plus MPC, accelerating adaptation to new rewards without labeled offline data.
> 
> Taken together, these works show a consistent trend: efficient learning and transfer now hinge on (i) simpler, universal heads, (ii) spectral regularity rather than hard constraints, (iii) implicit predictive objectives (JEPA) over reconstruction, (iv) aggressive but accurate optimizer state quantization, and (v) planning on reward‑agnostic feature accumulations. This combination improves scalability (parts, model size, horizon), stability under common optimizers (SGD/Adam/AdamW), and practical deployment (COCO‑style detection, Transformer fine‑tuning, and fast RL adaptation).

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, the five requested works are:
> 
> **1. Part–body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024, doc 08b70bc3)** — One-stage, anchor-free detector that links human parts to bodies via a single 2D part-to-body center offset on top of YOLOv5/YOLOv7-style anchor-free heads (multi-scale features, classification/localization/association branches, task-alignment + CE/MSE-style training). Reported metrics include AP, joint AP, conditional accuracy, MR-2, and precision/recall/F1 (vs. ED-Pose) on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; also generalizes to quadruped (AnimalPose, AP-10K).
> 
> **2. Spectral analysis of E/I-constrained RNNs ("Learning better with Dale's Law," NeurIPS 2023, doc e63a94c4)** — Shows Dale's-law (excitatory/inhibitory sign-rule) ColEI RNNs learn worse not because of sign constraints but because of multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization; recurrent DANN variants keep unimodal random-matrix spectra and match standard RNNs. Singular-value "transplant" experiments and normalized SVD entropy (NSE) link spectra to SGD optimization and learning performance (gradient clipping helps ColEI). Note: this paper is SGD-oriented; it does not specifically study AdamW.
> 
> **3. Theory of self-distillation/JEPA implicit bias ("How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features," NeurIPS 2024, doc 40fde037)** — Solves deep linear self-distillation (JEPA) vs. MAE dynamics, proving JEPA implicitly prioritizes "influential" features (large regression coefficient) and suppresses noisy features, with depth strengthening the bias; validated on ImageNet-1K via CCA alignment. The related contrastive-embedding-similarity paper (doc 160e1407) covers cosine-similarity objectives on CIFAR-10/100, but the JEPA implicit-bias theory itself is not demonstrated on MNIST/CIFAR-100.
> 
> **4. Memory-efficient 4-bit Adam/AdamW states (NeurIPS 2023, doc 8d5e1455)** — Compresses first/second moments to 4-bit using smaller block sizes, rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear quantizers (optionally factorized second moment, "4-bit Factor"). Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD (F1), ImageNet, E2E-NLG, MT, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning, with up to ~57.7% memory savings; LoRA is discussed as related parameter-efficient fine-tuning, not as an end-to-end LoRA method itself.
> 
> **5. Self-supervised RL transfer (RaMP, NeurIPS 2023, doc 528b3e89)** — Pre-trains multi-step Q-functions (Q-basis) on reward-free offline data using random neural-network features as pseudo-rewards, then fits a new reward by linear regression and plans via MPC, transferring across reward functions under shared dynamics while avoiding model-based compounding error (validated on Meta-World, Hopper, D'Claw).
> 
> **Development trend:** Across all five works the trajectory is toward greater *unification, theory-guided design, and efficiency/transfer*: (1) replacing multi-stage, anchor-based, heuristic pipelines with single-stage, anchor-free, end-to-end formulations (PBADet); (2) using spectral analysis (singular-value spectra, Hessian power-laws, NSE) to diagnose why constrained/depth networks train poorly and to guide optimization fixes rather than treating sign constraints or architectures in isolation; (3) providing exact/implicit-bias theory of self-distillation/JEPA objectives to explain which features SSL learns and why (influential vs. high-variance features); (4) pushing training memory down the precision ladder (32→8→4-bit) via smarter quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion) and factorization so large-model fine-tuning becomes feasible; and (5) making RL task-agnostic by disentangling dynamics from rewards through self-supervised random-feature Q-bases plus linear-regression planning, replacing brittle explicit models with implicit, transferable models. Common threads are task-agnostic/self-supervised pretraining, quantized/spectrally-informed optimization, and simple approximations (linear regression, MPC, dense per-pixel prediction) that trade accuracy minimally for scalability.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the provided collection, here are the matching papers and the development trend.
> 
> ## Papers found
> 
> 1. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — One-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association using a single part-to-body center offset on COCO-HumanParts/COCO, CrowdHuman, BodyHands. Built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 anchor-free heads with classification/localization/association branches and task-alignment (TOOD-style CE + regression) losses. Reports AP, Precision, Recall, F1 (e.g., vs ED-Pose: hands/feet F1 ~46–51 vs ~23–24), and ablation of association loss, multi-scale offsets, task alignment.
> 
> 2. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — Spectral analysis of recurrent E/I networks obeying Dale's sign rules (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs). Shows singular-value spectra at initialization matter more than sign constraints for learning; ColEI has multimodal/dispersed spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), while DANN/standard RNNs match quarter-circle random-matrix spectra. Introduces Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) as a pre-training predictor of performance; finds gradient clipping substantially stabilizes ColEI training; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and learning.
> 
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — Theory of the implicit bias of JEPA/self-distillation (MSE-style latent prediction with stop-gradient) vs MAE reconstruction in deep linear networks: JEPA prioritizes "influential" (high regression-coefficient, low-variance) features, with depth strengthening noise suppression; MAE mostly ignores this. Confirmed on ImageNet-1K via CCA of I-JEPA vs MAE features. Related: **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** analyzes cosine-similarity behavior of InfoNCE-style objectives (optimal negative-pair similarity, minibatch variance) on CIFAR-10/100 and proposes a variance-reduction auxiliary loss.
> 
> 4. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — Compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit for memory-efficient training/fine-tuning. Uses smaller blocks (B128) for the first moment, rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear quantization (or factorization) for the second moment. Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD (F1 ~94.5), ImageNet (Swin-T), WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA), saving up to 57.7% memory; discusses combination with LoRA (freezing pretrained weights, tuning low-rank parameters), sharding, and offloading.
> 
> 5. **Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning that Transfers using Random Features (RaMP, ICLR 2024)** — Self-supervised RL that transfers across reward functions: pretrains multi-step "Q-basis" functions on offline unlabeled trajectories using random features as pseudo-rewards (implicit dynamics modeling, no autoregressive compounding error), then fits the new reward via linear regression and plans with MPC. Validated on Meta-World, Hopper, D'Claw; NN random features outperform polynomial/Gaussian ones; adapts faster than MBPO/PETS/SF/CQL.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> 
> - **From multi-stage/heuristic to one-stage, unified, end-to-end designs**: PBADet replaces two-stage heuristics and anchor-based, body-to-part offset schemes with a single anchor-free part-to-body offset plus task-aligned training; RaMP likewise replaces explicit model-based dynamics (with compounding error) by implicit, model-free Q-basis learning plus simple planning.
> - **From empirical training to principled spectral/theoretical analysis**: the Dale's-Law work diagnoses optimization failures via singular-value spectra at initialization (NSE as a diagnostic), while the JEPA work explains SSL behavior through exactly solvable deep linear models; both use tractable analyses (deep linear networks, random-matrix theory) to guide practical architecture/objective design.
> - **Growing emphasis on memory/parameter efficiency**: optimizer states are pushed from 8-bit to 4-bit via better quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization), designed to be lossless in fine-tuning and complementary to LoRA/PEFT, sharding, and offloading.
> - **Shift toward task-agnostic/self-supervised pretraining and fast adaptation**: JEPA self-distillation and RaMP's random-feature pseudo-rewards both decouple representation/dynamics learning from the downstream task/objective, enabling transfer via linear regression, planning, or feature reweighting.
> - **Shared practical approximations and evaluation**: linear models/regression as analysis or recombination tools, MPC for planning, quantization for memory, gradient clipping for unstable spectra, and standardized metrics (AP, F1, Precision, MMLU, perplexity/accuracy) for validation.

### paperscope:trend:318 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle efficient and interpretable deep learning across perception and physical modeling, including: anchor-free part–body association in vision; training EI-constrained recurrent nets under Dale’s principle via spectral analysis; non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) that biases latent feature embeddings toward high-influence dimensions; memory-light optimizers that compress Adam/AdamW states to sub-byte levels for parameter-efficient Transformer fine-tuning (e.g., low-rank adapters end-to-end); and adaptive hierarchical graph simulators for time-series meshes. I’m looking for work that discusses squared-error metrics (MSE), cosine-similarity style objectives, cross-entropy loss, regularization trade-offs (quadratic penalties/Pareto), shallow predictors vs. feedforward classifiers, and reports Precision/F1/AUROC. **Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Across the five papers, a clear trend emerges toward methods that are both more efficient and more interpretable, with increasingly adaptive architectures that scale across perception (vision) and physical modeling. Key developments are:
> 
> 1) Replacing hand-crafted structures with adaptive, learned hierarchies
> - Physical simulation: EvoMesh learns time-evolving, data-adaptive graph hierarchies via differentiable Gumbel-Softmax node selection, improving long-range dependency modeling over fixed, precomputed hierarchies. This adaptivity reduces rollout errors (e.g., RMSE-All decreases vs. static multiscale baselines) and generalizes better to out-of-distribution mesh resolutions.
> - Perception (vision detection): PBADet moves from anchor-based, multi-stage association to one-stage, anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset. This reduces representation length (e.g., 5+K+2 vs. 6+K+2K) and scales seamlessly to more parts without degrading performance.
> 
> 2) Direction-aware and spectrum-aware message/feature propagation for interpretability and stability
> - Physical simulation: EvoMesh’s anisotropic message passing (learned edge-level weights) makes inter- and intra-level propagation direction-specific, and the learned weights align with regions of high temporal variation in physical quantities, increasing interpretability of information flow.
> - Dale’s Law-constrained RNNs: Spectral analysis identifies singular value distribution (and normalized SVD entropy) as the primary driver of learning quality, more so than sign constraints themselves. Designing EI RNNs (DANN variants) to have unimodal, clustered spectra improves stability and performance (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition) and clarifies why classic EI partitions struggled.
> 
> 3) Non-contrastive self-distillation that targets informative features
> - Representation learning: Deep linear analyses of JEPA vs. MAE show that both use squared-error objectives, but JEPA’s StopGrad self-distillation in latent space has an implicit bias toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients), avoiding noisy, high-variance components favored by MAE-style pixel reconstruction. This explains faster learning of semantic, predictive features without negative pairs, and clarifies when depth (encoder L) amplifies the bias toward influential directions.
> 
> 4) Memory-light optimization to scale training and fine-tuning
> - Optimizers: 4-bit Adam/AdamW states reduce training memory and communication costs (e.g., up to ~57.7% total memory reduction with offloading/FSDP in instruction tuning), while retaining accuracy across NLU (GLUE), QA (SQuAD EM/F1), image classification (Swin-T on ImageNet), machine translation (Transformer-Base on WMT14), and instruction tuning (LLaMA). Robust quantization is achieved by smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization (row/column-wise scales), and zero-point exclusion for the second moment; these address outlier patterns and the instability of near-zero moments. The approach is compatible with parameter-efficient regimes (e.g., LoRA codebase used in GPT-2 experiments), enabling larger models under fixed budgets.
> 
> 5) Methodological shifts in losses, metrics, and scalability
> - Losses/objectives: Squared-error (MSE) dominates in JEPA and physical simulation (RMSE); PBADet blends classification (softmax) with localization (IoU, DFL) and a task-alignment loss (α, β trade-offs between classification and localization); association loss uses L1 distances to learned offsets.
> - Metrics: Vision reports AP, MR-2, and mismatching rates; PBADet additionally reports Precision/Recall/F1 for part-body association. Simulation reports RMSE for one-step and long rollouts.
> - Benchmarks and architectures: Trends span YOLO and Transformer (Swin) in vision, MeshGraphNets-style GNNs in simulation, and RNN/Transformer families for sequence tasks; sequential MNIST and Penn Tree Bank capture time-series modeling in the Dale’s Law work.
> 
> Overall trajectory:
> - From fixed, heuristic structures and isotropic aggregation to data-adaptive, anisotropic hierarchies (PBADet, EvoMesh) that improve scalability and accuracy.
> - From opaque performance gaps to spectrum-level diagnostics (normalized SVD entropy) that predict stability and learning quality in EI-constrained recurrent nets.
> - From reconstruction-heavy SSL to JEPA-style latent prediction objectives that favor high-influence, lower-variance features with well-characterized training dynamics.
> - From 8-bit to 4-bit optimizer states that preserve convergence and downstream accuracy, making large Transformers and GNN-based simulators practical under tight memory budgets.
> These changes collectively deliver parameter/memory efficiency, better long-range modeling, and greater interpretability, while maintaining or improving task metrics across detection, simulation, and sequence modeling.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the context, the five papers matching your topics are:
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free part–body association using a single part-to-body center offset; reports AP and Precision/Recall/F1 versus ED-Pose.
> 2. **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) — training EI (excitatory–inhibitory) recurrent nets under Dale's principle; shows spectral properties (normalized SVD entropy) matter more than sign constraints, evaluated on MNIST-style and language tasks.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) analyzed via deep linear networks; latent-space prediction is biased toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features, with depth strengthening noise suppression vs. MAE.
> 4. **"4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW states from 8-bit to 4-bit (sub-byte) via smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, and factorization; lossless fine-tuning of RoBERTa/LLaMA and complements LoRA-style parameter-efficient tuning.
> 5. **EvoMesh** (ICML 2025) — adaptive hierarchical graph simulator for mesh-based time-series physical simulation, learning time-evolving hierarchies via differentiable (Gumbel-Softmax) node selection and anisotropic message passing, outperforming fixed-hierarchy GNNs by ~20%.
> 
> **Development trend:** Across the set, methods move from hand-designed, heuristic, or static components toward learned, adaptive, end-to-end differentiable designs: multi-stage/anchor-based detection → one-stage anchor-free offsets; sign-constrained EI nets → spectral analysis (SVD entropy) as a diagnostic and design guide; empirical SSL → exact characterization of implicit bias (why latent-space prediction is efficient); 8-bit → 4-bit optimizer states driven by moment-pattern analysis; and fixed multi-scale graph hierarchies → data- and time-adaptive hierarchies. Theory increasingly guides architecture (spectra, implicit bias), while efficiency (memory, one-stage inference, adaptive sparsity) is a common thread spanning both perception (vision, SSL) and physical modeling (mesh simulation).

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five matching papers and the development trend of their methods:
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part–body association via a single part-to-body center offset (vs. two-stage/anchor-based BPJDet, BodyHands), with task-alignment learning; reports AP, precision/recall/F1.
> 2. **Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — EI-constrained RNNs; shows learning quality is driven by the initial singular-value spectrum (normalized SVD entropy), not sign constraints; cross-entropy (MNIST/PTB) and MSE (adding) benchmarks.
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024) — deep-linear analysis of non-contrastive self-distillation: JEPA's squared-error latent objective biases features toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) dimensions, unlike MAE; CCA on ImageNet.
> 4. **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4 bits (rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization), near-lossless vs. 32-bit on GLUE/ImageNet/SQuAD/LLaMA fine-tuning; cross-entropy, F1, BLEU metrics; complements LoRA-style PEFT.
> 5. **EvoMesh** (ICML 2025) — adaptive hierarchical graph simulator for time-series meshes: learns time-evolving multi-resolution hierarchies with anisotropic message passing and differentiable (Gumbel-Softmax) node selection; MSE/RMSE-based rollout evaluation.
> 
> **Development trend:**
> - **From hand-crafted to learned/adaptive structure:** PBADet drops anchors and multi-stage heuristics; EvoMesh replaces fixed, pre-computed mesh hierarchies with data-adaptive, time-evolving ones. Structure is increasingly learned end-to-end.
> - **From constraints to principled analysis:** Dale's-Law work reframes the problem from sign constraints to spectral conditioning (NSE as a diagnostic), and JEPA analysis identifies the implicit bias of latent-space prediction — both shift design from "what to enforce" to "what dynamics/features to bias toward."
> - **From reconstruction to predictive latent objectives:** JEPA moves away from input-space reconstruction (MAE) toward latent self-distillation biased to high-influence features, improving perception efficiency.
> - **From precision to efficiency without loss:** 4-bit optimizer states push memory compression from 32→8→4 bits with near-lossless convergence, enabling larger Transformers under fixed memory and interoperating with parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
> - **Across the stack, the trend is efficiency + interpretability:** simpler/adaptive architectures (anchor-free detection, evolving hierarchies), theoretically explained learning dynamics (spectral, implicit-bias analyses), and sub-byte training memory — spanning perception (PBADet, JEPA) and physical modeling (EvoMesh, Dale's RNNs), with benchmarks from MNIST/ResNet-scale to large LLMs.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Integrated development trends across the five methods that match your pipeline components show a clear, time‑ordered shift toward end‑to‑end, adaptive, and resource‑efficient designs, with stronger theoretical guidance on what makes them stable and interpretable:
> 
> 1) Reliable, scalable hand/face→person association (HMI)
> • Trend in detection/association design (2018–2024): two‑stage, heuristic association → one‑stage, joint detection with compact targets → anchor‑free, part‑to‑body offsets.
> • Representative progression:
>   – Earlier: heuristics or two‑stage matching; anchor‑based joint detectors needed many offsets and degraded with more parts.
>   – PBADet (ICLR 2024): anchor‑free one‑stage detector adds a single part→body center offset per part, using multi‑scale feature maps and task‑alignment learning. This reduces representation length, simplifies decoding, scales to any number of parts, and is robust when some parts are invisible. Evaluations report AP/conditional accuracy/joint AP, mMR−2, and precision/recall/F1 (vs multi‑person pose), showing consistent gains. 
> • Takeaway for HMI: the field is converging on compact, anchor‑free, multi‑scale detectors that keep association explicit in the output target (center offsets), improving scalability and robustness under clutter.
> 
> 2) Memory‑tight fine‑tuning of large Transformers
> • Trend in optimizer states (2022–2023): 8‑bit states → 4‑bit states with targeted quantization and factorization, retaining full‑precision accuracy.
> • Representative progression:
>   – 8‑bit Adam required special embedding reparameterizations; block‑wise quantization with large blocks.
>   – 4‑bit (NeurIPS 2023): identify the second‑moment zero‑point failure mode and fix it (DE‑0 or linear mapping) while shrinking blocks (e.g., B128) and introducing rank‑1 normalization (row/column) to handle heterogeneous outliers; optionally factorize the second moment. Results: near lossless AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, MT, image classification, and instruction tuning (LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B), with large GPU memory savings and throughput gains under offloading—without needing special “stable embeddings.”
> • Takeaway for LoRA fine‑tuning: the trend is toward 4‑bit, zero‑aware, small‑block + rank‑1 schemes (and factorized second moment where applicable) that let you fine‑tune big Transformers within strict memory budgets while matching 32‑bit accuracy.
> 
> 3) Why self‑distilled representations focus on useful signals (JEPA vs MAE)
> • Trend in SSL objective choice (2021–2024): reconstruction (MAE) → joint‑embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) with stop‑grad.
> • Mechanistic insight (NeurIPS 2024): In deep linear models, JEPA exhibits an implicit bias toward high‑influence features (large regression coefficients), whereas MAE prioritizes high‑variance/co‑varying features (which can be noisy). Depth amplifies JEPA’s bias and speeds learning of predictive, low‑variance (semantic) features; critical learning times quantify the effect. Empirical studies (e.g., CCA on ImageNet‑64) match the theory.
> • Takeaway for representation design: using a JEPA‑style latent prediction objective (with stop‑grad) explains—and leverages—why self‑distillation sheds noisy pixels and locks onto task‑useful signals, especially as encoder depth increases.
> 
> 4) Biologically consistent RNNs (Dale’s Law) without losing performance
> • Trend in EI‑constrained training (2019–2023): naïve column‑sign constraints (ColEI) → architectures and initializations guided by spectral properties (e.g., DANNs), with stability predicted by singular‑value statistics.
> • Mechanistic insight (NeurIPS 2023): ColEI’s poor learning stems mainly from multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra (not just sign constraints). Making spectra unimodal/clustered (as in standard RNNs/DANNs) restores performance. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts trainability; network size and E:I ratio jointly shape spectra; gradient clipping helps.
> • Takeaway for EI‑consistent RNNs: enforce EI signs but control spectra (initialization/size/E:I ratio) to keep performance; NSE provides a pre‑training check for stability.
> 
> 5) Adaptive mesh simulators with evolving graph hierarchies
> • Trend in mesh‑based GNN simulators (2021–2025): single‑level message passing → fixed, precomputed hierarchies (bi‑stride, clustering, triangulation) → fully differentiable, data‑adaptive, time‑evolving hierarchies with learned anisotropy.
> • Representative progression:
>   – Fixed hierarchies (MGN, Lino’22, BSMS’23, Eagle’23, HCMT’24) improved long‑range propagation but were static and data‑independent.
>   – EvoMesh (ICML 2025): learns node‑selection probabilities via Gumbel‑Softmax (DiffSELECT) to build per‑step hierarchies; uses anisotropic message passing to learn directional weights intra‑ and inter‑level (REDUCE/EXPAND reuse learned weights); shows consistent RMSE reductions in one‑step and long‑rollouts, better OOD resolution behavior, and works on time‑varying meshes.
> • Takeaway for simulation: the field is moving to end‑to‑end differentiable, context‑aware hierarchy evolution and learned anisotropy, which strengthens long‑range coupling and generalization.
> 
> Cross‑cutting patterns and metrics you can reuse
> • Objectives/losses: L2/MSE‑style dynamics losses (EvoMesh; JEPA theory), classification cross‑entropy plus IoU/DFL for detection heads (PBADet). 
> • Optimizers: Adam/AdamW remain standard; compressed 4‑bit states now viable at scale. 
> • Metrics: 
>   – Detection/association: AP, mMR−2, conditional accuracy; Precision/Recall/F1 used when comparing to pose estimators.
>   – Dynamics: RMSE for one‑step and long‑horizon rollouts.
> • Scalability: each area replaced hand‑crafted, fixed structures with compact targets (PBADet), compressed states (4‑bit/Factor), implicit‑bias‑aware objectives (JEPA), spectrum‑aware EI designs (NSE), and differentiable graph evolution (EvoMesh).
> 
> Practical mapping to your pipeline
> • HMI association: adopt a one‑stage, anchor‑free, part→body‑offset head (PBADet) over multi‑stage matchers for accuracy/efficiency and simpler post‑processing.
> • Memory‑tight LoRA: pair LoRA with 4‑bit AdamW (small blocks, DE‑0/linear for v, rank‑1 normalization; factorized v where possible) to keep accuracy while fitting in tight GPU memory.
> • Representation learning: prefer JEPA‑style self‑distillation (stop‑grad) over pure reconstruction when you want features to ignore pixel noise; deepen the encoder to amplify the bias toward predictive features.
> • EI RNNs: enforce Dale’s Law but target unimodal/clustered singular‑value spectra (high NSE), adjust E:I ratio/width, and clip gradients—this preserves biological plausibility without sacrificing task performance.
> • Physics: run an adaptive, differentiable hierarchy (EvoMesh) with anisotropic intra/inter‑level propagation to capture long‑range, time‑varying dependencies; evaluate with RMSE for short/long rollouts.
> 
> Time‑line summary of the shift
> • 2021: Single‑level mesh GNNs (MGN); two‑stage/anchor detectors; ColEI RNNs struggle.
> • 2022–2023: Fixed hierarchies (bi‑stride, clustering, triangulation); 8‑bit → 4‑bit optimizers; DANNs and spectral analysis explain EI performance.
> • 2024: Anchor‑free, compact part→body association (PBADet); HCMT adds attention; JEPA theory explains implicit bias toward semantic (low‑variance) features.
> • 2025: EvoMesh makes hierarchies fully data‑adaptive and time‑evolving with anisotropic propagation, improving accuracy and generalization on complex, changing meshes.
> 
> These trends jointly support a resource‑constrained, end‑to‑end pipeline that (i) associates parts to people robustly, (ii) fine‑tunes large Transformers within tight memory using 4‑bit optimizers, (iii) relies on JEPA‑style self‑distillation to emphasize useful signals, (iv) keeps recurrent models biologically consistent by controlling spectra, and (v) runs adaptive, hierarchy‑evolving mesh simulators—evaluated with the MSE/CE losses and tracked via Precision/F1/AUROC or RMSE as appropriate.

**naive 最终答案**

> **结论：没有单一论文端到端覆盖这五条策略，但每条需求都有对应工作，且整体方法呈“从手工/静态/高精度/分阶段”向“自适应/动态/低比特/一体化”演进的趋势。**
> 
> **1) 手/脸与人身的可靠关联（HMI）— PBADet（ICLR 2024）**
> 趋势：从多阶段、锚点式（DARN、JointDet、BFJDet、Hier-R-CNN、Detector-in-Detector）演进到**单阶段、无锚点**；表示从“body-to-part”扩展表示（BPJDet，15维）转为更紧凑的“part-to-body”中心偏移（PBADet，10维），更简洁、可扩展、精度更高（AP、Precision/Recall/F1 提升显著）。
> 
> **2) LoRA + 压缩态优化器低显存微调 — 《4-bit Optimizers》(NeurIPS 2023)**
> 趋势：优化器状态从 32-bit → 8-bit 分块量化（Dettmers）→ **4-bit**（更小块 B128、融合行/列信息、第二矩去零点的线性量化与 Rank-1 分解），并与 LoRA 结合用于 LLaMA 等大模型微调，精度媲美 32-bit AdamW 且省显存最多 57.7%。
> 
> **3) 自蒸馏表征为何聚焦有用信号而非噪声像素 — 《Why JEPA…》(NeurIPS 2024)**
> 趋势：在“JEPA 隐空间预测”vs“MAE 像素重建”对比中，用深度线性网络动力学揭示隐式偏差——JEPA 偏向高影响（高 ρ）特征、抑制低方差/噪声特征，且**深度增强降噪能力**，从理论上解释自蒸馏表征比重建式方法更语义化。
> 
> **4) 生物一致的兴奋/抑制（Dale 定律）RNN — 《Why Dale's Law…》(NeurIPS 2023)**
> 趋势：从不含 E/I 约束的标准 RNN → 简单列约束（ColEI，学习差）→ 推广的 **Dale's ANN（DANN）** 递推化（E/I 投影重参数化），在不违背 Dale 定律下恢复性能。关键发现：性能由**初始谱性质**（单峰聚集奇异值、归一化 SVD 熵）决定而非符号约束，梯度裁剪可缓解差距。
> 
> **5) 随时间的自适应网格物理仿真图层次演化 — EvoMesh（ICML 2025）**
> 趋势：从手工/静态、启发式下采样的固定层次图（MGN、BSMS-GNN、HCMT）演进到**可微节点选择（Gumbel-Softmax）+ 各向异性消息传递（AMP）+ REDUCE/EXPAND 跨层传播**的时变、数据自适应图层次，端到端训练，平均比固定层次模型提升约 20%，并对时变网格/新分辨率具泛化性。
> 
> **关于评价指标**：MSE/RMSE（EvoMesh 物理预测）、交叉熵（4-bit 优化器的语言任务）、嵌入空间余弦相似度（对比/自蒸馏表征学习，如 JEPA、对比学习）、Precision/F1（PBADet、CEGA）都有对应工作采用；这些论文各自验证了相应策略，但没有一篇同时整合全部五条流水线。

**community 最终答案**

> **Are there works covering these strategies end-to-end?** No — the collection contains no single work that covers all five strategies in one integrated robotics pipeline. Each requirement is addressed by a separate paper:
> 
> 1. **Hand/face→person association (HMI)** — PBADet (`08b70bc…`): one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association (head/face/hands/feet) for HCI/robotics; reports AP, Precision/Recall/F1, mMR⁻².
> 2. **LoRA + compressed-state optimizers under tight GPU memory** — "4-bit Optimizers" (`8d5e14558f…`): 4-bit quantized Adam/AdamW optimizer states, applied to LLaMA fine-tuning, explicitly compatible with LoRA (freezing pretrained weights), up to ~57.7% memory savings.
> 3. **Self-distillation focusing on useful vs. noisy pixels** — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (`40fde037…`): deep-linear analysis of JEPA self-distillation, showing an implicit bias toward high-influence, low-variance (semantic) features and suppression of noisy features vs. MAE.
> 4. **Biologically consistent (E/I) recurrent models without losing performance** — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (`e63a94c4…`): explains why sign-constrained ColEI RNNs learn poorly and how recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) retain performance; identifies spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values) as the deciding factor.
> 5. **Adaptive mesh physics simulators with evolving graph hierarchies** — EvoMesh (`8eb80640…`): GNN mesh simulation with fully differentiable, time-evolving graph hierarchies and anisotropic message passing; evaluated with MSE/RMSE.
> 
> Your planned evaluation signals (MSE, cross-entropy/BCE, cosine similarity in embedding space, Precision/F1/AUROC) also appear across these and related papers (e.g., cosine embedding similarity analysis `160e1407…`; BCE in `c5ca0fc…`; AUC in DiffusionFake `fc4f3d1…`), but never combined in one work.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> 
> - **Part-body association (1):** Two-stage heuristics (pose-based arm-joint matching, BodyHands' learned association network) → one-stage anchor-based joint detection with per-part body-to-part offsets (BPJDet) → one-stage **anchor-free** with a single part-to-body center offset (PBADet), moving toward simpler, more scalable, unified detection+association.
> - **Memory-efficient fine-tuning (2):** Full-precision 32-bit optimizer states → block-wise 8-bit quantization (Dettmers) → **4-bit states** using smaller blocks, rank-1/row-column quantization, and zero-point-excluded linear quantizers, matched with parameter-efficient LoRA for lossless fine-tuning on LLaMA-7B–33B.
> - **Representation learning (3):** Input-space reconstruction (MAE) → **latent self-distillation (JEPA)**; analysis shows predicting in latent space biases toward predictive, low-variance semantic features and deprioritizes noisy pixels — a shift from reconstructing variance to predicting influence, with depth strengthening noise suppression.
> - **Recurrent E/I models (4):** Naive column-sign-constrained EI RNNs (ColEI) → reparameterized **Dale's ANNs (DANN)** that preserve E/I constraints while learning well; the key insight moved from "sign constraints are the problem" to "initial recurrent-weight spectral geometry (unimodal clustered singular values) is what determines learnability," with gradient clipping as a practical remedy.
> - **Mesh simulation (5):** Fixed, hand-crafted/static hierarchies (MGN, BSMS bi-stride, HCMT Delaunay/attention) → **adaptive, data-dependent, time-evolving hierarchies** (EvoMesh) via differentiable node selection and anisotropic message passing, improving long-term accuracy and zero-shot generalization to new mesh resolutions.
> 
> Overall the trend across all five is toward **simpler, unified, data-adaptive designs** (one-stage vs. multi-stage; learned/evolving structures vs. fixed hand-crafted ones; compressed parameter-efficient training) with analysis-driven understanding replacing ad-hoc constraints.

### paperscope:trend:330 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address efficient training and transfer across vision and robotics: anchor-free detectors that associate human parts with their parent bodies on common object benchmarks; active exploration for system identification to estimate masses/friction/articulation for sim-to-real control; low-bit (around 4-bit) optimizer states compatible with stochastic gradient and adaptive-moment methods; spectral analyses of excitatory/inhibitory recurrent nets that respect Dale-like constraints; and non-contrastive self-distillation in joint-embedding SSL (JEPA) that biases feature learning. Prefer works using transformer or residual (e.g., 50-layer) backbones, reporting precision/recall/F1 on COCO-style tasks, and comparing losses like mean-squared versus log-softmax, with support for lightweight adapter fine-tuning (low-rank) and regularization.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Across these five works (NeurIPS 2023–2024, ICLR 2024), a clear trend emerges toward methods that are (i) more sample/memory efficient, (ii) better targeted for transfer (vision ↔ robotics), and (iii) increasingly guided by principled analyses (spectral or information-theoretic) to scale reliably.
> 
> 1) Vision detection: from multi-stage, anchor-based to one-stage, anchor-free with scalable association
> - Earlier body–part association relied on two-stage heuristics or anchor-based heads that grow with the number of parts, degrading performance as part sets expand (cited in PBADet). The 2024 PBADet shifts to a one-stage, anchor-free design that adds a single part-to-body center-offset per location, keeping representation length fixed (5+K+2 vs. 6+K+2K) and scaling gracefully to more parts while improving accuracy on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, and CrowdHuman.
> - Training shifts from independent heads to task-aligned learning (TOOD-inspired), with IoU + DFL + classification and a lightweight association loss. This improves consistency between classification/localization and yields better Pareto behavior on AP vs. association errors (mMR−2) without the complexity of anchor hyperparameters.
> - Backbones migrate toward modern residual/YOLO stacks (comparisons include Faster/RetinaNet/FCOS with R50), and evaluation standardizes on COCO-style APs and, when relevant, precision/recall/F1 for part-level comparisons (e.g., ED-Pose vs. PBADet).
> 
> 2) Robotics sim-to-real: from passive/domain-randomized data to active exploration for one-shot system ID
> - Prior sim-to-real relied heavily on domain randomization; the 2024 ASID reframes transfer as “sim→real→sim→real”: (i) train an exploration policy in sim to maximize Fisher information, (ii) collect a single real trajectory, (iii) identify parameters (e.g., mass, friction, articulation, geometry), (iv) solve tasks in the updated simulator, then (v) zero-shot deploy.
> - The trend is from undirected exploration to targeted exploration that provably increases parameter identifiability (Fisher information). In practice, exploration learned in sim generalizes to real and typically needs only one real episode to build an accurate simulator for downstream control.
> - This enables robust transfer on manipulation tasks (rod balancing, shuffleboard) where policy success depends critically on mass/inertia/friction; naive DR or random exploration underperform, especially for one-shot tasks.
> 
> 3) Training efficiency: from 8-bit to robust 4-bit optimizer states that preserve convergence at scale
> - Earlier low-precision optimizers stopped at 8-bit. The 2023 4-bit optimizers show a shift to 4-bit states for Adam/AdamW by addressing two obstacles: (i) outlier structure (handled via smaller blocks and rank-1 normalization) and (ii) the zero-point failure for second moments (fixed by zero-excluding linear mapping). A hybrid factorized+quantized second moment further cuts memory.
> - Trend: make optimizer states the new scaling lever. This yields comparable accuracy to 32-bit across Transformers for NLU (GLUE), QA (F1 on SQuAD/SQuAD2.0), NLG (BLEU on E2E), vision classification (Swin-T on ImageNet-1k), machine translation (SacreBLEU), and instruction tuning (LLaMA), while materially reducing memory/communication and enabling larger models on fixed hardware (e.g., fine-tuning LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU with FSDP). This dovetails with adapter/fine-tuning workflows and optimizer offloading without changing model architectures.
> 
> 4) Theory-guided stability and scaling: spectral diagnostics for EI-constrained deep recurrent nets
> - Rather than treating Dale’s Law constraints as primarily sign constraints, the 2023 spectral perspective shows performance hinges more on the singular value spectrum at initialization. The field moves from ad-hoc E/I partitioning (ColEI) toward architectures and initializations (recurrent DANNs) that recover unimodal, clustered singular value distributions resembling standard RNNs.
> - A practical trend: use NSE (normalized SVD entropy) as a pre-training diagnostic to predict training behavior. As networks grow (or inhibitory ratios balance), ColEI spectra become less pathological and learning improves; gradient clipping helps, but robust spectral initialization is the main driver. This reframes biological plausibility and stability as a spectrum-shaping problem, not just a constraint problem, guiding scalable design choices.
> 
> 5) Representation learning: from MAE (MSE reconstruction) to non-contrastive JEPA (predictive in latent space)
> - With deep encoders (2024), JEPA-style self-distillation exhibits a distinct implicit bias: it prioritizes high-influence features (high regression coefficients), whereas MAE (MSE reconstruction) prioritizes high-variance/co-varying components—including noisy details. This clarifies why JEPA often reaches semantic features faster in practice, especially with deep encoders and vision backbones.
> - The trend is away from reconstruction loss (MSE) toward latent predictive objectives that avoid collapse via stop-gradients/predictors, with depth amplifying the beneficial bias (and highlighting caution for shallow encoders). Empirically (e.g., I-JEPA vs. MAE on ImageNet-1k), JEPA’s features align more with lower-variance, perception-relevant subspaces.
> 
> Cross-cutting themes
> - Scalability: anchor-free detection (fixed-size heads) scales to more parts; 4-bit optimizers scale models to larger parameter counts on fixed memory; EI-RNNs scale via spectral design (NSE) rather than solely sign constraints; JEPA scales feature quality with encoder depth; ASID scales data-efficiency to real by compressing real interaction to a single trajectory.
> - Transferability and evaluation: COCO-style APs, mMR−2, and precision/recall/F1 remain standard for detection; real-robot success rates (rod/shuffleboard) validate sim-to-real pipelines; NLP/vision MT/CLS/QA/NLG metrics (Accuracy, F1, BLEU, SacreBLEU) validate 4-bit optimizers across Transformers.
> - Losses and regularization: a shift from pure MSE reconstruction (MAE) to JEPA’s predictive latent losses; in detection, IoU/DFL/classification + task alignment improve head interaction; for EI-RNNs, gradient clipping and spectral radius control help but spectrum shape (unimodal clustering) is the decisive regularizer.
> 
> Overall development trend: Methods are converging on principled designs that reduce resource needs (one-stage detection heads, 4-bit optimizer states), target information where it matters (Fisher-information exploration; JEPA’s influential-feature bias), and use spectral or information-theoretic tools to predict and stabilize training (NSE, Fisher). These changes—appearing in 2023–2024—improve scalability, enable larger/stronger Transformer or residual pipelines under fixed hardware, and make sim-to-real transfer and real-world deployment more reliable with far less real data.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, the five papers that collectively address your topics are:
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) – One-stage, anchor-free part-body association detector. Extends anchor-free object representation (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) with a single part-to-body center offset, replacing BPJDet's cumbersome body-to-part offsets. Uses task-alignment learning; reports AP on COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman and precision/recall/F1 (e.g., hands/feet vs. ED-Pose on COCO), and extends to animal datasets.
> 2. **ASID** (ICLR 2024) – Active exploration for system identification in robotic manipulation. Decouples exploration/exploitation: trains a Fisher-information-maximizing exploration policy in simulation, deploys it once in the real world, identifies mass/friction/articulation parameters via optimization-based system identification, then trains a task policy in the corrected simulator for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer (rod balancing 6/9 vs DR 0/9; shuffleboard 7/10 vs 3/10).
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023) – Pushes optimizer-state precision from 8-bit to 4-bit for SGD(M)/Adam/AdamW via compression-based framework. Key ideas: smaller block size (B128) for the first moment; zero-point-excluded linear mapping and rank-1 normalization for the second moment, optionally factorized. Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E-NLG/WMT and enables LLaMA-7B training on one 80GB GPU.
> 4. **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023) – Spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory recurrent nets respecting Dale's law. Shows ColEI networks fail not mainly due to sign constraints but due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (from rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure); DANN RNNs keep unimodal random-matrix-like spectra and learn well. Introduces normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a pre-training predictor of performance.
> 5. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024) – Theoretical (deep linear network) analysis of non-contrastive self-distillation in joint-embedding SSL. Shows JEPA implicitly biases learning toward high-influence/low-variance ("slow") features, with depth strengthening noise suppression, unlike MAE which prioritizes by eigenvalue; verified on ImageNet via CCA with I-JEPA vs MAE.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> 
> - **From heuristics to principled, minimal representations**: PBADet replaces multi-stage/anchor-based detectors (BPJDet, Hier R-CNN) with a one-stage anchor-free single-offset formulation that scales to any number of parts.
> - **From blind data collection to targeted, information-theoretic exploration**: ASID shifts from domain randomization/random exploration toward Fisher-information-driven exploration, decoupling exploration from exploitation for efficient sim-to-real.
> - **From 8-bit to 4-bit and beyond via finer quantization statistics**: optimizer-state compression evolves from block-wise 8-bit to 4-bit using smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, and factorization—while keeping convergence lossless.
> - **From sign constraints to spectral conditioning**: the EI-RNN literature moves from "why sign constraints hurt" to identifying initial spectral properties (unimodality, NSE) as the true determinant of learnability, guiding better initializations/architectures.
> - **From empirical SSL to mechanistic understanding**: JEPA research progresses from architecture tricks (stop-gradient, predictors) to exact analyses of training dynamics, revealing implicit biases (feature prioritization, noise suppression) that explain why latent-space prediction beats pixel reconstruction.
> - **Cross-cutting**: works increasingly favor lightweight, parameter-efficient transfer (LoRA/low-rank adapters, fine-tuning/freezing search, L1/L2 regularization like LDReg), transformer/residual (ResNet-50, ViT, Swin) backbones, and rigorous reporting on COCO-style benchmarks (AP, precision/recall/F1).
> 
> Note: some preference criteria (e.g., explicit MSE-vs-log-softmax loss comparisons, low-rank adapter fine-tuning in the detection paper) are only partially or indirectly supported in the retrieved context; the optimizer paper discusses LoRA and SGD/Adam compatibility, and LDReg provides L1/L2 regularization for SSL.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, five papers collectively address these areas. Their development trend:
> 
> **1. PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — One-stage, anchor-free part-body association detection. It extends FCOS/TOOD-style anchor-free dense prediction (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) with a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO-WholeBody, COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman with AP, precision/recall/F1, and joint AP. Uses task-alignment learning; beats multi-stage/anchor-based BPJDet and HierR-CNN.
> 
> **2. ASID (ICLR 2024)** — Active exploration for system identification: trains a Fisher-information-maximizing exploration policy in simulation, deploys it once in reality, identifies mass/friction/stiffness/articulation, then trains the task policy in the corrected simulator for zero-shot sim-to-real transfer (beats domain randomization, random exploration, learned estimators).
> 
> **3. 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — Pushes optimizer-state precision from 8-bit to 4-bit, compatible with both SGD(M) and Adam/AdamW, via smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-exclusion, and factorized (low-rank) second moment. Matches 32-bit accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings; related to delta-tuning/low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
> 
> **4. Dale's Law spectral perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — Shows Dale-constrained EI RNNs (ColEI) learn poorly mainly because of the *initial recurrent-weight spectrum* (multimodal/dispersed singular values from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), not sign constraints; DANN EI RNNs match standard RNN spectra and learn well. Normalized SVD entropy predicts performance.
> 
> **5. JEPA self-distillation (NeurIPS 2024)** — Deep-linear analysis of non-contrastive self-distillation (BYOL/I-JEPA with stop-grad) showing JEPA implicitly biases toward high-influence, low-variance features and suppresses noise (unlike MAE's reconstruction bias); depth strengthens this. Verified on ImageNet via CCA. Companion work LDReg regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality to prevent collapse.
> 
> **Overall development trend:** methods move from multi-stage/heuristic pipelines to **streamlined unified one-stage formulations** (PBADet); from brute-force domain randomization to **minimal-data, information-driven sim-to-real transfer** (ASID); from full-precision to **memory-efficient, low-bit/factorized optimization with adapter-style fine-tuning** (4-bit optimizers); and from trial-and-error to **principled spectral/implicit-bias analyses guiding architecture and regularization** (Dale's-law RNNs, JEPA feature learning). Collectively they emphasize efficiency, transferability, and theoretically grounded design across vision detection, robotics control, and self-supervised representation learning.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five methods point to a coherent pipeline for a memory‑limited manipulation robot that watches humans and then interacts with objects, with clear time, scalability, and methodological shifts evident in the cited literature. 1) Perception front‑end: From anchor‑based, multi‑stage association to one‑stage, anchor‑free detectors. • Trend: 2017–2020 works (e.g., Mask R‑CNN derivatives, Hier R‑CNN) evolved to 2023–2024 one‑stage, anchor‑free designs. PBADet (ICLR 2024) replaces body‑to‑part offsets with a single part‑to‑body 2D center offset, reducing representation length from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2 and improving scalability as parts K increase. • Scalability: Multi‑scale anchor‑free heads generalize across parts and categories (humans, quadrupeds), with reduced post‑processing complexity and consistent one‑to‑one part‑to‑body assignments. • Evaluation trend: Beyond COCO AP series, PBADet reports mMR‑2 and adds precision/recall/F1 (vs ED‑Pose) to quantify association reliability; task‑aligned training (IoU loss, DFL, CE classification, plus L1 center‑offset association loss) regularizes detection‑association coupling. • Over time: Anchor‑free detectors proved more robust and flexible; ablations show task alignment and multi‑scale supervision are increasingly favored over anchor boxes. 2) Sim‑to‑real manipulation: From domain randomization to targeted system identification via active exploration. • Trend: ASID (ICLR 2024) shifts from training for robustness (domain randomization) to first maximizing Fisher information to collect highly informative real trajectories, then performing optimization‑based system identification (e.g., REPS/CEM) to refine a simulator, and finally training the downstream policy in the updated sim for zero‑shot transfer. • Data efficiency and scalability: Policies learned with PPO in a randomized sim are transferred once to real to collect a single informative episode; refined sims enable task learning with minimal labels and minimal real data (rod balancing, sphere striking, articulated opening, shuffleboard). • Over time: The design emphasis moves from broad DR to targeted parameter estimation (mass, friction, stiffness, articulation) with small real‑data budgets—improving sim‑to‑real reliability without sustained real‑world training. 3) Training efficiency under memory constraints: From 8‑bit to 4‑bit optimizers with quantization/factorization tailored to outlier patterns. • Trend: Dettmers‑style 8‑bit block‑wise quantization (2019–2022) is pushed to 4‑bit (NeurIPS 2023) by (a) smaller block sizes (e.g., B128) to track local outliers, (b) rank‑1 normalization (row/column scales per tensor entry), and (c) linear mappings that exclude zero to avoid second‑moment zero‑point failure. • Scalability: 4‑bit Adam/AdamW/SGD maintain comparable accuracy across NLU, MT, and vision tasks while cutting total training memory, enabling larger backbones and LoRA‑style low‑rank fine‑tuning on embedded GPUs; factorizing the second moment further reduces memory with small accuracy cost. • Over time: Focus shifts from uniform block quantization to outlier‑aware, tensor‑structure‑aware schemes and hybrid quantization+factorization, making low‑precision optimizers practical beyond 8‑bit. 4) Recurrent controller design under biological constraints: From sign‑constraint focus to spectral‑property control in EI networks. • Trend: Dale’s ANNs extended to recurrent architectures (NeurIPS 2023) show learning performance depends more on the singular‑value spectrum than on EI sign constraints alone. • Scalability: Spectral clustering (high normalized SVD entropy) improves learning; larger networks and balanced E/I ratios yield unimodal, compact singular‑value spectra and better stability; small networks or low inhibitory proportion produce multimodal, dispersed spectra and higher variance. • Over time: Guidance moves from enforcing sign rules to designing initializations/architectures that shape spectra, diagnosing pathology via normalized SVD entropy, and favoring EI architectures (e.g., DANNs) whose spectra resemble standard RNNs. 5) SSL pretraining for perception and downstream control: From input reconstruction (MAE) to latent prediction (JEPA) with self‑distillation and StopGrad. • Trend: Deep linear analyses (NeurIPS 2024) show JEPA objectives (latent‑space MSE with StopGrad) prioritize high‑influence (high regression‑coefficient) features—often more semantic—while MAE reconstruction prioritizes high‑variance features. Depth amplifies JEPA’s bias toward informative features; shallow encoders reduce this difference. • Scalability: Joint‑embedding SSL increasingly favored for perception tasks; JEPA‑style pretraining supports Transformer/ResNet backbones and adapts efficiently with low‑rank adapters (LoRA used in downstream GPT‑2 fine‑tuning in the 4‑bit optimizer study). • Over time: SSL shifted from input‑space MSE (MAE) to latent‑space predictive MSE (JEPA) plus collapse‑prevention (StopGrad), aligning feature selection with downstream discrimination. Cross‑method loss and regularization comparisons observed in practice • Detection vs representation learning losses: PBADet’s classification (CE) + IoU/DFL + association L1 pairs well with anchor‑free architectures, improving AP/mMR‑2 and precision/recall/F1; JEPA and MAE use mean‑squared losses in latent vs input spaces, respectively—JEPA’s latent prediction reduces sensitivity to unpredictable pixels compared to MAE. • Regularization trends: Task‑alignment in PBADet acts as a form of joint optimization regularization; JEPA avoids collapse via StopGrad (and related spectral/weight regularization in the literature); 4‑bit optimizers stabilize second‑moment quantization by excluding zero and using rank‑1 normalization; EI controllers use spectral metrics (NSE) to regularize architecture/initialization choices. Overall trajectory and integration • Time pattern: 2017–2020 multi‑stage/anchor‑based detection and broad DR give way to 2021–2024 anchor‑free association (PBADet), JEPA‑style SSL, targeted active exploration for system ID (ASID), and 4‑bit/low‑rank training for embedded deployment; recurrent EI controllers shift from sign constraints to spectrum‑aware design. • Scalability: Methods converge toward designs that scale—anchor‑free representations scale with parts; system ID scales across tasks with minimal real data; 4‑bit optimizers scale models within fixed memory; EI controller guidance scales with network depth/size; JEPA scales to large Transformers and adapts with LoRA. • Field change: A pipeline emerges—JEPA‑pretrained backbones (latent MSE), anchor‑free detectors for hand/face association (CE/IoU/DFL/L1), ASID’s Fisher‑max exploration for sim‑to‑real parameter estimation, spectrum‑aware recurrent control respecting EI rules, and 4‑bit optimizers enabling on‑board training/fine‑tuning. This reflects a broader shift from brute‑force robustness to targeted information acquisition, from heavy models to memory‑efficient training, and from rigid biological constraints to spectral design principles.

**naive 最终答案**

> **Recommended works (all from the provided collection):**
> 
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** – One-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association detector. A single part-to-body center offset replaces BPJDet-style body-to-part offsets; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts/COCO val and BodyHands with precision/recall/F1 (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs ED-Pose 31.51), plus joint AP and conditional accuracy ablations.
> 
> 2. **ASID: Active Exploration for System Identification (ICLR 2024)** – Sim-to-real pipeline that trains a Fisher-information-maximizing exploration policy in sim, deploys it once in the real world, identifies physical/geometry/articulation parameters (REPS/CEM), then trains the task policy in the corrected simulator for zero-shot transfer (rod balancing 6/9 vs DR 0/9).
> 
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** – Compresses SGD(M)/Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit via smaller blocks (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, and factorized second moment; ~57.7% memory savings, matching 32-bit accuracy, enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU (and a quantized-SGD convergence proof).
> 
> 4. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** – Guidance for recurrent controllers with excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints: the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints; ColEI column-sign partitioning gives multimodal spectra, while DANN EI parameterization matches standard RNN spectra; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts training success.
> 
> 5. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** – Deep-linear analysis of JEPA self-distillation implicit bias: JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high regression coefficient) features and suppresses noise with encoder depth, unlike MAE; ImageNet I-JEPA experiments confirm faster alignment with the perceptual low-variance subspace. For pretraining transformer/residual backbones and low-rank adaptation, pair with **NFTS (ICLR 2024)** (searches adapter placement/frozen layers for ResNet/ViT, incl. self-supervised DINO-pretrained ViT) and the **Hessian power-law paper (ICML 2025)** (LoRA fine-tuning spectra, generalization indicators).
> 
> **Loss/regularization comparisons available:** the JEPA paper contrasts latent-space (squared) prediction vs reconstruction losses and depth-dependent noise suppression; the shallow-ReLU gradient-flow paper analyzes square loss implicit bias (rank minimization) and regularization via small initialization; LDReg adds L1/L2 regularization to SSL losses against dimensional collapse; the Hessian paper relates power-law spectra, weight decay, batch size, and LoRA to generalization.
> 
> **Development trend:** methods move from heavy pipelines toward label- and memory-efficient, theory-guided designs — multi-stage/anchor-based association → single-offset anchor-free detection; random/domain-randomized sim2real → one-episode Fisher-information-driven active identification; 32→8→4-bit optimizer states for low-memory training; sign-constrained RNN design guided by spectral (SVD/NSE) analysis; reconstruction/contrastive SSL → non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) with characterized implicit bias, plus parameter-efficient low-rank/adapters for few-shot deployment — jointly enabling a memory-limited robot that watches people, estimates physics with minimal real data, and adapts pretrained backbones with few labels.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the provided collection, here are the works that together cover your stack, plus the development trend.
> 
> ## Suggested works
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part-to-body detector (hands/face/body): PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc…`). One-stage, anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts (COCO-derived), BodyHands, and CrowdHuman. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO val it reports per-part precision/recall/F1 (e.g., all parts: Precision 39.41, Recall 63.09, F1 48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51); on BodyHands it leads hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP.
> 
> 2. **Active exploration for physical-parameter estimation / sim-to-real: ASID** (ICLR 2024, doc `cbd087e…`). Decouples exploration and exploitation: trains a Fisher-information-maximizing exploration policy in sim, collects ~one real episode, runs system identification (REPS/CEM) on geometry/articulation/mass/friction/stiffness, then trains the task policy in the corrected simulator for zero-shot transfer. Validated on sphere manipulation, laptop articulation, rod balancing, shuffleboard.
> 
> 3. **4-bit optimizer for SGD/Adam-style training: "4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e145…`). Quantizes optimizer states to 4-bit for Adam/AdamW (framework generalizes to SGDM, etc., with a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M)); uses smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment; up to 57.7% memory savings and fits models on a single 80 GB GPU.
> 
> 4. **Recurrent controllers with excitatory/inhibitory sign rules, spectral analysis: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c…`). Studies RNNs obeying Dale's Law (E/I sign constraints; ColEI vs DANN architectures). Shows the singular-value spectrum at initialization—not sign constraints per se—drives learning; introduces normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as a predictive diagnostic and shows gradient clipping mitigates instability.
> 
> 5. **JEPA self-distillation implicit bias for SSL pretraining + low-rank adaptation:**
>    - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde03…`). Proves JEPA-style latent-space prediction (squared-error objective) is biased toward high-influence/low-variance ("slow") features, whereas MAE-type reconstruction prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; the bias only emerges with deep encoders; ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the perceptual PCA subspace than MAE.
>    - **Adaptation with low-rank adapters:** LoRA (Hu et al., 2022, referenced throughout) and the Hessian-structure study (doc `582d13…`) analyze LoRA fine-tuning of pretrained TinyLlama (power-law Hessian spectra of adapters); NFTS (doc `aa60be…`) searches residual/TSA adapters on pretrained ResNet-18/ViT-small backbones for few-shot adaptation.
> 
> ## Comparisons of MSE vs classification losses and regularization
> - The JEPA paper contrasts the squared-error latent-prediction loss (JEPA) with the squared-error reconstruction loss (MAE), isolating implicit-bias differences between the two objectives.
> - LDReg (doc `5152606…`) compares L1 vs L2 regularization terms on SSL (no significant difference) and shows that overly strong dimensionality regularization triggers collapse; it improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE representations (ResNet-50, ViT-B) including COCO detection/segmentation transfer.
> - "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (doc `160e14…`) analyzes InfoNCE-style (classification-like) losses, showing optimal negative-pair similarity and an auxiliary variance-reduction regularizer that improves top-1 accuracy and temperature robustness.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> - **Detection:** from multi-stage, anchor-based part detectors (BPJDet, Hier-R-CNN) toward **one-stage, anchor-free, single-offset formulations** that scale to many parts with better precision/F1 and fewer parameters.
> - **Sim-to-real:** from passive domain randomization to **active, information-theoretic (Fisher-information) exploration** that decouples exploration from exploitation, minimizing real-world data (≈1 episode) before zero-shot transfer.
> - **Optimization:** from 8-bit to **4-bit optimizer-state quantization** with dedicated quantizers for moment outlier patterns, plus factorization—enabling large-model training on memory-limited GPUs while matching full-precision accuracy.
> - **Recurrent/neural-science models:** from "sign constraints hurt learning" folklore to **spectral analyses showing initialization spectra (e.g., NSE) matter more than sign constraints**, guiding architecture/initialization design for E/I networks.
> - **SSL/pretraining:** from reconstruction (MAE) to **JEPA-style self-distillation**, whose implicit bias toward high-influence, low-variance features is theoretically characterized (deep linear analysis), with parameter-efficient **low-rank/residual adapters (LoRA, TSA)** used to adapt pretrained transformer/ResNet backbones, and regularization (LDReg, variance-reduction) used to counter dimensional collapse.
> 
> Caveat: the collection contains no single paper explicitly comparing mean-squared vs classification losses end-to-end on a manipulation robot; that comparison is supported only indirectly (JEPA squared-error objectives vs contrastive/InfoNCE losses, and LDReg's L1/L2 regularization ablations).

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five method families show a common shift toward scalability, principled objectives/regularization, and provable or benchmarked performance under modern constraints (compute, privacy, biological structure).
> 
> 1) Human part–body association (COCO-style benchmarks)
> - Trend: From anchor-based, multi-stage body→part schemes to one-stage, anchor-free, part→body association with compact representation and simple decoding.
> - Why: Anchor-free heads and a single 2D part-to-body center offset avoid the 2K growth in representation as the number of parts K increases (PBADet uses length 5+K+2 vs 6+K+2K for prior BPJDet), preserving accuracy and robustness as parts scale.
> - Scale/metrics: Multi-scale features with task-aligned learning deliver state-of-the-art or competitive AP on COCOHumanParts and strong Precision/Recall/F1 vs pose baselines; consistent gains on BodyHands (AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP) and lower mismatching rates, confirming better scalability as part sets grow.
> 
> 2) Deep recurrent nets under Dale’s Law (E/I constraints)
> - Trend: From assuming sign constraints are the main bottleneck to focusing on spectral properties as the dominant factor for learnability and scale.
> - Why: Spectral analysis shows ColEI RNNs have dispersed, multimodal singular-value spectra that harm learning, whereas DANN-style EI architectures match standard RNNs’ unimodal spectra and learn well. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) reliably predicts performance.
> - Scale/regularization: Larger networks and more balanced E/I ratios improve spectra and learning; spectrum transplant experiments show spectrum matters more than sign constraints. This reframes biological constraints as a spectral-regularization design problem that scales with width and inhibitory fraction.
> 
> 3) Self-supervised JEPA vs MAE
> - Trend: From pixel-space reconstruction (MSE/CE) to latent prediction with self-distillation and stop-grad, targeting predictive (high-influence) features and avoiding noisy pixels.
> - Why: Exact dynamics in deep linear models show critical-time ordering differs: MAE learns high-covariance directions (λ), but JEPA (especially with depth) prioritizes directions with large regression coefficients (ρ), i.e., features most useful for predicting y. Temporal models show JEPA focuses on slow/predictive components.
> - Scale/metrics: Depth amplifies JEPA’s bias toward predictive features; representations assessed via CCA indicate faster alignment with bottom-variance (semantically useful) subspaces. This yields efficient, scalable training compared to reconstruction on large-scale vision (e.g., ViT/ImageNet setups).
> 
> 4) Memory-efficient optimization (4-bit states for Adam/AdamW)
> - Trend: From 8-bit states to robust 4-bit optimizers by explicitly handling optimizer-state outliers and the zero-point failure mode of v (second moment).
> - Why: Moments exhibit row/column outliers and quantizing v to zero explodes 1/sqrt(v). The fix combines smaller blocks (B128), zero-free mappings (DE-0/Linear), and rank‑1 normalization to capture mixed outlier patterns.
> - Scale/benchmarks: End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning of large LMs (LLaMA 7B/13B/33B) matches full-precision accuracy, with up to 57.7% total memory reduction and 2×+ larger models trainable under the same GPU memory budget (e.g., OPT‑6.7B on 80GB; LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU). Parity is shown on GLUE (NLU), SQuAD (QA), ImageNet-1k (CLS, Swin‑T), WMT14 (MT), and E2E‑NLG, demonstrating scalable, accurate training with Adam/AdamW and compatibility with offloading/FSDP.
> 
> 5) Differentially private RL with self‑play (trajectory‑wise JDP & LDP)
> - Trend: From single-agent DP-RL to multi-agent, two-player zero-sum Markov games with trajectory-level protection and near-optimal regret.
> - Why: A general DP-Nash-VI (optimistic Nash VI) privatizes counts and uses Bernstein-type bonuses; regret reduces to the best non-private multi-agent results when ϵ→∞ and strictly generalizes the best single-agent DP bounds.
> - Scale/theory: Under ϵ-JDP, regret = Õ(√(H^2SABT) + H^3S^2AB/ϵ) with privacy as a lower-order additive term; under ϵ-LDP, regret = Õ(√(H^2SABT) + S^2AB√(H^5T)/ϵ). Both definitions ensure trajectory-wise privacy and scale with horizon H, states S, actions A/B, and time T, providing clear privacy–utility trade-offs.
> 
> Cross-cutting trends
> - Scalability by design: Anchor-free detection compresses representation as parts grow; 4-bit optimizers expand feasible model sizes on fixed hardware; JEPA’s depth-driven bias accelerates learning of predictive features; DP-RL extends to multi-agent self‑play with regret guarantees.
> - Regularization moves from heuristics to principles: spectral control (NSE) for Dale-compliant RNNs; task-aligned learning and Bernstein bonuses; quantization mappings/normalization tailored to optimizer statistics; JEPA’s implicit bias toward high‑influence features.
> - Practical metrics and modern benchmarks: AP/Precision/F1 on COCO/BodyHands; GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/WMT/E2E/LLaMA for efficiency–accuracy; privacy via JDP/LDP regret; representation quality via CCA.
> - Timeline: 2023 focused on understanding limits and efficiency (spectral analysis under Dale’s law; 4‑bit optimizers). 2024 emphasizes scalable, single‑stage anchor‑free association on COCO, principled JEPA theory for predictive features, and trajectory-private self‑play RL—converging toward methods that scale in parts/agents/model size while remaining efficient, robust, and theory‑backed.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five recent papers matching your criteria, based only on the provided context:
> 
> **(a) PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — One-stage, anchor-free part-body association detection. It extends anchor-free object detection with a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale feature maps, giving one-to-one part-to-body correspondence. Benchmarked on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, and CrowdHuman, reporting AP (AP.5:.95, AP.5, AP_M, AP_L), Precision/Recall/F1, and mMR-2; it beats BPJDet, HierR-CNN, and ED-Pose (e.g., joint AP 85.98 on BodyHands; AP 43.0 on COCO-HumanParts).
> 
> **(b) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — Analyzes deep recurrent nets under biologically inspired E/I (excitatory/inhibitory) constraints via spectral analysis. It shows poor learning of simple E/I-partitioned RNNs (ColEI) comes mainly from pathological (multi-modal, dispersed) singular value spectra at initialization, not sign constraints; DANN recurrent nets match standard RNN spectra and learn well. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at init predicts performance.
> 
> **(c) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — Studies joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA/self-distillation) vs. MAE pixel reconstruction using deep linear networks. It explains the implicit bias: predicting in latent space prioritizes high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features and suppresses noisy pixel targets, with critical-time dynamics showing how feature embeddings evolve (aligning faster with low-variance perceptual PCA subspace, confirmed on ImageNet-1K).
> 
> **(d) "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** — Memory-efficient Adam/AdamW with 4-bit quantized optimizer states (smaller blocks B128 for first moment; zero-point-excluding linear/Rank-1 normalization and factorization for second moment). Matches 32-bit accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, WMT14, and supports end-to-end LoRA-style fine-tuning of LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on Alpaca (up to 57.7% memory savings).
> 
> **(e) "Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play"** — Extends Joint DP (JDP) and Local DP (LDP) to two-player zero-sum episodic Markov games with trajectory-level protection, via optimistic Nash value iteration (DP-Nash-VI) with privatized Bernstein bonuses. Provides regret bounds (JDP: Õ(H²SABT + H³S²AB + H²S²AB·E_ε,β), E≈Õ(H/ε); LDP: E≈Õ(H√K/ε)) that generalize the best single-agent DP-RL and non-private multi-agent results.
> 
> **Development trend summary:** The methods all move toward *simpler, more scalable, and more efficient* designs: (a) from multi-stage/anchor-based detection to a single unified one-stage anchor-free head with one offset; (b) from naive biological sign-constraint insertions to understanding *why* they fail (spectra) so constraints can be applied without hurting learning; (c) from pixel-level reconstruction toward latent-space prediction with theoretical analysis of the implicit regularization; (d) pushing optimizer-state precision down from 8-bit to 4-bit (and factorized) to enable larger models on fixed memory, including efficient fine-tuning; and (e) extending DP guarantees from single-agent to self-play/multi-agent settings with matching (near-optimal) regret bounds. Across all five, the common theme is preserving accuracy/robustness while gaining efficiency, scalability, and formal guarantees, validated on modern benchmarks (COCO-style datasets, ImageNet, GLUE, LLM fine-tuning).
