> Based on the available collection, I can identify papers for all five areas. Here is the summary:
> 
> ## Matching papers
> 
> **(a) Human part–body association (PBADet)** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection* (ICLR 2024). Anchor-free, one-stage detector; adds a single part-to-body center offset on top of YOLOv5/v7-style anchor-free heads. Benchmarked on COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; reports AP (e.g., 42.7/41.5 AP on COCO-HumanParts, joint AP 85.98) and Precision/Recall/F1 vs. ED-Pose (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> **(b) Dale's law / E-I RNNs from a spectral perspective** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023). Shows poor learning of column-partitioned E/I (ColEI) RNNs comes from the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed), not sign constraints; recurrent DANN variants have RNN-like spectra and learn well. Introduces normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a spectrum-pathology diagnostic; experiments on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> 
> **(c) JEPA / latent prediction vs. pixel targets** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). Uses fully solvable deep-linear toy models (Gaussian generative models; static and temporal flickering settings) to show JEPA learns high-influence (high-ρ) features and step-wise feature ordering that avoids noisy pixel variance, while MAE orders by covariance λ; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace. (The toy settings in this paper are Gaussian/temporal models rather than MNIST/CIFAR-100 classification; no document in the collection matches JEPA specifically on MNIST/CIFAR-100.)
> 
> **(d) 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW + LoRA** — *4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States* (NeurIPS 2023). Quantizes first moment with smaller blocks (B128/DE) and second moment with zero-point-excluding linear quantizer/rank-1 normalization or factorization; matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, E2E-NLG, WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca instruction tuning (up to 57.7% memory saved; LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU). The paper cites LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning as complementary techniques, but its own end-to-end fine-tuning experiments use full (non-LoRA) AdamW; no document in the collection explicitly reports 4-bit states with LoRA fine-tuning.
> 
> **(e) DP reinforcement learning with self-play** — *Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play* (Qiao & Wang). Extends Joint DP (JDP) and Local DP (LDP) to two-player zero-sum episodic Markov games with trajectory-level protection; algorithm DP-Nash-VI privatizes Bernstein-type bonuses. Regret: JDP Õ(H²S²AB·T + H³S²AB + H²S²AB·E_{ε,β}) with E_{ε,β}=Õ(H/ε); LDP uses E=Õ(H√K/ε); includes lower bounds and PAC bounds, generalizing the best single-agent DP-RL and non-private self-play results.
> 
> ## Development trend across these methods
> - **Detection (a):** from multi-stage/anchor-based heuristics (Zhou et al., BPJDet) toward single-stage, anchor-free, dense per-pixel prediction with one universal offset — fewer hyperparameters, scale-invariant to many parts, one-to-one part→body association, and better accuracy/robustness.
> - **Recurrent nets (b):** from brute-force sign constraints (ColEI) to reparameterized E/I architectures (DANN), with the insight that initialization spectral properties (singular-value distribution, NSE) — not constraints per se — determine learnability; enables biologically faithful models that train well.
> - **SSL (c):** from pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) toward latent-space prediction (JEPA), with theory showing latent prediction's implicit bias (high-influence features, depth-dependent noise suppression) explains why it avoids noisy pixel targets; analysis moves from empirical observations to exact dynamics of feature learning order.
> - **Optimization (d):** from full-precision/8-bit states to 4-bit states via careful analysis of moment outlier patterns, smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, and factorization — pushing memory efficiency while preserving lossless convergence at scale (LLaMA-33B).
> - **DP-RL (e):** from single-agent DP regret minimization to multi-agent/trajectory-level guarantees (JDP and LDP) via private counting with Bernstein bonuses, giving near-optimal regret bounds and matching non-private multi-agent baselines.
> 
> Overall, the trend is: (i) simpler, more scalable designs (anchor-free, one-stage; 4-bit states; end-to-end fine-tuning); (ii) theory-driven explanations replacing heuristics (spectral analysis, implicit-bias dynamics, regret bounds); and (iii) evaluation on modern benchmarks (COCO-family, ImageNet, GLUE, LLaMA instruction tuning) with practical metrics (AP/F1, accuracy, memory, regret).

> {'answer': "End‑to‑end trend summary across the four components you need (2019–2024), based strictly on the cited papers:\n\n1) Detection: from multi‑stage, anchor‑based to one‑stage, anchor‑free, scalable association\n- Earlier association pipelines relied on two stages or anchor‑based heads; recent work (ICLR 2024, PBADet) moves to a one‑stage, anchor‑free head that encodes a single part‑to‑body center offset.\n- Scalability: representation length no longer grows with the number of parts; the single offset remains valid even when some parts are invisible. This improves robustness and simplifies decoding while supporting many parts without degrading detection.\n- Practical shift: task‑aligned learning (from TOOD) replaces centerness branches; multi‑scale heads are retained for size variability; evaluation expands beyond AP to include association‑aware metrics (mMR‑2) and, when compared to pose, F1/Precision are reported.\n\n2) Pretraining for perception: from MAE reconstruction to JEPA self‑distillation that down‑weights noisy pixels\n- MAE reconstructs pixels and tends to prioritize high‑variance, sometimes uninformative details.\n- Newer JEPA/self‑distillation (NeurIPS 2024) shows a distinct implicit bias: with deeper encoders, JEPA prioritizes “influential” (high‑regression‑coefficient) features in latent space and avoids noisy, unpredictable pixels—matching the empirical shift toward semantic features needed for perception.\n- Practical recipe: stop‑gradient teacher/online encoders and prediction in representation space; empirically faster perception gains than MAE and well‑suited to ViT/Transformer families.\n\n3) Training efficiency under tight memory: from 8‑bit states to robust 4‑bit Adam‑family optimizers, plus adapters\n- Prior low‑precision states stabilized at 8‑bit; the 2023 work pushes to 4‑bit by addressing two blockers revealed in measurements of optimizer moments: (a) complex outlier patterns across rows/columns and (b) the zero‑point failure for the second moment.\n- Technique evolution: smaller blocks + rank‑1 normalization over rows/columns for first/second moments; exclude zero from the mapping (or use a linear map) to fix Adam’s v‑term; optionally combine with factorization for even lower memory.\n- Scope and compatibility: works with AdamW on Transformers across NLU, MT, image classification and instruction tuning; integrates cleanly with adapter‑style fine‑tuning (e.g., LoRA on LLaMA), delivering large memory savings and maintaining accuracy and throughput.\n\n4) Auditability/causality: from CI‑only discovery to rank‑based identification with hidden variables\n- CI‑based (PC/FCI) yields limited identifiability when latent confounders exist. The 2024 RLCD framework uses rank constraints (t‑separation) on sub‑covariances to (i) detect latent variables, (ii) determine their cardinalities, and (iii) recover the Markov equivalence class (over observed and latent) under weaker graphical conditions than prior rank‑based work.\n- Algorithmic trend: a three‑phase search (CI‑skeleton via rank tests; rank‑deficiency driven cluster discovery; refinement) partitions variable groups for scalability and uses canonical correlations to test ranks. Empirically, RLCD improves F1/SHD over baselines on synthetic and real data and supports graphs where observed nodes can be adjacent and latents can be confounders, mediators, or effects.\n\nCross‑cutting evaluation and objectives\n- Metrics broaden from AP to include association‑aware miss‑rate (mMR‑2) and, when comparing detectors vs pose estimators, F1/Precision; causal discovery reports F1/SHD; optimization papers keep standard task scores while reporting detailed memory/time.\n- Losses in these works match your plan: squared‑error objectives are central in the JEPA linear analysis and in rank testing (Gaussian covariances), while standard cross‑entropy is used for downstream classification and language tasks under low‑precision optimization.\n\nWhat this means for your pipeline\n- Detector: adopt the one‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑body offset head (PBADet) for scalable hand/face‑to‑person association with simple decoding and stable training on multi‑scale features.\n- Pretraining: prefer JEPA‑style self‑distillation over MAE to emphasize influential, semantic features and avoid noisy pixels—especially effective with deep encoders.\n- Training at 4‑bit: use the 4‑bit AdamW states with rank‑1 normalization and zero‑point‑free second‑moment quantization; combine with adapters (e.g., LoRA) on Transformers for further memory savings while preserving accuracy.\n- Causal audit: use RLCD’s rank‑based discovery to uncover operator‑behavior relations even with unobserved factors, leveraging canonical‑correlation rank tests and the three‑phase search to obtain a latent‑augmented causal structure.\n\nTime‑ordered signals of the trend (most recent → earlier)\n- 2024: PBADet generalizes one‑stage anchor‑free association and scales to many parts; RLCD extends rank‑based discovery to flexible latent structures with observed adjacencies; JEPA theory explains why joint‑embedding prediction yields semantic, less‑noisy features.\n- 2023: 4‑bit optimizer states mature from 8‑bit via rank‑1 normalization and zero‑point fixes, enabling practical fine‑tuning of large Transformers with adapters while matching full‑precision accuracy.\n\nIn short: the field is converging on (i) anchor‑free, single‑offset association heads for scalable detection, (ii) JEPA self‑distillation for semantic pretraining, (iii) 4‑bit Adam‑family optimizers plus adapters for resource‑constrained training, and (iv) rank‑based causal discovery to audit systems even with hidden factors—all evaluated with standard task scores plus F1/Precision and memory/time, and trained with squared‑error/entropy objectives where appropriate."}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, the set of papers that guides these components end-to-end is:
> 
> **1. Detection — PBADet (ICLR 2024, Gao et al.)**
> "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association." A one-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/v7 backbones with anchor-free heads) that associates hands, face, etc. with the correct person via a single part-to-body center offset, with branches for box, class, and association prediction, supervised by task-alignment learning (from TOOD). Outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN; vs. the pose estimator ED-Pose it yields substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands and feet.
> 
> **2. Pretraining — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, Littwin et al.)**
> Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with self-distillation (online encoder predicts target encoder's latent output). Deep-linear analysis shows JEPA has an implicit bias toward high-influence, low-variance ("slow") features, avoiding noisy, uninformative pixel-level features that MAE-style reconstruction learns; ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace than MAE.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient training — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023, Li et al.)** (with NFTS, ICLR 2024, as adapter-fine-tuning complement)
> 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW: smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, rank-1 normalization and a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment, plus optional Adafactor-style factorization ("4-bit Factor"). Matches 32-bit AdamW accuracy on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning with up to 57.7% memory savings; the paper situates itself alongside delta-tuning/LoRA-style adapter approaches that only tune a small parameter subset. NFTS complements this by using NAS (SPOS supernet) to decide per-layer adapter insertion and freeze/fine-tune choices for pretrained Transformers/ResNets.
> 
> **4. Causal analysis — RLCD (ICLR 2024)**
> "RLCD: A Flexible Rank-Based Method for Latent Causal Discovery." Uses rank-deficiency constraints on sub-covariance matrices (with canonical-correlation tests) instead of plain conditional independence, so it can locate unobserved latent variables acting as confounders, mediators, or effects—including hierarchical latent structure—and recover the Markov equivalence class under much weaker graphical conditions than Hier. Rank; without latents it asymptotically matches PC. Evaluated with F1/SHD on synthetic and real data (Big Five personality/operator-behavior network analysis).
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> - **Detection**: from multi-stage, anchor-based, heuristic matching (two-stage hand-body association, BPJDet's one-to-many body-to-part offsets) → unified one-stage anchor-free detection with a single, always-valid part-to-body center offset, making association scalable to any number of parts without accuracy loss.
> - **SSL pretraining**: from pixel-space reconstruction (MAE), which tends to learn noisy/uninformative features, → JEPA latent-space self-distillation, with theory (deep linear analysis) explaining why predicting in latent space implicitly prioritizes semantic, low-variance features and suppresses noisy pixels.
> - **Optimization/tuning**: from 32-bit (and 8-bit block-wise) optimizer states → 4-bit states via finer-grained quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion) plus factorization, achieving lossless accuracy with large memory savings, increasingly combined with parameter-efficient (adapter/LoRA/delta-tuning) strategies and automated search over adapter placement.
> - **Causal discovery**: from conditional-independence-only methods (PC/FCI) that are poorly informative about latent factors → rank-based (trek-separation) constraints on covariances, which reveal unobserved confounders/mediators and hierarchical latent structure under weaker assumptions, asymptotically generalizing PC when no latents exist.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, the four papers that best cover these components end-to-end are:
> 
> **1. PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc…`) — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association detector for hands/faces↔person, using a single part-to-body center offset (F1/Precision evaluation).
> 
> **2. "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde03…`) — joint-embedding predictive architecture/self-distillation that predicts in latent space and suppresses noisy pixels, unlike pixel-reconstruction (MAE).
> 
> **3. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e145…`) — 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW (with rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization), evaluated on LLaMA fine-tuning/instruction tuning with LoRA-style adapters on Transformers under limited GPU memory.
> 
> **4. RLCD** (ICLR 2024, doc `f8eb4c3…`) — rank-based latent causal discovery that uncovers causal relationships with unobserved factors via rank-deficiency constraints on sub-covariance matrices (evaluated with F1/SHD; standard losses incl. squared error/entropy fit its linear model).
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> - **Detector:** multi-stage/anchor-based two-stage pipelines (DA-RNN, JointDet, HierR-CNN, BPJDet body-to-part offsets) → a streamlined one-stage, anchor-free design with a single, always-valid part-to-body offset, task-alignment, and scalability to many parts (a universal framework).
> - **Pretraining:** generative pixel-reconstruction (MAE) that captures noisy, uninformative variance → joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) with a theoretical implicit bias toward high-influence/low-variance "slow" semantic features, formalizing why noise is avoided.
> - **Optimization:** 32-bit → 8-bit block-wise states → 4-bit states via smaller blocks, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization and factorization, achieving lossless convergence and up to ~57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B on one GPU) and working with delta/LoRA-style fine-tuning.
> - **Causal analysis:** conditional-independence-only methods (PC/FCI) that cannot handle latents well → rank-constraint-based discovery that locates latent variables, determines cardinalities, and recovers the full Markov equivalence class under much weaker graphical conditions (reducing to PC when no latents exist).
> 
> Together they form an end-to-end stack: PBADet for detection/association, JEPA-style self-distillation for robust pretraining, 4-bit Adam optimizer states for memory-efficient adapter fine-tuning, and RLCD for auditable causal analysis under unobserved factors.

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five works converge along five complementary axes, each advancing scalability, efficiency, and interpretability while broadening applicability across vision, sequences/time series, and molecular design.
> 
> 1) Interpretable and synthesizable molecular generation (2025): The field is moving from expert-curated or heuristic grammars to multi‑modal, foundation‑model–guided induction. Foundation Molecular Grammar (FMG) replaces hand‑written vocabularies with MMFM‑induced, image‑and‑text aligned substructures and uses LLM chain‑of‑thought plus tournament feedback to select chemically sound rules. The result is a scalable, more data‑efficient pipeline that preserves formal grammar guarantees while improving synthesizability and class specificity, signaling a shift toward interpretable, MMFM‑assisted graph languages rather than opaque neural generation.
> 
> 2) Self‑supervised learning by predicting in latent space (2024): Joint‑Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) formalize a move away from pixel‑space reconstruction (which chases noisy, high‑variance features) toward latent‑space prediction that prioritizes influential, predictive features. Analytically, deep encoders intensify a bias toward high regression‑coefficient directions (MSE in latent space), explaining faster convergence to semantic features and offering a principled path for robust pretraining; JEPA’s temporal model additionally clarifies how slow, predictive features emerge in time‑series/video.
> 
> 3) Spectral analysis of EI‑constrained recurrent nets (2023): Work on Dale’s Law RNNs reframes the core difficulty from sign constraints to spectral pathologies. Performance trends improve as methods manage the singular‑value spectrum (unimodal, clustered) rather than only enforcing EI signs, with Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) predicting learnability. Over time, results show small, I‑sparse networks learn worse (dispersed spectra), while larger or more balanced E/I nets learn well—even on sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and the adding problem—highlighting a shift toward spectral diagnostics and initialization over hand‑crafted architectural constraints for time‑series modeling.
> 
> 4) Anchor‑free, one‑stage human part–body detection (2024): Detection is trending from multi‑stage/anchor‑based pipelines to one‑stage, anchor‑free association with compact representations. PBADet replaces body‑to‑part vectors with a single part‑to‑body center offset on multi‑scale feature maps, scaling gracefully with the number of parts and avoiding invalid offsets when parts are occluded. Trained with SGD and task‑aligned losses on COCO‑HumanParts/COCO‑WholeBody, it improves joint association metrics and, when contrasted with pose estimation, yields better Precision/Recall/F1 for part‑body pairing under the same COCO setting. This trend emphasizes simpler heads, tighter losses, and dataset‑scale training for robust association.
> 
> 5) Memory‑efficient training via low‑bit optimizer states (2023): Optimizer‑state compression has moved from 8‑bit to practical 4‑bit states by addressing outliers and the zero‑point failure mode in the second moment. Using smaller blocks, rank‑1 (row/column) normalization, and linear mappings that exclude zero for v, 4‑bit Adam/AdamW match full‑precision across diverse Transformers (e.g., Swin‑T, RoBERTa‑L, GPT‑2, LLaMA) and tasks (ImageNet classification, GLUE, SQuAD, MT, instruction tuning). Factorized v further reduces memory; with optimizer offloading, throughput improves. The unifying trend is drop‑in, optimizer‑agnostic memory savings (SGD/Adam/AdamW) that scale model size without sacrificing accuracy.
> 
> Cross‑cutting observations and metrics:
> - Losses/metrics: JEPA formalizes MSE in latent space; PBADet employs task‑aligned classification/IoU/L1; part‑association benchmarking reports Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO. 
> - Feature embeddings and attention: PBADet builds on modern detector heads and multi‑scale features; FMG’s interpretable substructures act as modular, human‑understandable “embeddings” for molecules; JEPA’s latent prediction emphasizes feature selectivity over pixel detail.
> - Time‑series modeling: Both JEPA’s temporal model and Dale’s Law RNNs underline a trend toward principled dynamics—slow/influential features and spectrum‑aware initialization/diagnostics—over ad‑hoc constraints.
> 
> Overall trajectory: From 2023–2025, methods evolve toward (i) principled implicit biases (spectral control, latent‑space prediction), (ii) leaner representations (anchor‑free association, single‑offset vectors), and (iii) scalable efficiency (4‑bit optimizer states), while (iv) preserving or increasing interpretability (formal grammars guided by MMFMs). This combination yields systems that are easier to scale, more data‑efficient, and better aligned with domain constraints across molecules, detection, and sequence modeling.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers addressing each theme
> 
> 1. **Interpretable & synthesizable molecular generation with multi-modal models** — *Foundation Molecular Grammar (FMG)*: uses multi-modal foundation models (MMFMs) to induce an interpretable molecular graph language; renders molecules as images, describes them as text, aligns modalities via prompt learning, and excels in synthesizability, diversity, and data-efficiency. Related: *CoBO* (correlated latent-space Bayesian optimization with synthesizable recommendations; aligns latent-space distances with objective values via Lipschitz/correlation loss, yielding smoother latent landscapes).
> 
> 2. **Self-supervised learning predicting in latent space to avoid noisy pixel features** — *"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"*: analyzes self-distillation (JEPA) vs. MAE in deep linear networks, showing JEPA's latent-space prediction is implicitly biased toward high-influence, low-noise features, suppressing noisy ones; depth strengthens this. Related: *LDReg* (local-dimensionality regularization to prevent dimensional collapse in SSL, improving representation quality), *HASSOD* (fully self-supervised detection from DINO features), and *RaMP* (self-supervised RL with random features).
> 
> 3. **Spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory constraints in recurrent nets** — *"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"*: compares ColEI (column sign-constrained E/I) vs. DANN RNNs; shows poor learning is due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), not sign constraints; proposes Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) as a pre-training diagnostic; tested on sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, adding problem, object recognition.
> 
> 4. **Anchor-free human part–body detection trained on COCO** — *PBADet*: one-stage, anchor-free part–body association using a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale features with task-alignment learning; trained on COCO-HumanParts and evaluated on COCO validation, outperforming BPJDet/HierR-CNN/ED-Pose (e.g., all-parts Precision 39.41, Recall 63.09, F1 48.52 vs. ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51).
> 
> 5. **Memory-efficient training with low-bit (4-bit) optimizer states** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"*: quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller block size, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional factorization); matches 32-bit accuracy on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet (Swin-T)/E2E-NLG/WMT14/LLaMA fine-tuning with up to 57.7% memory savings; includes convergence proof for quantized SGD(M). Related: *BSO/T-BSO* (binary-weight spiking online optimization, SGD with cosine annealing, memory to O(n²L/32), CIFAR-10/100 results).
> 
> ## Supporting aspects requested
> 
> - **Feature embeddings**: covered by JEPA (latent feature bias), CoBO (latent embeddings, Pearson correlation >0.7, smooth landscapes), LDReg (embedding dimensionality), and contrastive-learning embedding analysis (negative-pair similarity variance reduction, top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100).
> - **MSE/CE losses**: JEPA analysis (predictive regression in latent space), CoBO (Lipschitz/align losses), Hessian paper (training loss landscape, label-noise robustness), shallow ReLU gradient-flow analysis (square/MSE loss), G-Sim (MSE/Wasserstein loss in time-series simulation).
> - **Precision/F1, MNIST/CIFAR-100**: PBADet reports Precision/Recall/F1 (COCO); Hessian paper uses MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 (LeNet/ResNet18, power-law spectra, test error correlations); LDReg and BSO report CIFAR-10/100 accuracy; G-Sim and RLCD report F1. **SVHN does not appear in this collection** — no retrieved work uses it. ResNet-50 appears only in LDReg (ImageNet, not the 4-bit optimizer paper, which uses Swin-T/Transformer/LLaMA).
> - **Time-series modeling**: *Synthcity* (benchmarking tabular/time-series/survival synthetic data with LSTM, GRU, RNN, TCN, Transformer, InceptionTime architectures and fidelity/utility/privacy metrics), *ChaosBench* (S2S climate forecasting; deterministic/probabilistic/physics-based spectral metrics; autoregressive error accumulation), G-Sim (interpretable simulator generation, MSE/MMD/Wasserstein, causal F1), and RNN baselines in G-Sim (GRU, DyNODE, Transformer trained with Adam/AdamW).
> 
> ## Development trend
> 
> Across these works the trend is a shift from raw accuracy to **efficiency, interpretability, and understanding of learning dynamics**:
> 
> - **Interpretability is increasingly induced by foundation models** rather than expert annotation (FMG's MMFM-derived grammar vs. hand-written grammars), while latent-space methods seek smoother, better-aligned embeddings (CoBO).
> - **SSL has moved from pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) to latent-space prediction (JEPA)**, with theory explaining why latent prediction avoids noisy features, and regularization (LDReg) to prevent dimensional collapse.
> - **Biologically constrained RNNs** advanced from naive sign-constrained E/I partitioning to spectral-aware designs, showing spectral properties (singular-value distribution, NSE) matter more than sign constraints.
> - **Detection** evolved from two-stage, anchor-based part-body pipelines to one-stage anchor-free dense prediction with a single scalable part-to-body offset and task alignment.
> - **Optimization** is being pushed to ever-lower precision (32→8→4-bit states) with dedicated quantizers/factorization, achieving lossless convergence at drastically reduced memory (e.g., LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
> - A parallel thread uses **spectral/loss-landscape analysis** (Hessian power laws, SVD entropy, implicit bias) as diagnostics that predict generalization before or during training, and **benchmarking frameworks** (Synthcity, ChaosBench) now systematically cover diverse modalities including time series.

> ## Papers addressing the five topics
> 
> 1. **Interpretable & synthesizable molecular generation with multi-modal models**
>    - **Foundation Molecular Grammar (FMG)** — uses multi-modal foundation models (MMFMs) to induce an interpretable molecular graph language: molecules rendered as images, described as text, aligned via prompt learning. Excels in synthesizability, diversity and data efficiency on MOSES, with expert-validated GPT-4o case studies.
> 
> 2. **Self-supervised learning predicting in latent space to avoid noisy pixel features**
>    - **Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** — analyzes JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture) vs. MAE; latent-space prediction is biased toward high-influence features and suppresses noise (ImageNet/I-JEPA + CCA confirm faster alignment with perceptual low-variance subspace).
>    - **LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning** — counters (local) dimensional collapse, improving representation quality/transfer (ResNet-50, ViT-B on ImageNet; COCO detection).
> 
> 3. **Spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory constraints in recurrent nets**
>    - **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — shows E/I (Dale's law) RNNs learn poorly because of the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed), not sign constraints; introduces normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a performance predictor. Benchmarks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> 
> 4. **Anchor-free human part–body detection trained on COCO**
>    - **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLOv5/v7 backbones; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts; beats ED-Pose in precision/recall/F1 on COCO val.
> 
> 5. **Memory-efficient training of Transformers/ResNet-style CNNs with SGD/Adam/AdamW and 4-bit optimizer states**
>    - **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW (and the SGDM family) first/second moments to 4-bit via small blocks, rank-1 normalization and zero-point exclusion; matches 32-bit accuracy on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T (ImageNet), GPT-2, Transformer-Base (WMT14), LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
>    - Supporting: **MLMC compression** (2-bit quantized distributed SGD on CIFAR-10 ResNet-18) and **BSO** (binary-weight online spiking training with per-layer moments on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, DVS, GSC).
> 
> ## Supporting works for the requested aspects
> - **Feature embeddings**: *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet top-1); *GEEA* (mutual VAE over entity embeddings); *HASSOD* (DINO features for self-supervised detection); *GWM-E* (embedding-level multi-modal message passing).
> - **MSE / CE losses**: *GEEA* explicitly uses CE (decoder prediction) and MSE (post-reconstruction of joint embeddings); GNN edge-embedding paper uses MSE on Ising marginals; JEPA latent-space prediction is MSE-style.
> - **Precision/F1**: *PBADet* (precision/recall/F1 vs ED-Pose), *GEEA* (P/R/F1), *G-Sim* (F1 for causal structure), *RLCD* (F1 on synthetic causal graphs), *CMA* (F1=0.81 on AD consensus graph).
> - **MNIST / CIFAR-100 (SVHN not present in this collection)**: *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* uses LeNet/ResNet-18/FCN on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 with SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/etc.; the Dale's-law paper uses sequential MNIST; 4-bit optimizer paper uses ImageNet; **SVHN was not found in the retrieved context**.
> - **Time-series modeling**: *Synthcity* (regular/irregular time series, LSTM/GRU/Transformer/TCN/InceptionTime architectures, time-series generative models like TimeGAN/FourierFlows); *ChaosBench* (S2S climate forecasting with physics-based spectral metrics); *DAML* (decision-aware spatiotemporal count forecasting, likelihood-vs-BPR tradeoff); *G-Sim* (simulation models of COVID-19/supply chain, MSE/Wasserstein losses); RNN papers inherently handle sequential data.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> - **Molecular generation**: from expert-annotated/manual graph grammars and heuristic rules → foundation-model-driven automatic grammar induction that aligns image/text modalities in-context, buying interpretability, synthesizability and data efficiency without expert curation.
> - **Self-supervised learning**: from pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) → latent-space prediction (JEPA) to ignore noisy features, backed by theory of implicit bias (deep linear networks) and regularization against dimensional collapse; SSL is also moving into object detection via pseudo-labeling (HASSOD).
> - **Biologically constrained RNNs**: from blaming sign constraints for poor learning → spectral analysis (random-matrix theory, singular-value spectra, NSE) showing initialization spectra are the key, guiding architectures (DANN) that respect Dale's law and still train well.
> - **Part–body detection**: from multi-stage, anchor-based, heuristic association (body-to-part offsets, separate matching networks) → unified one-stage anchor-free detectors with a single part-to-body offset, task-alignment losses, and scalable multi-part association; evaluation shifts from AP-only to AR and precision/recall/F1.
> - **Memory-efficient training**: from 32-bit optimizer states and 8-bit optimizers → 4-bit (and binary/2-bit) states via better quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization), achieving lossless accuracy and enabling larger models on limited GPUs; the same compression mindset extends to distributed SGD and spiking networks.
> 
> Overall, the trend is **unification and simplification** — single frameworks/offsets, latent-space modeling to avoid raw noise, spectral diagnostics for architecture design, and aggressive low-bit compression — all validated on standard benchmarks (MOSES, ImageNet, MNIST/CIFAR, COCO, GLUE, LLaMA) with both loss-based and precision/F1-based metrics.

Gold 1：

> Across these five works, several clear development trends emerge around modeling choices, optimization/regularization, efficiency, and scalability. 
> 
> 1) Stronger inductive biases and spectra-aware training in recurrent deep networks
> - Shift from enforcing biological sign constraints (excitatory/inhibitory) to targeting spectra: Dale’s-law RNNs show that singular-value spectra at initialization—and their clustering measured by normalized SVD entropy (NSE)—predict learning more than sign constraints themselves. Larger networks and more balanced E/I ratios yield unimodal, well-clustered spectra and better performance (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, natural object recognition); small nets with few inhibitory units have multimodal, dispersed spectra and learn worse. Gradient clipping stabilizes training, and spectral metrics like NSE become practical design tools. Trend: from architecturally enforcing EI signs to spectra-aware initialization, diagnostics, and scaling to larger networks for stable optimization.
> 
> 2) From reconstruction to prediction in self-supervised learning—and depth-amplified implicit bias
> - Deep linear analyses show a systematic move from masked reconstruction (MAE, MSE in input space) to joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA/self-distillation with StopGrad in latent space). A key trend is depth-dependent implicit bias: with deeper encoders, JEPA prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficients), i.e., more predictive and less noisy subspaces, while MAE prioritizes highly covarying (often higher-variance) features. This persists in linear temporal models where JEPA favors slowly varying, predictable components. Result: predictive JEPA-type objectives learn semantically useful features faster (in the training-time sense) as depth increases, while reconstruction remains agnostic to influence and more tied to input variance.
> 
> 3) Resource-efficient fine-tuning: optimizer-state quantization from 8-bit to 4-bit, with structure-aware normalization
> - Optimizer memory becomes the bottleneck for large models; methods evolve from 8-bit to 4-bit Adam states by (i) using smaller blocks and rank-1 (per-row and per-column) normalization to handle heterogeneous outliers in moments, and (ii) fixing a zero-point artifact in second-moment quantization (excluding zero via linear mapping) that otherwise distorts update directions. Factorization of the second moment can be combined with 4-bit quantization for further savings. These 4-bit optimizers retain accuracy across NLU (e.g., GLUE), QA (SQuAD EM/F1), image classification (Swin-T on ImageNet-1k), MT (WMT14), and instruction tuning (LLaMA), while reducing memory and preserving throughput (especially with fused ops/offloading). Trend: practical, task-robust 4-bit state approximations and per-row/column statistics replace coarse block-only schemes; memory savings unlock larger-model fine-tuning on limited hardware.
> 
> 4) Anchor-free, one-stage association with task-aligned regularization replaces multi-stage or pure CE training
> - Body–part association progresses from two-stage, anchor-based or heuristic matching to a one-stage, anchor-free detector (PBADet) with a single part-to-body center offset. This representation scales linearly with the number of parts (5+K+2 vs 6+K+2K), remains valid even with occlusions, and simplifies decoding. Training goes beyond plain cross-entropy by adopting task-aligned learning (from TOOD): an alignment metric couples classification and localization, selecting top-K anchors for supervision. Trend: unified, scalable, and efficient association heads with alignment-based regularization outperform multi-stage or anchor-based designs and maintain accuracy as part sets grow.
> 
> 5) Sensor-faithful, time-resolved NeRFs: modeling raw lidar transients over t
> - NeRF supervision moves from auxiliary point clouds to raw time-resolved photon count histograms from single-photon lidar. A transient, time-resolved volume-rendering equation (with two-way transmittance, 1/r^2 falloff, and convolution with the measured impulse response) allows direct rendering of lidar histograms along time t. Space-carving regularization suppresses spurious density where measurements indicate free space. Using efficient NeRF backbones (Instant-NGP/NerfAcc), these models enable novel-view synthesis of transients and recover improved geometry and conventional appearance from few views (2–5). Trend: explicit sensor/image-formation modeling—at picosecond timescales—yields better few-view reconstruction and opens new simulation/use cases for robotics, autonomous driving, and remote sensing.
> 
> Cross-cutting trends
> - Regularization beyond CE and beyond simple parameter constraints: task alignment (association), space carving (lidar NeRFs), spectrum-aware initialization (EI RNNs), and log-domain losses for high dynamic range (transients) all improve stability and accuracy.
> - Scalability manifests along different axes: (i) handling many parts with constant overhead (PBADet), (ii) training stable EI RNNs by scaling network size/E–I balance guided by spectral diagnostics, (iii) fine-tuning progressively larger Transformers with 4-bit optimizer states, and (iv) learning geometry/appearance from fewer views by modeling raw transient physics.
> - Time as a first-class dimension: temporal transients in NeRFs (explicit t), temporal learning dynamics in JEPA (feature learning order/critical time), and sequence tasks for RNNs (e.g., sequential MNIST) reflect a broader emphasis on exploiting temporal structure rather than treating it as a byproduct.
> 
> Overall trajectory
> - Recent methods converge on principled, physics- or theory-grounded biases (spectral diagnostics, latent prediction bias, sensor-accurate renderers) coupled with efficiency (4-bit optimizers) and scalable formulations (anchor-free, one-stage heads). This combination yields robust performance with fewer views, more parts, or less memory—while broadening the output space from RGB/depth to raw, time-resolved sensor signals.

**naive 最终答案**

> I found papers matching all five topics. Note: one detail in topic (3) — the 4-bit optimizer paper in the collection does **not** report CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 F1/Precision metrics (it uses Swin-T on ImageNet, RoBERTa/GPT-2/Transformer on NLP, LLaMA fine-tuning); those specifics cannot be verified from the context.
> 
> **The five papers:**
> 
> 1. **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly (NeurIPS 2023)** — E/I (Dale's law) constraints in RNNs; shows spectral properties (multimodal singular-value spectrum, measured by normalised SVD entropy) matter more than sign constraints, validated on sequential MNIST, with SGD/gradient-clipping training.
> 2. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** — implicit bias of joint-embedding predictive (JEPA, self-distillation with MSE in latent space) vs masked reconstruction (MAE, MSE in data space), analyzed via deep linear networks (exact ODE dynamics); JEPA prioritizes high-influence features, MAE prioritizes variance, confirmed on ImageNet-1K with I-JEPA/MAE.
> 3. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4 bits: smaller block size (B128) plus rank-1 normalization using both row- and column-wise scales, and a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment; matches full-precision accuracy on Swin-T, RoBERTa-L, Transformer, GPT-2, LLaMA.
> 4. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage anchor-free part–body association detector; extends FCOS/TOOD-style anchor-free representation with a single part-to-body center offset, supervised not by plain cross-entropy but by a task-alignment scheme (IoU + DFL + classification + dedicated association loss with top-K aligned anchors).
> 5. **Transient Neural Radiance Fields (NeurIPS 2023)** — time-resolved NeRF that renders single-photon lidar photon-count transients over time t using a time-resolved volume-rendering equation, enabling novel-view synthesis of transients plus improved 3D reconstruction from few (2–5) views.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:** The work moves from **understanding/analyzing** learning to **engineering efficiency and new sensor modalities**. Early works (1, 2) diagnose *why* networks behave as they do — decomposing performance gaps into spectral vs. sign-constraint factors, and deriving the implicit bias that makes latent-space prediction favor informative features over reconstruction — i.e., theory-driven guidance for architecture/objective design. The later works (3–5) translate such understanding into practical gains: (3) pushes optimizer-state quantization from 8 to 4 bits with finer-grained (row+column) quantization and zero-point handling to make memory-efficient fine-tuning lossless; (4) replaces hand-crafted multi-stage/anchor pipelines with a single unified one-stage anchor-free detector where an extra association head is trained via task-alignment rather than plain classification; (5) extends NeRF from rendering RGB to rendering raw physical measurements (transients) by respecting the sensor's image-formation model. Common threads: simpler/unified representations, physics- or theory-grounded losses instead of generic ones, and pushing toward raw-data-level fidelity (transients, quantized states) while preserving accuracy.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the available documents, the five topics map to these papers:
> 
> 1. **Spectral/regularization in SGD-trained networks & E/I RNNs**: *"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"* (NeurIPS 2023) — shows ColEI (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs learn worse than standard RNNs/DANNs on sequential MNIST not because of sign constraints but because of their multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum at initialization; normalized SVD entropy predicts performance. Complemented by *"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"* (ICML 2025) — well-trained nets (LeNet on MNIST, CNNs, ViT, LLMs) show power-law Hessian spectra tied to generalization and batch-size phases.
> 
> 2. **Implicit bias of JEPA vs MAE**: *"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"* (NeurIPS 2024) — in deep linear models, JEPA (predictor in latent space, MSE-type objective) prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses noise, while MAE (masked reconstruction) only follows high-variance features; ordering depends on depth and critical times, confirmed with I-JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet (Transformers, CCA). *"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"* covers the cosine-similarity contrastive side (positive alignment, negative-pair separation, mini-batch variance).
> 
> 3. **4-bit memory-efficient Adam fine-tuning**: *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit via smaller block sizes (B128), row-wise/column-wise (rank-1) normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizers, and second-moment factorization. Note: the context's benchmarks are Swin-T on ImageNet-1k (accuracy ~80.8), RoBERTa-L on SQuAD (F1 ~94.5), Transformer-Base on WMT14, and LLaMA fine-tuning; CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 metrics as described are not in this paper.
> 
> 4. **Anchor-free part–body association**: *"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"* (ICLR 2024) — a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale anchor-free features, supervised with TOOD-style task-alignment (alignment metric t = s^α·u^β selecting top-K anchors) plus an association loss, beating BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts and ED-Pose on hands/feet precision-recall-F1.
> 
> 5. **Time-resolved lidar NeRFs**: *"Transient Neural Radiance Fields for Lidar View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction"* (NeurIPS 2023) — a time-resolved volume-rendering equation renders raw single-photon lidar photon-count histograms (transients over t) from novel views, yielding better geometry/appearance from only 2–5 views than point-cloud-supervised NeRFs.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> - **From heuristics to spectral/implicit-bias theory**: performance differences (EI RNNs, SSL objectives, generalization) are increasingly explained by measurable spectra (singular values, Hessian power laws, SVD entropy) and provable implicit biases (feature-learning order/critical times in deep linear networks), then validated on real CNNs/Transformers/LLMs.
> - **From coarse to fine-grained compression**: optimizer-state precision drops (8→4-bit) while quantization granularity becomes finer (block-wise, row/column/rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization) to retain full-precision accuracy at larger scales.
> - **From multi-stage, anchor-based pipelines to unified one-stage designs**: part–body association collapses to a single offset, and plain cross-entropy is upgraded to task-alignment-based supervision that couples classification and localization quality.
> - **From post-processed supervision to raw sensor physics**: NeRF moves from using point clouds as auxiliary depth supervision to modeling the actual lidar image-formation model (time-resolved transients), enabling new-view sensor simulation and better few-view 3D reconstruction.

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five works (2019–2024) converge on three themes: scaling under real‑world constraints, moving from surrogate/heuristic supervision to physically/architecturally faithful objectives, and making training feasible on tight compute.
> 
> 1) Part–body association in crowded scenes (detection):
> - Shift from multi‑stage, anchor‑based pipelines and heuristic matching to one‑stage, anchor‑free designs. PBADet (ICLR’24) replaces body→part offsets with a single part→body center offset, plus task‑aligned learning. This yields simpler decoding, better robustness in crowds, and, critically, scalability: the representation size no longer grows with the number of parts (supports multiple parts without accuracy loss).
> - Training remains efficient (SGD with standard detectors like YOLOv5/7), and evaluation is broadening beyond AP to crowd‑specific metrics (MR−2, mMR−2) and even F1/Precision for part detection/association when compared to pose estimators.
> - Trend: anchor‑free, multi‑scale, task‑aligned formulations that scale to more parts and crowded scenes with lower overhead while improving association accuracy.
> 
> 2) Lidar view synthesis and reconstruction (transient NeRF):
> - Move from using lidar point clouds only as auxiliary supervision for RGB NeRFs to modeling the lidar’s native image formation. Transient NeRFs (NeurIPS’23) render raw time‑resolved photon count histograms by extending volume rendering along time t and convolving with the system impulse response.
> - This physical modeling at picosecond scales improves geometry from few views and, for the first time, enables novel‑view synthesis of lidar transients—useful for simulating raw measurements in planning (autonomy/robotics/remote sensing).
> - Trend: from point‑cloud surrogates to full transient rendering that captures the sensor’s timing and radiometry, with accelerated NeRF backends (Instant‑NGP/NerfAcc) for practicality.
> 
> 3) Memory‑lean fine‑tuning of large Transformers (4‑bit optimizers):
> - Compression pushes optimizer states from 8‑bit to 4‑bit (NeurIPS’23) by analyzing first/second‑moment outlier patterns. Key steps: smaller block sizes for m, zero‑point removal plus linear mapping for v (to avoid catastrophic small‑value quantization), and rank‑1 normalization; optionally factorize v for further savings.
> - Result: AdamW at 4‑bit matches 32‑bit accuracy across RoBERTa, GPT‑2, Swin‑T, and LLaMA instruction tuning, with large memory reductions and throughput gains under offloading—enabling fine‑tuning under tight GPU budgets.
> - Trend: from format changes alone to distribution‑aware quantization (and factorization) tailored to optimizer moments, unlocking 4‑bit training stability at scale.
> 
> 4) Objective choice in self‑supervised pretraining (JEPA vs MAE):
> - Analytical deep‑linear results (NeurIPS’24) show JEPA‑style latent prediction (self‑distillation with stop‑grad) has an implicit bias toward “influential” (high regression‑coefficient) features, while MAE’s pixel‑space squared‑error prioritizes high‑variance (often noisy) components. The JEPA bias strengthens with encoder depth L and flips feature learning order when variance and influence disagree.
> - Temporal generative tests further support JEPA’s preference for predictive, lower‑variance “slow” features—aligning with the desire to avoid pixel‑reconstruction noise.
> - Trend: replacing pixel reconstruction with latent prediction to steer learning toward semantically predictive features, with depth amplifying the effect.
> 
> 5) Excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) architectural constraints and learning dynamics:
> - Dale’s‑law RNNs: the main limiter is not signs per se, but spectral pathologies of the recurrent weight matrix. The community moves from naïve ColEI sign constraints (multimodal, dispersed singular spectra, unstable learning) to DANN‑style EI architectures that match standard RNN performance by achieving unimodal clustered spectra.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) emerges as a predictive metric of trainability; performance worsens for small networks and low inhibitory ratios due to spectral dispersion, and improves with larger width even if the largest singular value grows—highlighting the role of the entire spectrum.
> - Trend: biologically inspired constraints are reconciled with learnability by prioritizing spectral health at initialization; spectrum (not just sign) governs stability and sample efficiency in time‑series tasks.
> 
> 6) Training regimes, metrics, and toolchains:
> - Optimizers: SGD remains standard in detection; Adam/AdamW is the norm for Transformers, with low‑bit states now practical. 
> - Metrics: beyond AP, crowd‑aware MR−2/mMR−2 for detection, F1/Precision/Recall for part association and QA (SQuAD), and PSNR/LPIPS plus depth L1 for rendering/geometry.
> - Acceleration: widespread use of Instant‑NGP/NerfAcc to keep physically faithful rendering (including transient lidar) tractable.
> 
> Overall trajectory (2023–2024):
> - Move from heuristics/surrogates (two‑stage association, point‑cloud supervision, pixel reconstruction, sign‑only EI constraints) to principled objectives and parameterizations that respect the data‑generation process (transient lidar rendering), the optimizer’s statistics (4‑bit, zero‑point‑aware quantization), the representational goal (JEPA’s latent prediction bias), and architectural biology (spectral properties under Dale’s law). These shifts simultaneously improve scalability (more parts, few‑view lidar, larger models on limited GPUs) and robustness (crowds, unstable spectra), aligning method design with the needs of robotics stacks that must associate parts to bodies, simulate sensors along time t, and fine‑tune large Transformers under strict memory budgets while tracking task metrics such as F1 and Precision.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains works addressing all four of your building blocks. The development trends across them are:
> 
> **1. Detection with part–body linking (PBADet, ICLR 2024).** Trend: from **two-stage** pipelines (heuristic matching in Zhou et al. 2018; learned association scores in BodyHands 2022) and **anchor-based body-to-part offsets** (BPJDet) toward a **one-stage anchor-free** detector using a single **part-to-body center offset**. This removes representation redundancy (length 15→10), stays valid under occlusion, scales to any number of parts, and uses multi-scale features + task-alignment loss. It reports AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, and notably beats the pose estimator ED-Pose on **Precision/Recall/F1** for hands/feet, and is trained with **SGD** on tight GPU budgets (4×V100, mixed precision).
> 
> **2. Raw single-photon lidar simulation/reconstruction (Transient NeRF, NeurIPS 2023).** Trend: from lidar/point-cloud **supervision of RGB-only NeRFs** (DS-NeRF, Urban NeRF) toward modeling the actual **time-resolved volume rendering equation** on raw SPAD photon-count histograms. It renders **transient (x–y–t) views**, incorporating single-bounce transport, sensor impulse response, and Poisson noise, built on efficient Instant-NGP/NerfAcc hash grids — giving SOTA few-view (2–5) geometry and appearance.
> 
> **3. Memory-lean Transformer fine-tuning (4-bit optimizers, NeurIPS 2023).** Trend: **32-bit → 8-bit block-wise → 4-bit optimizer states**, via smaller block size (B128), row+column (rank-1) normalization, a zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the second moment, and factorization. It matches 32-bit AdamW across RoBERTa/Swin/GPT-2/Transformer/LLaMA, cutting memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
> 
> **4. JEPA vs pixel reconstruction, EI constraints, and objective analyses.**
> - *JEPA* (NeurIPS 2024): trend from input-space **reconstruction (MAE)** toward **latent-space predictive (JEPA/self-distillation)** pretraining; theory shows JEPA implicitly biases toward high-influence, low-variance features and avoids noisy ones.
> - *Dale's Law* (NeurIPS 2023): trend from "sign constraints impair learning" toward showing the impairment stems mostly from **spectral properties** (multimodal/dispersed singular values) of the recurrent weight matrix; redesigned DANN architectures learn well while respecting E/I constraints.
> - *Objective analyses on MNIST/CIFAR-100*: contrastive-learning work analyzes **cosine-similarity** objectives (InfoNCE optimal negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1), mini-batch variance effects) on CIFAR-10/100; a Hessian-structure study trains LeNet/ResNet on **MNIST/CIFAR-100 with SGD/Adam**, while the JEPA paper contrasts latent (similarity-based) vs squared-error reconstruction objectives.
> 
> **Overall trend:** a move from multi-stage/heuristic, representation-heavy, full-precision and pixel-reconstruction approaches toward **unified one-stage anchor-free formulations**, **sensor-physics-aware neural rendering**, **aggressively quantized/factorized optimizer states**, **latent-space self-supervised objectives**, and **principled spectral/objective analyses** — all aimed at better performance under tight compute budgets.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — four works in this collection collectively cover all your needs:
> 
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free detection with part–body association. It links hands/face/feet to bodies in crowded scenes via a single part-to-body center offset, replacing two-stage heuristic/learned association (Zhou 2018, BodyHands) and anchor-based BPJDet's bulky body-to-part offsets. Evaluated with AP, precision, recall, and F1 on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman.
> 
> 2. **Transient Neural Radiance Fields (NeurIPS 2023)** — renders raw single-photon lidar time-resolved photon-count histograms from novel views using a time-resolved (along t) volume rendering equation with Poisson noise, plus intensity/depth maps. Built on hash-grid Instant-NGP/NerfAcc for efficiency; outperforms point-cloud-supervised RGB NeRFs (DS-NeRF, Urban NeRF) from 2–5 views, directly serving lidar simulation for robotics planning.
> 
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — memory-lean fine-tuning of large Transformers by compressing Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4 bits: smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the second moment, plus optional factorization. Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD (F1), ImageNet, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning, cutting memory up to ~57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
> 
> 4. **Self-supervised analyses** — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024) shows JEPA-style latent prediction is implicitly biased toward high-influence features vs MAE's pixel-reconstruction (squared-error) objective, explaining JEPA's advantage; "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" analyzes cosine-similarity structure of contrastive embeddings, proving optimal positive/negative similarities and adding a variance-reduction loss that improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet; "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023) analyzes excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) sign-constrained networks, tracing poor training to the initial recurrent weight spectrum (not the sign constraints) and showing gradient clipping mitigates it — tested on sequential MNIST and object-recognition benchmarks.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:**
> - **Detection**: multi-stage/anchor-based → unified one-stage anchor-free detection with built-in part–body association (simpler representations, better scalability, and direct F1/Precision evaluation).
> - **Lidar/rendering**: RGB NeRF with preprocessed point-cloud supervision → transient NeRF that models and renders the raw time-resolved sensor measurement itself, improving few-view geometry and appearance.
> - **Optimizers**: full 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit state compression, with increasingly fine-grained quantization (block-wise → rank-1/zero-point-excluded → factorized), enabling large-model fine-tuning under tight GPU budgets with negligible accuracy loss.
> - **Self-supervised learning**: pixel-reconstruction (MAE) → JEPA latent-space prediction, backed by theoretical analysis of implicit bias and cosine-similarity statistics; E/I-constrained architectures are analyzed mechanistically (spectral structure) and fixed via training interventions rather than discarded.

</details>

### paperscope:trend:372 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) selecting a small subset of open, unlabeled text to warm‑start fine‑tuning large language models using feature embeddings and distributional matching (rather than full continued pretraining), compatible with SFT/LoRA workflows and reported with F1/Precision style metrics; (2) memory‑lean training via compressing optimizer states to very low bitwidth while keeping Adam/AdamW/SGD behavior for Transformer backbones; (3) analyses of non‑contrastive self‑supervised objectives that predict in latent space (vs reconstruction losses like MSE) and their implicit bias in deep networks; (4) a spectral perspective on recurrent models with separate excitatory/inhibitory units (Dale‑style constraints) for stability/interpretability; and (5) an anchor‑free, one‑stage detector that associates parts to their parent instances on whole‑body benchmarks (e.g., COCO‑like), with attention backbones and standard detection metrics. Prefer works that discuss fine‑tuning, self‑supervised learning, cosine‑style similarity/embeddings, and common optimizers (Adam/AdamW).Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five methods converge on a common theme: replace brute‑force data/compute with principled, scalable mechanisms that preserve or improve task performance under tight budgets.
> 
> 1) Pre‑fine‑tuning via small, unlabeled subsets (ICLR 2024, GOT‑D)
> - Shift in objective: from “distribution matching” that ignores the pre‑training distribution to “pre‑training distribution shifting.” GOT‑D selects samples whose gradients (from the dual of an optimal transport objective) most efficiently pull the pre‑training distribution toward the target task. This corrects the mismatch seen when the fine‑tuned model still behaves like a mixture of pre‑training and fine‑tuning data (low‑data, few‑epoch regime).
> - Scalability and practicality: OT with entropy regularization and GPU parallelism scales to millions of samples in minutes. Selection budgets are small (e.g., 50k), yet deliver consistent gains across detoxification, domain adaptation, and GLUE; results are reported with standard downstream metrics (e.g., F1, accuracy), and the pipeline uses feature embeddings (e.g., distilled‑BERT) to compute distances.
> - Evolution over time: from continued pre‑training on massive corpora to lightweight pre‑fine‑tuning that measurably reduces target data/compute while improving final fine‑tuning efficacy.
> 
> 2) Memory‑lean training with low‑bit optimizer states (NeurIPS 2023, 4‑bit optimizers)
> - Bitwidth progression: from 16‑bit/8‑bit states to 4‑bit states for Adam/AdamW/SGDM without sacrificing training dynamics on Transformer backbones.
> - Technical advances enabling the drop to 4‑bit: smaller block sizes to handle heterogeneous outliers in moments; rank‑1 (row/column) normalization; and zero‑point‑free quantization for the second moment to avoid catastrophic direction errors. A hybrid with factorization further reduces memory.
> - Outcomes and scale: comparable or better performance on language (GLUE, SQuAD), machine translation, image classification, and instruction tuning tasks; large memory savings enable bigger models/training under fixed budgets. Implementations integrate with standard toolchains (AdamW, SGD) and parameter‑efficient code paths (e.g., LoRA codebase used for some experiments), keeping workflows familiar while improving throughput/memory.
> 
> 3) Non‑contrastive SSL that predicts in latent space (NeurIPS 2024, JEPA analysis)
> - Objective shift: from reconstruction losses (e.g., MSE in MAE) to joint‑embedding predictive objectives (self‑distillation JEPA). In deep linear analysis, JEPA exhibits an implicit bias toward high‑influence (predictive, low‑variance) features, whereas MAE prioritizes high‑covariance (possibly noisy) features.
> - Depth dependence and learning dynamics: deeper encoders amplify JEPA’s bias, producing step‑wise, greedy feature acquisition that favors semantically useful directions early. This explains empirical reports that JEPA‑style pretext tasks often learn more task‑relevant representations faster than reconstruction.
> - Trend: theoretical grounding for the community’s move from reconstruction toward prediction in latent space, clarifying when and why non‑contrastive SSL leads to better data/compute efficiency.
> 
> 4) Spectral perspective for EI‑constrained RNNs (NeurIPS 2023, Dale’s Law)
> - Problem reframed: poor performance of sign‑constrained (E/I) RNNs (Column EI) is shown to stem primarily from pathological singular‑value spectra (multimodal, dispersed), not sign constraints alone.
> - Architectural evolution: recurrent DANNs (EI networks inspired by fast inhibitory circuits) achieve unimodal, clustered spectra similar to standard RNNs, yielding strong learning while respecting Dale’s Law.
> - Stability/interpretability metric: normalized SVD entropy (NSE) emerges as a practical predictor of trainability; larger networks and balanced E/I ratios improve spectra and performance. The field trend is toward spectral diagnostics and initialization/design that preserve stability and learning under biological constraints.
> 
> 5) Anchor‑free, one‑stage part‑to‑body association (ICLR 2024, PBADet)
> - Representation shift: from body‑to‑part (anchor‑based, multi‑stage) to part‑to‑body center offsets in an anchor‑free, one‑stage detector. This reduces representation length (from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2), avoids invalid offsets when parts are occluded, and scales to arbitrary part sets without exploding complexity.
> - Training/runtime pragmatics: built atop modern one‑stage heads (e.g., YOLOv5/7 with anchor‑free heads), task‑alignment learning (à la TOOD) replaces centerness branches; standard optimizers (SGD) and multi‑scale features are used. Evaluated with standard detection metrics (AP, mMR) on COCO‑style whole‑body benchmarks (BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts), with qualitative/quantitative improvements and simpler decoding.
> - Trend: unify detection and association in a single forward pass with reduced overhead, improving scalability and robustness in crowded/occluded settings.
> 
> Cross‑cutting trajectory (2019–2024)
> - From heuristics to principled, theory‑backed tools: OT‑gradient selection for pre‑fine‑tuning; spectral analysis for EI networks; dynamical analyses for SSL objectives. These theories now directly inform practical pipelines.
> - From more data/precision to smarter data/precision: lightweight pre‑fine‑tuning replaces massive continued pre‑training; 4‑bit optimizer states (plus factorization) replace memory‑heavy training states; anchor‑free, offset‑based detection replaces anchor‑heavy multi‑stage association.
> - Constant compatibility with standard stacks: methods integrate with common optimizers (Adam/AdamW/SGD), SFT/parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning codepaths, and mainstream backbones (Transformers/YOLO), and report standard metrics (F1/Precision/Recall, AP, BLEU), easing adoption at scale.
> 
> Net effect: Across data selection, optimization, representation learning, biologically constrained RNNs, and detection, the field is converging on scalable, compute‑aware designs that are theoretically motivated and empirically validated—achieving more with less while maintaining compatibility with prevailing training/fine‑tuning workflows and benchmarks.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers matching your criteria (all from the provided collection):
> 
> 1. **Data-selection warm-start for LLM fine-tuning** — *GOT-D: Optimizing Gradient-based Data Selection for Pre-fine-tuning Large Language Models* (ICLR 2024). Selects a small subset of open unlabeled text to pre-fine-tune LLMs, using sentence-transformer feature embeddings + optimal-transport distributional matching (nudging the pretraining distribution toward the target) instead of full continued pretraining; reported with F1/GLUE/toxicity metrics, scaling to millions of samples in ~1 GPU hour.
> 
> 2. **Memory-lean training via low-bit optimizer states** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023). Compresses Adam/AdamW (and SGDM-style) first/second moments to 4-bit via smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, and factorization; keeps Adam/AdamW convergence on Transformers (RoBERTa, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) with up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 
> 3. **Implicit bias of latent-space SSL objectives** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes non-contrastive JEPA objectives that predict in latent space vs. reconstruction (MAE/MSE); shows via deep linear networks that JEPA is biased toward high-influence features, while reconstruction prioritizes high-variance/noisy subspaces.
> 
> 4. **Spectral view of Dale-constrained recurrent models** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023). Shows that for E/I (excitatory/inhibitory) recurrent networks, the singular-value spectrum at initialization (multimodal, dispersed in ColEI) matters more than sign constraints for stability/learning; proposes normalized SVD entropy as a diagnostic.
> 
> 5. **Anchor-free one-stage part–body association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Detects parts (hands, face) and associates them to parent bodies via a single part-to-body center offset on COCO-WholeBody/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman, using YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones, task-alignment learning, and standard AP/F1 metrics.
> 
> **Development trend across the five works:**
> 
> - **Efficiency of adaptation**: from expensive full continued pretraining toward principled, cheap data selection (embeddings + distributional matching) that warms up fine-tuning, and from 32-bit/8-bit optimizer states toward 4-bit quantized/factorized states, keeping standard optimizers' (Adam/AdamW) behavior while enabling larger models on limited memory.
> - **Self-supervised learning**: from contrastive to non-contrastive latent-space prediction (JEPA), with theory replacing heuristics — deep-linear analyses revealing implicit bias (influential vs. variance-explaining features) rather than relying on reconstruction losses.
> - **Recurrent/structured models**: from treating sign constraints (Dale's Law) as the cause of poor learning to spectral analysis showing initialization spectra dominate; diagnostics (NSE) guide architecture/initialization design for stability and interpretability.
> - **Detection**: from multi-stage/anchor-based part detectors to unified one-stage anchor-free designs where association is a single learned offset, scaling to whole-body benchmarks with better AP/F1 — a general move toward simpler, joint, end-to-end formulations.
> 
> Common thread: replacing heuristic/expensive components (data, optimizer states, losses, constraints, association pipelines) with principled, cheaper, and theoretically motivated alternatives that preserve or improve standard metrics.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers from the collection that best match your criteria:
> 
> 1. **Data selection for warm-starting fine-tuning**: *Get More for Less: Principled Data Selection for Warming Up Fine-Tuning in LLMs* (GOT-D, ICLR 2024) — selects a small subset from open unlabeled data via the gradient of an Optimal Transport (distributional-matching) distance, shifting the pre-training distribution toward the target; runs on embeddings (sentence-transformer nearly as good as distilled BERT), is used for "pre-fine-tuning" rather than full continued pretraining, and reports F1/GLUE improvements (e.g., +1.04–3.13% over vanilla BERT). Note: it is selection for fine-tuning generally, not explicitly LoRA-specific.
> 
> 2. **Memory-lean training via low-bit optimizer states**: *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023) — compresses Adam/AdamW (and SGDM) first/second moments to 4-bit (block B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantization), keeping Adam/AdamW behavior on Transformer backbones (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) with up to 57.7% memory savings, evaluated on F1/GLUE etc.
> 
> 3. **Non-contrastive SSL objective analysis**: *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024) — analyzes non-contrastive JEPA objectives that predict in latent space (vs. MAE-style MSE reconstruction), proving an implicit bias toward high-influence ("slow") features in deep networks, unlike reconstruction losses that prioritize high-variance/noisy features.
> 
> 4. **Spectral perspective on Dale-constrained RNNs**: *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023) — studies recurrent E/I (excitatory/inhibitory) models with Dale-style sign constraints; shows the initial recurrent-weight singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed for simple ColEI partitioning vs. unimodal for DANN/standard RNNs) matters more than sign constraints for stability/learning, with normalized SVD entropy as a predictive diagnostic.
> 
> 5. **Anchor-free part-body detection**: *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free detector associating parts to their parent bodies via a single part-to-body center offset; validated on COCO-WholeBody-style/COCO-derived benchmarks (COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman) with standard AP/F1 metrics. Caveat: it uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 CNN backbones (anchor-free heads), not attention/Transformer backbones.
> 
> **Development trend of their methods**:
> - **Efficiency**: Data/optimizer-level efficiency moves from full continued pretraining to cheap distribution-matched *data selection* over embeddings (GOT-D), and from 32-bit optimizer states to *4-bit quantized moments* that preserve Adam/AdamW convergence (4-bit optimizers) — both enable fine-tuning of larger LLMs on limited GPUs.
> - **From empirics to theory**: SSL work shifts from designing contrastive/reconstruction losses to *characterizing implicit bias* of latent-space prediction objectives (JEPA vs. MAE) via deep linear network dynamics; likewise, Dale-constrained RNN analysis moves from sign-constraint debates to *spectral properties* at initialization as the determinant of trainability/stability.
> - **From two-stage/anchor-based to one-stage/anchor-free**: Part-body association evolves from heuristic matching or anchor-based multi-offset representations (BPJDet) to a *single part-to-body offset* in one-stage anchor-free detectors, simplifying representation and post-processing while keeping detection quality.
> - **Common thread**: emphasis on *embedding/representation-level reasoning* (feature embeddings in selection, latent-space prediction in SSL, spectral singular-value analysis in RNNs), *standard optimizers (Adam/AdamW)* in efficiency work, and *distributional matching* as a principled principle across data selection.

</details>

### paperscope:trend:378 — 评分与执行路径对照

I’m also interested in near‑linear runtime discussions, SFT backbones, ResNet‑50 baselines, and clean‑label subsets used for calibration.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.
