Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper development trends by topic:
> 
> (a) One‑stage anchor‑free part–body association detectors:
> - Shift from two‑stage, anchor‑based and heuristic association (e.g., earlier YOLO/Faster‑RCNN baselines, ResNet‑50 backbones in COCOHumanParts tables) toward one‑stage, anchor‑free designs with task‑aligned learning (TOOD/FCOS) and multi‑scale dense heads.
> - Representation evolves from body‑to‑part offsets (BPJDet) to a single part‑to‑body center offset (PBADet), reducing representation from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2 and simplifying post‑processing (distance‑based decoding instead of complex matching).
> - Scalability improves with the single offset remaining valid even under occlusion and as the number of parts grows; performance gains are reported across AP, F1, Precision, and mMR−2 on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman.
> - Training remains practical (SGD, task alignment, multi‑scale heads), while evaluation moves beyond AP to include joint association metrics (conditional accuracy, joint AP) reflecting the method’s end‑to‑end association quality.
> 
> (b) Spectral analyses of EI recurrent nets:
> - The focus moves from sign constraints (simple Column EI) to spectral properties at initialization as the primary determinant of training quality under squared‑error (adding problem) and log‑loss (sequential MNIST, language modeling).
> - Findings show Column EI produces dispersed, multimodal singular value spectra; well‑performing RNNs/DANNs are unimodal/clustered (quarter‑circle law). Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) emerges as a pathology measure predicting learning outcomes.
> - Practical design trend: tune inhibitory ratio and network width to control spectrum (more clustering at larger size or more balanced E/I), use gradient clipping for stability, and target spectra resembling standard RNNs to enable robust training across deep networks.
> 
> (c) Joint‑embedding self‑supervision vs. masked reconstruction:
> - Movement away from masked autoencoding towards JEPA/self‑distillation objectives that predict latent targets (StopGrad) to avoid noisy features.
> - In deep linear settings, JEPA exhibits an implicit bias toward high‑influence features (large regression coefficients), especially as encoder depth increases, whereas MAE prioritizes highly covarying components; this explains empirical robustness to noise.
> - Experiments span classic vision datasets (MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR‑100) and a simple temporal model, highlighting time‑series implications and the depth‑dependent shift in learning order under squared losses.
> 
> (d) Anytime‑valid RCPS for low‑risk deployment:
> - Progression from batch RCPS to sequential, anytime‑valid guarantees via e‑processes/betting that hold simultaneously over time steps.
> - Introduction of active labeling budgets: label only informative points using inverse propensity‑weighted martingales; incorporate predictors to reduce variance and improve utility under a fixed budget.
> - Characterization of log‑optimal labeling/predictor design and regret bounds links estimation error directly to the wealth process growth rate, enabling label‑efficient online calibration.
> 
> (e) Instruction‑tuned, permissively licensed code LLMs:
> - Transition from synthetic, non‑permissive instruction sources to large, permissive corpora (COMMITPACK) built from Git commits—natural alignment of human instructions (messages) and code changes.
> - Expansion of evaluation beyond HumanEval Python synthesis to HUMANEVALPACK (repair, explain, synthesize) across six languages; synthesis performance is nearing saturation, pushing research toward repair/explanation.
> - Fine‑tuning base code models (e.g., StarCoder 16B, CodeGeeX2 6B) on filtered high‑quality subsets (COMMITPACKFT + natural language data) improves generalization across languages and tasks, with performance correlating to pretraining language weight; practical diagrams and pass@1 metrics standardize evaluation.
> 
> Cross‑cutting characteristics observed over time:
> - Scalability and efficiency: detectors reduce representation and post‑processing complexity; RCPS methods reduce labels via active sampling; JEPA avoids noisy subspaces with depth‑dependent selection; code LLMs rely on permissive, large‑scale but filtered datasets for efficient instruction tuning.
> - Training/evaluation modernization: anchor‑free, task‑aligned detection heads; spectrum‑aware EI RNN design; self‑distillation in SSL; e‑process‑based anytime guarantees; multi‑task, multi‑language code benchmarks.
> - Metrics diversify to capture end‑to‑end utility: AP/F1/Precision/mMR−2 in detection, NSE for spectral health, pass@k for code tasks, and time‑uniform risk bounds for RCPS, reflecting a broader shift toward rigorous, deployment‑oriented validation.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Research found per area
> 
> **(a) Part–body association detection** — PBADet (ICLR 2024): a one-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/v7 backbones) that replaces multi-stage, anchor-based, body-to-part offset designs with a **single part-to-body center offset**. It guarantees one-to-one part–body correspondence, simplifying post-processing, and reports precise metrics (Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP on BodyHands; AP/MR on COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman; Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose).
> 
> **(b) Spectral analyses of biologically constrained RNNs** — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023): compares standard RNNs, ColEI (column-constrained excitatory/inhibitory), and recurrent DANNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition. It shows the **initial recurrent weight spectrum (not sign constraints) governs learning**; ColEI has multimodal/dispersed singular values; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization predicts final error; gradient clipping helps. Related spectral/optimization studies: power-law Hessian spectra of well-trained networks (SGD vs random init; many optimizers; batch-size phases; LoRA vs full fine-tuning), and gradient-flow analysis of shallow ReLU nets under square loss with small initialization.
> 
> **(c) Joint-embedding self-supervision** — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024): analyzes JEPA self-distillation (predicting **latent targets**) vs MAE (masked reconstruction in input space). It proves JEPA prioritizes high-influence/low-noise features (biased toward high regression coefficients, increasingly with depth), while MAE learns high-variance, noisy features; validated with deep linear networks and ImageNet I-JEPA vs MAE experiments (CCA with PCA subspaces). Related: JEPA focuses on slow features; LDReg regularizes local dimensionality for SSL (ResNet-50/ViT baselines).
> 
> **(d) Anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets** — "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets": extends RCPS to sequential, adaptively collected data with **e-process/betting (testing-by-betting) formulations**, Ville's inequality guarantees, **active labeling under a label budget**, inverse-propensity weighting, and ML-based risk predictors as control variates (optimal predictor = conditional risk; optimal labeling policy ∝ conditional risk std). Label-efficient on simulations and ImageNet.
> 
> **(e) Instruction tuning of code LLMs** — OctoPack: permissively licensed CommitPack (4TB Git commits) + HumanEvalPack (fix/explain/synthesize across 6 languages); instruction-tunes StarCoder (SFT) into OctoCoder (46.2% pass@1 Python, best permissively licensed model). NEFTune: adding noise to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning (LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval 29.8→64.7), with embedding-similarity analysis (top singular values, token-flip/nearest-neighbor projections). TuCo: decomposes transformer forward passes into pre-training/fine-tuning components, using **embedding-space projection diagrams and angular similarity** (projection norms) to quantify per-prompt tuning contribution. CodeSteer: SFT+DPO fine-tuning of Llama-3.1-8B for code/text steering.
> 
> **Cross-cutting interests:** near-linear/output-sensitive runtime appears in parametric DP for ML (Clarkson-based cell enumeration) and in the one-hour GOT-D data-selection pipeline; **SFT backbones** (StarCoder, Llama-3.1-8B); **ResNet-50 baselines** (LDReg SSL); **clean-label vs noisy-label spectral analyses** and clean gold-standard calibration subsets (Hessian paper, DSL paper, GOT-D clean variants).
> 
> ## Development trend summary
> 
> - **(a)** From multi-stage, anchor-based, body-to-part offset detectors (BPJDet, HierR-CNN) toward **single-stage, anchor-free, part-to-body offsets** with task-alignment learning — fewer hyperparameters, scalable to many parts, simpler post-processing, better AP/F1 metrics.
> - **(b)** From treating sign constraints as the cause of poor EI learning to **spectral-property explanations** — moving from static analysis of trained weights toward **initialization-time spectral diagnostics** (NSE, power-law Hessian structure) that predict trainability/generalization across optimizers and losses, including LoRA vs full fine-tuning.
> - **(c)** From reconstruction-based SSL (MAE) to **latent-space prediction (JEPA/self-distillation)**, with theory showing an implicit bias toward influential, noise-free features; trend is toward *explaining* why latent prediction generalizes (deep linear dynamics, critical times, spectral/feature-ordering analysis).
> - **(d)** From static, one-shot risk control (RCPS, conformal) to **sequential, anytime-valid guarantees via e-processes/betting**, combined with **active labeling and learned risk predictors** to reduce label cost while preserving guarantees.
> - **(e)** From closed-source/distillation-based instruction data to **permissively licensed datasets and open models**, with full SFT (OctoPack, CodeSteer) and embedding-level tricks (NEFTune noise, TuCo decomposition with angular/projection diagrams) for improving and *interpreting* instruction-tuned code LLMs, evaluated on HumanEval-style execution benchmarks (pass@1).
> 
> Overall trend: **simplification of pipelines (one-stage, anchor-free, latent prediction, anytime-valid sequential guarantees) paired with increasingly principled spectral/statistical analyses (initialization spectra, Hessian power laws, e-processes, implicit biases) and openness/permissiveness (open data, open models, embedding-level interpretability)**.
> 
> *Note:* the specific classic datasets MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 for JEPA experiments are not all directly present — the JEPA analysis uses ImageNet; sequential MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 appear in the RNN/Hessian works.

**community 最终答案**

> I have gathered substantial evidence across the five research areas. Let me summarize the development trend of the methods.
> 
> ## Development Trend Summary
> 
> **(a) One-stage anchor-free part–body association.** PBADet (ICLR 2024) is the representative work. Development: traditional methods moved from two-stage heuristics/anchor-based detectors (e.g., hand-body heuristic matching, BodyHands, anchor-based BPJDet with body-to-part center offsets) toward a single one-stage anchor-free detector. The trend is toward simpler, more scalable representations: instead of growing the object representation with each body part (BPJDet's length-15 representation), PBADet uses one compact part-to-body center offset (length-10) over multi-scale feature maps, with classification/localization/displacement branches, task-alignment learning, and streamlined post-processing that guarantees one-to-one part–body correspondence. It reports precise metrics (Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP, and higher Precision/Recall/F1 vs. ED-Pose) and is a universal framework extending even to quadruped part–body association.
> 
> **(b) Spectral analyses of biologically-constrained RNNs.** "Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023) shows the trend from attributing poor EI-network learning to sign constraints toward understanding it via the spectral properties of the recurrent weight matrix at initialization. Spectral analyses (singular-value distributions, Marchenko-Pastur/quarter-circle laws, normalized SVD entropy) reveal that the ColEI partitioned spectrum is multimodal/dispersed while standard RNNs and Dale's ANNs (DANN) are unimodal/clustered; initialization spectra matter more than sign constraints, and gradient clipping plus SVD-entropy diagnostics predict training success. Relatedly, "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" shows how SGD optimization shapes deep networks—well-trained nets exhibit power-law Hessian spectra while random-initialized ones do not, linking initialization/optimizer choice to generalization across squared-error-like and classification settings.
> 
> **(c) Joint-embedding self-supervised learning predicting latent targets.** The JEPA/deep-linear self-distillation analysis ("How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features", NeurIPS 2024) is the conceptual anchor: the trend is from masked reconstruction (MAE, which predicts in data space and picks up noisy pixels) toward joint-embedding predictive architectures that predict latent targets, which carry an implicit bias to learn high-influence features and suppress noise. Experiments (e.g., CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet with ResNet backbones, plus MNIST-style linear-network dynamics in the related spectral work) confirm latent-space prediction yields cleaner representations. Supporting SSL work (embedding-similarity analysis on CIFAR/ImageNet with ResNet-18/50 baselines; LDReg regularization) reinforces the trend toward feature-quality regularization rather than raw reconstruction.
> 
> **(d) Anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets.** "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" extends Bates et al.'s static RCPS to the sequential/streaming setting. The trend is from single-shot conformal-style risk control toward time-uniform, anytime-valid guarantees valid under adaptive data collection and adaptive stopping, built on e-processes and testing-by-betting (gambling with virtual wealth, Waudby-Smith–Ramdas betting e-processes), inverse propensity weighting for active labeling, control-variate predictors from the ML model to reduce variance, optimal labeling policies proportional to conditional risk std-dev, and regret bounds for label-efficient convergence toward β*. This supports low-risk deployment with explicit label budgets.
> 
> **(e) Instruction tuning of permissively-licensed code LLMs.** OctoPack (OctoCoder) represents the trend: rather than distilling closed OpenAI-API models (PanGu-Coder2, WizardCoder, InstructCodeT5+—considered non-permissive), it instruction-tunes open models (StarCoder) end-to-end on permissive data (4TB CommitPack of Git commits, filtered CommitPackFT, OASST), evaluated on HumanEvalPack (code synthesis/repair/explanation across 6 languages, pass@1/pass@k). Ablations show CommitPackFT is critical for repair, natural-language targets for explanation, and mixing data helps. The overall trend is toward end-to-end instruction tuning on open, permissively-licensed data (with parameter-efficient methods like LoRA and noisy-embedding augmentation NEFTune as complementary techniques) rather than imitation of closed models.
> 
> **Overall cross-cutting trend.** The five lines of work share a common direction: replacing complex, rigid, or closed components with simpler, open, and theoretically-grounded ones—anchor-based multi-stage detection → single compact anchor-free offset; sign-constraint explanations → spectral/initialization diagnostics; masked pixel reconstruction → latent-target prediction; static fixed-time guarantees → anytime-valid e-process/betting guarantees; and closed-model distillation → permissively-licensed end-to-end (or LoRA) instruction tuning—each validated with precise metrics, classic baselines (ResNet-50, HumanEval, MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100), clean-label calibration data, and runtime/regret analyses.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper development trends (2016–2025) that match the query’s needs converge along five axes: vision association in crowds, low‑bit optimization for memory, self‑supervised pretraining bias, transformer‑based conditional guidance for code/text, and biologically constrained RNNs.
> 
> 1) Vision: from anchor‑based, multi‑stage to anchor‑free, one‑stage association (2019→2024)
> - Earlier pipelines (Faster R‑CNN/YOLO anchors; body‑to‑part offsets) struggled to scale across many parts and occlusions. PBADet (ICLR’24) extends anchor‑free detectors (FCOS/TOOD) with a single part‑to‑body center offset head on multi‑scale features, replacing K body‑to‑part offsets with one offset per part.
> - Trend characteristics: (a) scalability: representation length drops from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2, letting one model handle variable part sets; (b) robustness: one‑to‑one part‑to‑body decoding simplifies association in crowds; (c) learning: task‑aligned classification/localization (IoU + DFL + CE) replaces centerness, improving consistency; (d) practice: trained with SGD on COCO‑style data; evaluated with AP and mMR on COCO‑HumanParts/CrowdHuman. Net result: anchor‑free, one‑stage designs become the default for COCO‑style crowded association tasks.
> 
> 2) Optimizers: from 32‑bit/8‑bit to 4‑bit states without accuracy loss (2022→2023)
> - After 8‑bit Adam, the frontier moved to 4‑bit Adam/AdamW states via finer normalization and quantization. Key advances: (a) smaller blocks and rank‑1 (row/column) normalization to handle heterogeneous outliers in the first/second moments; (b) removal of the zero‑point in second‑moment quantization (linear mapping) to avoid catastrophic update spikes; (c) optional factorization of the second moment when tensor‑shaped.
> - Trend characteristics: (a) memory/throughput: 4‑bit states reduce optimizer memory ≥2× over 8‑bit and improve offloaded training throughput; (b) generality: comparable accuracy on RoBERTa‑L/Swin‑T/GPT‑2 and LLaMA instruction tuning; (c) optimizers: AdamW/Adam remain standard; SGD still used in detection. Net result: low‑bit (down to 4‑bit) optimizer states become a practical default for tight‑memory fine‑tuning and pretraining.
> 
> 3) SSL pretraining: from pixel reconstruction (MSE) to latent prediction (JEPA) to avoid noisy features (2022→2024)
> - MAE‑style reconstruction in pixel space (MSE) emphasizes high‑variance, sometimes uninformative features. Deep linear analysis shows JEPA/self‑distillation with stop‑grad introduces an implicit bias: deep encoders prioritize influential (high regression‑coefficient) features over merely high‑variance ones, especially as depth increases.
> - Trend characteristics: (a) objective shift: from minimizing pixel MSE to predicting latent targets; (b) noise avoidance: JEPA favors semantically predictive, lower‑variance features over noisy pixels; (c) depth matters: the bias toward influential features strengthens with deeper encoders. Net result: self‑supervised pipelines increasingly prefer JEPA‑style latent prediction (often with cosine/alignment losses) when the goal is robust, semantic representations rather than raw reconstruction.
> 
> 4) Reasoning/control: from prompt heuristics to transformer‑based conditional guidance with SFT/DPO (2023→2025)
> - Heuristic system prompts and single‑model code interpreters under‑utilize symbolic computation. CodeSteer (ICML’25) introduces a small, fine‑tuned controller (SFT then DPO) that conditions a larger Task‑LLM over multiple turns, deciding when to write code vs. natural language, adapting strategy, and finalizing answers.
> - Trend characteristics: (a) controller–policy separation: a compact SFT backbone (transformer) learns to guide a larger model; (b) training: multi‑turn SFT (emphasizing late turns) plus DPO over guidance pairs; (c) checkers: self‑answer (code‑based verification) and symbolic‑complexity scoring make the controller code‑aware; (d) generalization: trained for GPT‑4o but transfers to Claude/Mistral/GPT‑3.5; (e) results: large, consistent gains on symbolic tasks vs. code interpreters and CoT‑only models (o1/R1). Net result: multi‑turn, transformer‑based conditional guidance with SFT/DPO becomes the dominant pattern for deciding code vs. text and exploiting symbolic tools.
> 
> 5) EI RNNs: from sign constraints to spectrum‑aware design for stability and learning (2016→2023)
> - Classical ColEI (column excitatory/inhibitory) constraints learned poorly, initially blamed on sign limits. New evidence shows spectral properties at initialization matter more: ColEI yields multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra; learning improves when spectra are unimodal/clustered (high normalized SVD entropy). Recurrent Dale’s ANNs (DANNs) match standard RNN learning by aligning spectra.
> - Trend characteristics: (a) what to control: singular‑value spectrum (not just signs) determines stable gradients and performance; (b) design knobs: E/I ratio, network size, gradient clipping; (c) diagnostics: normalized SVD entropy predicts trainability; (d) implication: for time‑series modeling under Dale’s Law, prioritize spectral shaping at init for stable, inhibitory/excitatory‑constrained RNNs. Net result: EI‑respecting RNNs become practical by targeting spectrum clustering instead of only enforcing sign constraints.
> 
> Cross‑cutting practice and losses
> - Optimizers and fine‑tuning: Adam/AdamW dominate (with 4‑bit states increasingly standard); SGD remains common in detection. Instruction/SFT fine‑tuning and DPO are routine in reasoning controllers; end‑to‑end full‑parameter FT appears in all domains; LoRA is used in some codebases but was not required here.
> - Objectives: detection blends classification (CE‑style) with IoU/DFL; SSL trends away from pixel‑MSE toward latent prediction; symbolic controllers rely on SFT/DPO rather than reconstruction. 
> 
> Overall trajectory (2019–2025)
> - Vision detection: anchor‑free, one‑stage multi‑head models that scale cleanly with parts (COCO‑style crowds).
> - Training efficiency: optimizer states compressed from 32‑bit→8‑bit→4‑bit with accuracy preserved and offload speedups.
> - Representation learning: self‑supervision shifts from reconstruction (MSE) to predictive latent alignment (JEPA) to avoid noisy features.
> - Reasoning/control: specialized transformer controllers (SFT/DPO) steer large LLMs between code and text, with verifier tools.
> - Neuroscience‑inspired RNNs: performance hinges on spectral initialization (NSE) rather than EI sign constraints alone.
> 
> These trends collectively satisfy the stack’s needs in the query: (i) anchor‑free part‑body detection on COCO‑style data with high precision; (ii) tight‑memory training via 4‑bit AdamW/SGD states; (iii) self‑supervised pretraining that avoids noisy pixel MSE (JEPA bias); (iv) a transformer‑based, SFT/DPO‑trained controller that chooses code vs. text; and (v) EI RNNs whose stable spectra enable principled excitatory/inhibitory time‑series modeling.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains papers covering every major component of your stack. Summary and method-development trend:
> 
> **1. Anchor-free detection (vision module)**
> - **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage, anchor-free part-body association detection — a single part-to-body center offset links hands/face to the correct person, evaluated on COCO-WholeBody/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman (body, left/right hand, face). Extends FCOS/TOOD dense prediction + task-alignment learning.
> - *Trend*: multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines (Faster R-CNN, RPN-based DA-RNN, two-stage BodyHands/BPJDet) → unified one-stage anchor-free representation with dense per-pixel prediction and one-to-one part–body association, cutting hyper-parameters and post-processing.
> 
> **2. Low-bit optimizers (tight GPU memory)**
> - **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023): pushes Adam/AdamW/SGD(M) optimizer states to 4 bits via smaller block size, rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluded linear quantization for the second moment; matches 32-bit accuracy while saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
> - *Trend*: 32-bit → 8-bit (block-wise) → 4-bit states, with better outlier handling (rank-1/row+column normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization) to make aggressive quantization lossless.
> 
> **3. JEPA-style implicit bias (self-supervised pretraining)**
> - **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024): with deep linear networks it proves JEPA (latent prediction, non-contrastive self-distillation) prioritizes high-influence/"influential" features, while MAE-style pixel reconstruction (MSE) prioritizes high-variance, often noisy, features — exactly the latent-prediction-over-reconstruction preference you want.
> - *Trend*: reconstruction-based SSL (MAE, MSE/cosine pixel alignment) → joint-embedding predictive / latent-prediction objectives, now backed by theory on implicit bias and noise suppression.
> 
> **4. Transformer conditional guidance for code/text (reasoning agent, SFT/DPO)**
> - **CodeSteer** (ICML 2025): a small steering model (Llama-3.1-8B) fine-tuned with multi-turn **SFT + DPO** decides per-turn whether the TaskLLM should solve via Python code or natural-language reasoning, guided by symbolic/self-answer checkers; boosts GPT-4o from 53.3→86.4 on SymBench.
> - Related: Neural Comprehension (CoNN + LM with sparse gating) and TokenSignature (deciding CoT vs direct answer).
> - *Trend*: pure text CoT reasoning → hybrid code/text routing; large-model reasoning steered by specialized small models trained with SFT then DPO.
> 
> **5. EI RNN spectral analyses (physiological time-series RNN)**
> - **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023): shows sign-constrained E/I (ColEI) networks fail mainly due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization, not the sign constraints themselves; DANN-style E/I RNNs keep stable, random-matrix (quarter-circle) spectra; Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) predicts learnability.
> - *Trend*: incorporating E/I constraints empirically → spectral analysis (SVD spectra, NSE) as a diagnostic/design principle for stable, learnable constrained RNNs.
> 
> **6. Practical fine-tuning, regularization, CE vs MSE**
> - **LoRA + memory tricks**: RTB fine-tunes diffusion/LLMs with **LoRA** plus stochastic timestep subsampling to fit gradients in memory; the Hessian paper (ICML 2025) analyzes LoRA fine-tuning (and finds LoRA doesn't induce full-fine-tuning power-law Hessian structure); NEFTune/QLoRA use LoRA-based instruction tuning.
> - **Regularization**: **NEFTune** (ICLR 2024) adds scaled noise to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning, reducing overfitting (higher train loss, lower test loss) and large gains on AlpacaEval — a lightweight regularizer.
> - **CE vs MSE trade-off**: no dedicated paper on this; the closest are the JEPA-vs-MAE analysis (MSE pixel reconstruction vs latent prediction), Universal Guidance (cross-entropy classifier guidance vs general losses), and data-selection/regression papers (MSE regression vs logistic cross-entropy).
> 
> **Overall trend**: a clear move toward (a) unified one-stage/anchor-free perception; (b) extreme-but-lossless state quantization for memory-constrained training; (c) latent-predictive (JEPA) SSL with theoretical implicit-bias justification instead of noisy pixel reconstruction; (d) hybrid code/text reasoning steered by SFT/DPO-trained small models; (e) spectral-principled design of biologically constrained RNNs; and (f) parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) combined with memory tricks and noisy-embedding regularization. Two caveats: there is no paper specifically titled "End-to-end LoRA" (only LoRA-as-a-tool across RTB/NEFTune/Hessian papers), and CE-vs-MSE trade-offs are only addressed indirectly through the JEPA/MAE and guidance papers.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains papers covering nearly all requested pieces, with a couple of caveats.
> 
> **Coverage per topic**
> - **Anchor-free detection**: PBADet — one-stage, anchor-free part‑body (hands/face→person) association via a single part‑to‑body center offset on multi‑scale features (YOLOv5/7 backbones, task‑alignment learning), evaluated on COCO‑style datasets (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands).
> - **Low‑bit optimizers**: "4‑bit Optimizers" — quantized AdamW/SGD(M) states with smaller blocks (B128), rank‑1 normalization, zero‑point‑excluded linear mapping for the second moment, and factorized variants; ~57% memory savings at parity with 32‑bit AdamW.
> - **JEPA implicit bias**: "Why JEPA Self‑Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" — deep‑linear analysis showing JEPA latents bias toward high‑influence (low‑variance, perceptual) features whereas MAE/reconstruction tracks variance; supports latent prediction over pixel reconstruction.
> - **Code/text conditional guidance**: CodeSteer — a small Llama‑3.1‑8B model fine‑tuned with multi‑turn SFT + DPO to steer a larger LLM between Python and natural language (SymBench, symbolic/self‑answer checkers).
> - **EI RNN spectral analysis**: "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" — ColEI vs DANN networks, singular‑value spectra, normalised SVD entropy (NSE), spectrum transplants, E/I ratio and size effects.
> - **Fine‑tuning/regularization/LoRA**: partially covered — NEFTune (noisy‑embedding regularization for instruction fine‑tuning), Themis (LoRA fine‑tuning with observation dropout), Hessian power‑law paper (LoRA‑only fine‑tuning does not induce the power‑law Hessian structure of full fine‑tuning), NFTS (searching fine‑tune/adapter placement). 
> - **CE vs MSE trade‑offs**: no dedicated paper; CE/MSE appear only incidentally (e.g., cross‑entropy in classifier guidance, square loss in ReLU implicit‑bias theory). A dedicated CE‑vs‑MSE analysis is **not** established here.
> 
> **Development trend**
> - Detection: multi‑stage, anchor‑based, heuristic association → **one‑stage anchor‑free dense prediction with an explicit part‑to‑body offset and task‑alignment**, i.e., end‑to‑end and scalable to many parts.
> - Optimization: 32‑bit → 8‑bit → **4‑bit optimizer states**, with the trend toward finer‑grained quantization (smaller blocks, rank‑1/row‑column normalization, zero‑point handling, factorization) to keep convergence lossless under tight GPU memory.
> - Self‑supervised pretraining: reconstruction (MAE, variance‑dominated) → **latent prediction (JEPA/self‑distillation)**, with theory moving from empirical results to *implicit‑bias* explanations (critical times, feature influence) and regularization (LDReg against dimensional collapse).
> - Reasoning agents: single‑modality CoT or code → **explicit code/text switching steered by a specialized small model via SFT→DPO** plus checkers; preference optimization (DPO) layered on SFT becomes standard.
> - EI RNNs: from sign‑constrained architectures that train poorly → **spectral diagnostics (NSE) and designs (DANN) whose spectra resemble standard RNNs**, showing spectra matter more than sign constraints; stable spectra via balanced E/I and size.
> - Fine‑tuning: full fine‑tuning → **parameter‑efficient LoRA** with lightweight regularization (noisy embeddings, dropout), and spectral/Hessian analyses used to understand and predict fine‑tuning behavior.

### paperscope:trend:390 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle scalable and reliable deep learning across vision, sequences, and RL: (a) a single-pass, anchor-free detector that associates human parts with the correct person; (b) analyses of recurrent nets that enforce excitatory/inhibitory sign structure and show how the singular-value spectrum at initialization, more than the sign constraints, drives learning; (c) theory for joint-embedding/self-distillation objectives (JEPA-style) in deep linear models explaining why latent prediction with cosine-like similarity and MSE/CE surrogates biases toward high-influence features; (d) memory‑lean training by quantizing Adam/SGD states to around 4 bits with smarter block/row/column scaling and zero‑free quantizers; and (e) a top‑down, LLM‑guided strategy/option generator for RL that turns natural-language subgoals into shaped rewards for Transformer agents. Please include works that discuss regularization, feature embeddings, and report metrics like F1/Precision/AUROC, and that are relevant to time‑series or vision backbones (e.g., ResNet/Transformers) and standard losses (cross‑entropy vs MSE).Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': "Development trend across the five works (2019–2025) shows a clear shift toward scalable, reliable learning via (i) simpler, more general representations in vision; (ii) principled controls of sequence model dynamics; (iii) latent-space, self-distilled representation learning; (iv) memory-lean training at optimizer/state level; and (v) top‑down, LLM‑guided exploration in RL. Together these trends reduce sample/compute/memory costs while improving stability and task coverage across vision, sequences, and control.\n\n1) Vision (part–body detection): from multi‑stage, anchor‑based to one‑stage, anchor‑free, scalable association (2024)\n- Earlier joint detectors encoded body→part offsets per part (complexity grows with number of parts K). PBADet replaces this with a single 2D part→body center offset, learned in an anchor‑free head with task‑alignment (TOOD) losses and standard SGD.\n- Trend in scalability: representation length drops from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2, keeping accuracy while supporting arbitrary part sets and occlusions. This improves AP/mMR−2/conditional accuracy on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman and yields higher Precision/Recall/F1 than pose estimators in matched comparisons.\n- Field shift: anchor‑free, multi‑scale heads (YOLOv5/7/8) generalize across human and even animal part‑to‑body association, emphasizing robust feature embeddings over hand‑crafted anchors.\n\n2) Sequences (RNNs with Dale’s Law): from sign constraints to spectrum‑aware initialization and diagnosis (2023)\n- Conventional E/I sign constraints (ColEI) harmed learning; the key driver proved to be the singular‑value spectrum at initialization, not the sign constraint itself.\n- Trend in reliability: moving to spectrum‑aware designs (e.g., recurrent DANNs, or ColEI with improved spectra) yields unimodal, clustered singular values (good NSE—normalized SVD entropy) and better stability/generalization on time‑series benchmarks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, language modeling).\n- Practical knobs that scale: network size, E/I ratio, and gradient clipping affect spectrum pathology; NSE emerges as a simple, predictive regularization/diagnosis metric for deep networks, especially small models where spectra are most fragile.\n\n3) Representation learning (JEPA vs. MAE): from pixel reconstruction to latent prediction that prioritizes influential features (2024)\n- Theoretical trend: deep linear analysis shows JEPA‑style self‑distillation (with MSE/CE surrogates and cosine‑like similarity) is biased toward high‑influence features; depth strengthens this bias. MAE prioritizes high‑variance directions; JEPA prioritizes predictive, low‑noise semantics.\n- Field shift: explains why modern joint‑embedding/self‑distillation objectives on Transformers produce robust feature embeddings for downstream tasks and why replacing reconstruction with latent prediction improves semantic selectivity.\n\n4) Training at scale: from 8‑bit to 4‑bit optimizer states with structure‑aware quantization (2023)\n- Memory trend: optimizer states drop from 8‑bit to 4‑bit by (i) smaller blocks, (ii) rank‑1 (row/column) normalization that captures heterogeneous outliers, and (iii) zero‑free quantizers to avoid “zero‑point” collapse in second moments. A hybrid path (4‑bit m, factorized v) further reduces footprint.\n- Reliability & portability: works across Transformers and CNNs (RoBERTa‑L on GLUE/SQuAD F1, Swin‑T on ImageNet, GPT‑2 on E2E‑NLG BLEU, Transformer MT on WMT14), matching 32‑bit accuracy; enables much larger models under fixed memory (e.g., from OPT‑1.3B to OPT‑6.7B; LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU). Compatible with Adam/SGD and offloading, improving throughput.\n\n5) RL exploration: from bottom‑up trial‑and‑error to top‑down, LLM‑guided strategy distributions with reward shaping (2025)\n- Method trend: a Strategist builds a distribution over policies (low‑entropy, high‑value) via an LLM‑generated strategy tree (approaches and plans), then translates natural‑language sub‑goals into dense, learned shaping rewards (trained with MSE) to guide PPO/EDE.\n- Sample‑efficiency & coverage: consistently faster convergence and discovery of more complex behaviors (e.g., breeding in Crafter) versus PPO/EDE baselines; the LLM (a Transformer) acts as conditional guidance at the strategy level, while the policy remains domain‑agnostic.\n- Unification with (4): memory‑lean optimizers and top‑down priors are complementary—quantized states make larger strategy‑conditioned agents practical; top‑down signals reduce environmental trials.\n\nCross‑cutting patterns and timelines\n- 2023: Foundations for reliability and scale—spectral diagnostics for EI RNNs (NSE) and 4‑bit optimizer states (rank‑1 normalization; zero‑free quantization). These improve stability and capacity without hurting accuracy, and they slot neatly into standard Adam/SGD training.\n- 2024: Representation built in latent space—JEPA theory clarifies why cosine‑/MSE/CE‑based self‑distillation learns predictive, semantically rich embeddings; vision moves to simpler, anchor‑free association heads that scale to many parts without re‑engineering.\n- 2025: Planning moves top‑down—strategy distributions and LLM‑derived shaping rewards guide RL to complex, long‑horizon solutions with fewer samples, and interoperate with stronger exploration (EDE) and standard backbones.\n\nWhat this means for “scalable and reliable deep learning”\n- Simpler, more general representations (anchor‑free links; latent prediction) and principled control of dynamics (spectra, NSE) reduce brittleness across vision and sequences.\n- Memory scaling at the optimizer/state level (4‑bit, factorized v) unlocks larger Transformers and longer training runs under fixed hardware, while maintaining standard losses (cross‑entropy for classification; MSE for regressors/shapers) and metrics (AP, BLEU, F1/Precision, etc.).\n- Top‑down, Transformer‑based conditional guidance (LLMs) supplies high‑level structure that bottom‑up RL lacked, accelerating exploration without bespoke action spaces.\n\nEvidence mapped to the requested entities\n- Optimizers/losses: SGD (PBADet), Adam (4‑bit optimizers; Strategist’s shaper training), CE vs. MSE (JEPA analysis; CE classification in detectors; MSE for reward‑shaping regressor).\n- Feature embeddings and cosine similarity: JEPA theory formally links latent prediction with cosine‑like similarity to semantic feature selection.\n- Transformers/CNNs: used across Swin‑T, RoBERTa, GPT‑2, LLaMA (4‑bit); LLMs (Transformers) guide RL strategies; YOLOv5/7 anchor‑free heads for detection.\n- Time‑series modeling: EI RNN analyses on adding/sequential‑MNIST/language modeling expose spectral causes of failure and fixes.\n- Metrics: AP/mMR−2/Precision/Recall/F1 for detection/pose comparisons; F1 on SQuAD, BLEU on E2E‑NLG, accuracy/correlation on GLUE, MT SacreBleu.\n\nIn short: from 2023→2025, the field converges on making deep systems both larger and safer to train (4‑bit, spectrum control) while learning more useful features (JEPA) and exploring more intelligently (LLM‑guided strategies). In vision, anchor‑free association compresses the problem while improving accuracy; in RL, top‑down strategy distributions and shaped rewards deliver the same kind of scalability and reliability that memory‑lean optimizers and latent‑space learning brought to supervised settings."}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the five papers that match each requested topic:
> 
> **(a) Vision / detection — PBADet** (doc `08b70bc…`): "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association." Single-pass, anchor-free detector that links human parts (hands, face, feet) to the correct body via a single part-to-body center offset; no anchors, no two-stage association networks. Uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 CNN backbones, multi-scale feature maps, task-alignment learning, and reports Precision/Recall/F1 and AP on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> 
> **(b) Sequences / recurrent nets — Dale's Law** (doc `e63a94c4…`): "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023). Analyzes RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNNs) on sequential MNIST, adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition. Using spectrum "transplant" experiments it shows the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed vs. unimodal, clustered) matters more than the sign constraints for learning; introduces normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as a pre-training diagnostic. Uses softmax/CE for classification/language and MSE for the adding problem.
> 
> **(c) JEPA/self-distillation theory — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`, NeurIPS 2024). Solves the learning dynamics of deep linear self-distillation (JEPA) vs. MAE under MSE-style latent objectives. Shows JEPA's implicit bias prioritizes "high-influence" (high-regression-coefficient ρ) features, while MAE orders by variance λ; the bias strengthens with depth (critical-time/depth-separation results). Related work discusses spectrum modulation and weight regularization (LDReg/WERank) to prevent collapse; ImageNet-1K CCA experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns to low-variance perceptual subspace faster than MAE.
> 
> **(d) Memory-lean training — 4-bit optimizers** (doc `8d5e1455…`): "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023). Quantizes Adam/AdamW (and SGD-family) first/second moments to 4 bits using a smaller block size (B128), smarter rank-1 (row+column) normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear/DE-0 quantizers for the second moment, optionally with factorization. Evaluated on RoBERTa-L, Swin-T (vision Transformer), GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B across NLU, image classification, QA (F1), NLG (BLEU), MT, instruction tuning — matching 32-bit with ~43–58% memory savings.
> 
> **(e) RL / LLM-guided options — Strategist** (doc `a40dc270…`, ICML 2025): "Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation." LLM-built Strategy Trees generate natural-language strategies/sub-goals (option-spirited), evaluated for value/feasibility/specificity, then converted into shaped rewards for RL agents (PPO/EDE) in the Crafter environment, improving sample efficiency and complex behaviors vs. vanilla PPO and DreamerV3. Theory shows sample complexity scales with strategy entropy rather than the full state-action space.
> 
> **Cross-cutting aspects you asked about:** Regularization/embeddings appear in (b) gradient clipping, (c) spectrum/weight regularization and feature-embedding bias, and (d) weight decay/optimizer settings; F1/Precision metrics are reported in (a) and (d, QA-F1); vision backbones (Swin-T, YOLO/CNN, ViT-related SSL) appear in (a), (c), (d), while (b) covers sequence/language models; both cross-entropy (classification/LM) and MSE (adding/regression/latent) losses are used across (b), (c), (d). AUROC and time-series backbones (e.g., LSTM/TCN, anomaly detection) do **not** appear in these five papers — the collection's other time-series work (e.g., the Synthcity library, G-Sim, RaMP) uses such metrics/backbones but is not among the matched topics.
> 
> **Development trend of the methods:** The set shows a clear shift toward *scalability and reliability via simpler, more principled designs*: (a) moving from multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines to one-stage anchor-free end-to-end detection; (b) replacing the "sign constraints are the culprit" view with spectral-at-initialization analysis that guides better EI-network initialization; (c) moving from empirical SSL to exact dynamical-theory accounts of why latent prediction (JEPA) beats reconstruction (MAE); (d) pushing optimizer-state precision from 8-bit down to 4-bit via data-aware (rank-1, zero-excluded) quantizers to democratize large-model training; and (e) shifting RL from bottom-up trial-and-error to top-down LLM-prior-guided strategic exploration with shaped rewards. Overall, the trend is from heuristic/empirical engineering toward theory-grounded, efficiency-driven (memory- and sample-wise), and prior-informed methods that preserve or improve standard metrics.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers found
> 
> **(a) PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024)
> Single-pass, anchor-free detector that associates human parts (hands, face, feet) with the correct person via a single part-to-body center offset (vs. BPJDet's body-to-part offsets). Built on YOLOv5/v7 backbones with classification, localization and displacement branches plus task-alignment loss. Beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts and reports precision, recall, and F1 (vs. ED-Pose), joint AP, MR-2.
> 
> **(b) Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Analyses RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs) on sequential MNIST, language modeling, object recognition. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the **singular-value spectrum at initialization (multimodal, dispersed) drives learning more than the sign constraints themselves**; normalised SVD entropy predicts performance. Sign constraints impair learning (~0.7–1%) but don't explain the full gap (~2.3%).
> 
> **(c) Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024)
> Theory for JEPA/self-distillation in deep linear networks: latent-space prediction (cosine-like similarity, MSE/CE surrogates) has an implicit bias toward **high-influence features (large regression coefficients)**, unlike MAE which favors high-variance/noisy features; the bias only holds for deep encoders. ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace (CCA).
> Related in the same community: *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (InfoNCE/SigLIP embedding-similarity analysis, variance-reduction regularization), and **LDReg** (regularization against local dimensional collapse, improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE on ResNet-50/ViT-B), and HASSOD (self-supervised detection with AR metrics).
> 
> **(d) 4-bit Optimizers: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Quantizes Adam/AdamW/SGD states to ~4 bits: smaller blocks (B128) for the first moment, **rank-1 normalization (row+column scales)** and **zero-free linear quantizer (DE-0/linear, excluding zero point)** for the second moment, optionally factorized (4-bitFactor). Matches 32-bit accuracy on GLUE (F1/accuracy), SQuAD (F1), ImageNet with Swin-T, E2E-NLG, machine translation; up to 57.7% memory savings; LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU.
> 
> **(e) Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation** (Strategist, ICML 2025)
> LLM-guided (top-down) strategy/option generator: builds a hierarchical Strategy Tree of natural-language strategies/subgoals, evaluates value/feasibility, and **translates subgoals into shaped rewards** (learned sub-goal progress scorer + environment reward) for Transformer-based agents (PPO; beats DreamerV3 on modified Crafter). Theory: sample complexity scales with strategy entropy rather than state-action space.
> 
> ## Development trend
> 
> - **Detection:** from two-stage/anchor-based heuristic pipelines → unified single-pass anchor-free frameworks where association is a by-product of the representation (PBADet), with task-alignment losses instead of hand-crafted matching.
> - **RNN/EI analysis:** from blaming sign constraints per se → diagnosing initialization spectra (SVD entropy) as the dominant factor, guiding initialization/architecture design.
> - **SSL theory:** from empirical observations → exact deep-linear analyses of implicit bias (JEPA vs MAE), complemented by regularization methods (LDReg, variance-reduction) to counter collapse/dimensional collapse.
> - **Memory-efficient training:** from 8-bit block-wise quantization → 4-bit states with finer row/column (rank-1) scaling, zero-point exclusion, and factorization, achieving lossless convergence across vision and language backbones.
> - **RL:** from bottom-up trial-and-error/experience-driven hierarchies → top-down LLM-generated strategy trees with zero-shot reward shaping, with theory linking strategy concentration to sample-complexity gains.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Development trends across the five works show a consistent shift toward strategies that make learning and inference more sample‑, compute‑, and memory‑efficient, while improving stability and scalability across domains (vision, language, and control). The evolution is time‑stamped and thematically aligned as follows:
> 
> 1) 2023 → Memory efficiency in optimization moves from 8‑bit to 4‑bit states
> - Trend: Optimizer state precision drops from 8‑bit to 4‑bit without accuracy loss, making full fine‑tuning feasible under tight memory.
> - Method advances: 4‑bit Adam/AdamW states via (i) smaller blocks to track outliers, (ii) zero‑point‑free quantization of the second moment, and (iii) rank‑1 normalization; optional factorization for sublinear memory on second moments.
> - Scalability: Validated on large Transformers (RoBERTa‑L, Swin‑T, Transformer‑Base, GPT‑2, LLaMA) across NLU, QA (F1/EM), MT (BLEU), and image classification (accuracy), delivering 30–58% total memory savings and preserving task scores.
> 
> 2) 2023 → Stability for biologically constrained RNNs shifts from sign constraints to spectral design
> - Trend: Dale’s‑Law RNNs transition from poorly performing “column E/I” implementations to architectures guided by spectral properties.
> - Method advances: Spectrum transplant experiments and Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) reveal spectra—not sign constraints—primarily determine learnability; higher NSE (more clustered singular values) predicts better performance.
> - Scalability/Design rules: Stability improves with larger width and balanced E/I ratios; guidance applies across tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, language modeling, naturalistic object recognition) using standard training (PyTorch, gradient clipping).
> 
> 3) 2024 → Real‑time association in vision consolidates to single‑stage, anchor‑free detection
> - Trend: From two‑stage or anchor‑based joint detection to one‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑body association.
> - Method advances: PBADet introduces a single 2D part→body center offset on multi‑scale heads with task‑aligned learning; keeps representation length fixed as parts grow, simplifying post‑processing.
> - Scalability/Metrics: Outperforms prior baselines on BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, and CrowdHuman with higher AP/Joint‑AP and lower MR/mMR; reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs. pose baselines; compatible with YOLOv5/7 backbones for fast deployment.
> 
> 4) 2024 → Self‑supervised pretraining pivots from reconstruction to predictive embeddings (JEPA)
> - Trend: MAE‑style pixel reconstruction gives way to JEPA/self‑distillation that predicts in latent space, emphasizing informative features over high‑variance noise.
> - Method advances: Deep linear analysis shows JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (high regression‑coefficient) features; depth amplifies this bias, explaining faster emergence of semantic features compared to MAE with CE/MSE/cosine‑style objectives.
> - Practical implication: Theory clarifies when and why JEPA‑like objectives yield more useful representations for downstream tasks than reconstruction.
> 
> 5) 2025 → RL planning moves from bottom‑up exploration to top‑down, LLM‑guided strategies
> - Trend: From single‑plan, bottom‑up learning to distributions over policies with explicit specificity–value trade‑offs and strategy trees.
> - Method advances: The Strategist frames the Strategy Problem (low‑entropy, high‑value policy sets), builds approach/plan nodes with an LLM, and converts natural‑language sub‑goals into dense shaping rewards via a distilled ResNet‑18; plug‑and‑play with PPO/EDE.
> - Scalability/Metrics: On Crafter variants, top‑down guidance speeds convergence and elicits more complex behaviors (e.g., breeding), improving task returns under fixed sample budgets.
> 
> Cross‑cutting patterns
> - Compute/memory scalability: 4‑bit optimizer states, factorization, and FSDP‑style training enable full fine‑tuning of larger Transformer backbones under constrained GPUs.
> - Architectural simplification for scale: One‑stage anchor‑free detection (fixed 2D offset) scales to many parts/persons; spectral criteria (NSE) provide size/ratio rules for stable E/I RNNs; JEPA leverages depth to focus on predictive features.
> - Standard training/evaluation: Methods use standard optimizers (Adam/SGD), regularization (e.g., task‑aligned learning, gradient clipping), and common metrics (AP, MR/mMR, Precision/Recall/F1, BLEU, accuracy) across language, vision, and RL.
> 
> Time‑ordered arc (what changes over time)
> - 2023: Practical training bottlenecks tackled first—memory (4‑bit optimizers) and stability in E/I RNNs (spectral metrics).
> - 2024: Inference/training pipelines simplified for scale—single‑stage anchor‑free association in vision; JEPA’s theory explains why predictive embeddings outperform reconstruction for semantics.
> - 2025: Exploration itself becomes strategic—LLMs encode domain knowledge into low‑entropy, high‑value strategy sets, then translate them into learnable rewards for off‑the‑shelf RL.
> 
> Overall: The field is converging on methods that (i) reduce resource demands (4‑bit, factorization), (ii) enforce principled stability/structure (spectral criteria, anchor‑free heads), and (iii) elevate learning from bottom‑up trial‑and‑error to top‑down, knowledge‑guided exploration—while remaining compatible with Transformer/ResNet backbones and standard metrics.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection covers all these pieces. Development trend of each line:
> 
> **1. LLM→RL planning (Strategist):** From bottom-up RL (trial-and-error, hand-designed hierarchies, manual reward shaping) toward **top-down planning** — LLMs generate Strategy Trees that are translated zero-shot into sub-goal reward signals for an RL policy, narrowing the policy search space and cutting sample complexity.
> 
> **2. Memory-efficient training:** Trend is pushing optimizer-state precision down: 32-bit → 8-bit → **4-bit Adam/AdamW states** (smaller block sizes, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, optional second-moment factorization), matching full-precision accuracy with large memory savings (e.g., LLaMA-7B on one GPU). Complemented by parameter-efficient **LoRA fine-tuning** (Themis, NFTS adapters, Hessian-spectrum studies comparing LoRA vs full fine-tuning) and data-selection pre-fine-tuning for small budgets.
> 
> **3. Part-body detection (PBADet):** From two-stage pipelines (detect hands/bodies separately, then a learned association network or heuristic matching) toward **one-stage, anchor-free detectors** with a single part-to-body center offset, built on YOLO backbones, reporting Precision/Recall/F1/AP — more streamlined and scalable for real-time hand/face-to-person association.
> 
> **4. E/I sequence stability (Dale's Law RNNs):** From simple column-constrained E/I (ColEI) networks that train poorly and unstably (multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra) toward DANN-style architectures whose spectra match standard RNNs (unimodal, clustered singular values). Key finding: **spectral properties matter more than sign constraints**, with normalized SVD entropy predicting stability/performance — guiding designs that honor E/I structure with good spectra.
> 
> **5. JEPA/self-distillation understanding:** From empirical claims ("JEPA learns semantic features") to theoretical analysis on deep linear networks showing an **implicit bias toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features**, with noise suppression strengthening with encoder depth (vs. MAE, ordered mainly by eigenvalue λ); verified via PCA/CCA on ImageNet.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection contains papers covering all five pieces, though AUROC is not the headline metric in most of them (F1/Precision are reported in PBADet; QA-F1 in the 4-bit optimizer paper).
> 
> **Paper mapping**
> 1. **LLM → reward signals for RL**: *Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation* (Strategist) — LLM builds a Strategy Tree and translates strategies into shaped rewards (node-specific LLM scores distilled into a ResNet-18 student), used with PPO/EDE/DreamerV3 backbones on Crafter.
> 2. **Tight GPU memory / low-bit states / LoRA**: *4-bit Optimizers* — 4-bit Adam/AdamW states via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, and second-moment factorization; lossless accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU). LoRA end-to-end fine-tuning is analyzed in *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (TinyLlama + LoRA; power-law Hessian does not emerge with LoRA as with full fine-tuning); LoRA fine-tuning is also used in Themis.
> 3. **Fast single-stage hand/face→person association**: *PBADet* — one-stage, anchor-free, part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5/v7 backbones; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN/BodyHands and reports AP, mMR-2, and Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose for hands/feet/face.
> 4. **E/I-structured stable sequence models with spectral properties**: *Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly* — ColEI vs DANN; finds the initial singular-value spectrum (unimodal, random-matrix-like) matters more than sign constraints, with normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicting performance and gradient clipping mitigating instability.
> 5. **JEPA self-distillation feature bias**: *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* — deep-linear analysis showing JEPA implicitly prioritizes high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) low-variance features, increasingly with depth, suppressing noisy features (unlike MAE which orders by eigenvalue λ); validated with I-JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet via CCA. Related: *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (cosine/InfoNCE similarity, negative-pair similarity, variance-reduction loss) and LDReg (local dimensional collapse regularization).
> 
> **Development trend of methods**
> - **RL**: bottom-up trial-and-error / hand-crafted sub-goals and manual reward engineering → LLM-assisted RL (action priors, sub-goal generation) → fully top-down "strategist" agents that search over strategy trees and convert text strategies into dense rewards zero-shot, with distillation to cut LLM calls and decaying shaping weights; goal is lower sample complexity and plug-and-play gains on existing RL algorithms.
> - **Memory-efficient training**: full-precision optimizer states → 8-bit (Dettmers) → 4-bit with finer-grained quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 row/column normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization); combined with LoRA/activation compression/checkpointing, and increasingly *analyzed* (Hessian power-law spectra, LoRA vs full fine-tuning generalization) rather than just benchmarked.
> - **Part/body detection**: multi-stage pipelines with heuristic matching or separate association networks → one-stage anchor-based extended representations (BPJDet) → one-stage anchor-free with a single part-to-body offset (PBADet); trend is toward simpler, scalable representations that handle many parts without degrading detection accuracy.
> - **E/I sequence models**: naive column-wise sign-constrained RNNs (ColEI) that train poorly → spectral diagnosis (multimodal/dispersed singular values, NSE) and architectures like DANN that keep good random-matrix spectra; trend is that spectral properties at initialization, not constraints per se, determine stability/learning, guiding better initialization and gradient clipping.
> - **JEPA/SSL**: contrastive methods with negative pairs and MAE pixel reconstruction → non-contrastive self-distillation with stop-gradient (BYOL/SimSiam/I-JEPA) → theoretical (deep-linear) accounts of implicit bias (priority to high-influence, low-variance "perceptual" features, noise suppression that deepens with depth) plus regularization against dimensional collapse (LDReg) and embedding-similarity analysis.
> 
> All use standard Transformers/ResNet/YOLO backbones and standard regularization (weight decay, gradient clipping, stop-grad, task-alignment losses); you can adapt them piecewise as a blueprint, but note the exact evaluation mix (AUROC in particular) is not consistently reported across all of them.

</details>

### paperscope:trend:396 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle memory- and data‑efficient deep networks across diverse tasks: (i) self‑supervised/self‑distillation objectives (e.g., MSE vs cross‑entropy with cosine similarity) for learning feature embeddings; (ii) anchor‑free, attention‑based detection on COCO with reporting in Precision/F1; (iii) memory‑efficient AdamW‑style training with sub‑byte states enabling end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning; (iv) spectral/regularization perspectives for recurrent time‑series modeling (e.g., Dale’s Law) to improve interpretability and stability; and (v) unsupervised methods that learn to solve combinatorial problems like TSP without labels. Preference for works that compare CE vs MSE, use MNIST/COCO‑scale benchmarks, and discuss practical training trade‑offs.Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Across these five works, several clear development trends emerge toward memory- and data‑efficient deep networks, with time and scalability characteristics explicitly reflected. 1) Self-supervised/self-distillation objectives for embeddings: Recent JEPA-style approaches (2024) move away from reconstruction losses (MAE) toward non-contrastive self-distillation with StopGrad. In deep linear analyses, JEPA shows a depth-dependent implicit bias to learn high‑influence (high regression‑coefficient) features and prioritize low‑variance, semantic components, yielding faster, stepwise feature acquisition. Practical trade‑offs include: depth strongly modulates feature selection; JEPA’s stability hinges on spectral alignment rather than negative pairs; and empirical validation on ImageNet-scale PCA and temporal models confirms representational focus shifts over training. 2) Anchor-free, attention-based detection on COCO: Detection has transitioned (2023→2024) from anchor-based (e.g., YOLO heads, BPJDet) to anchor-free designs (PBADet, ICLR 2024) that encode part–body associations with a single center offset. This reduces representation length (5+K+2 vs 6+K+2K), scales to many parts without inflating output channels, and simplifies decoding. On COCOHumanParts, PBADet matches or improves AP and achieves lower mMR−2; on COCO validation images the method reports Precision/Recall/F1 improvements over ED-Pose, highlighting both accuracy and robustness gains as anchor-free task-aligned learning (TOOD) and multi-scale features mature. 3) Memory-efficient AdamW training with sub‑byte states: Optimizer compression has progressed from 16/8‑bit (2022) to 4‑bit states (NeurIPS 2023), enabling large-model finetuning under tight memory (e.g., end-to-end instruction tuning for LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B). Key advances include smaller block sizes for first moment, rank‑1 normalization and zero‑point‑free linear quantization for second moment to avoid catastrophic update directions, and hybrid factorization+quantization for further savings. This yields comparable accuracy to full‑precision AdamW across ImageNet classification (Swin‑T), GLUE/SQuAD, WMT14 MT, and GPT‑2 NLG, while cutting optimizer memory and communication overhead (beneficial for offloading and sharded training). 4) Spectral/regularization perspectives for recurrent time‑series modeling: Instead of enforcing Dale’s Law by sign constraints alone, the 2023 spectral perspective shows singular‑value spectra (not just EI signs) dominate RNN performance and stability. Normalised SVD entropy predicts learning quality; spectrum transplant experiments reveal spectral properties matter more than sign constraints; and performance improves with balanced E/I ratios and larger widths. Practical stability trade‑offs (e.g., gradient clipping) and tasks spanning adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and natural object recognition indicate a shift toward interpretable, spectrum-aware EI architectures (DANN RNNs) with better training reliability. 5) Unsupervised combinatorial solvers (TSP): Methods have moved from label-heavy SL/RL toward UL with surrogate losses and local search (NeurIPS 2023). UTSP trains an expressive SAG GNN to produce non‑smooth heat maps (via band‑pass filters that avoid oversmoothing), then uses best‑first k‑opt guided by these maps. This reduces search space dramatically (≥99% edge coverage on TSP‑100 validation), scales to 1,000-node instances, and uses ~0.2% of the training samples and ~10% of parameters compared to SL/RL, while matching or outperforming contemporary learning baselines. Overall trends: • From anchors to anchor‑free: simpler, scalable representations with task-aligned learning improve COCO performance while reporting AP and F1/Precision/Recall. • From reconstruction to JEPA self‑distillation: deeper predictors favor influential features; training cost and stability improve without labels/negatives. • From 8‑bit to 4‑bit optimizers: refined quantization (smaller blocks, rank‑1 scales, zero‑point exclusion) plus factorization enables end‑to‑end large model finetuning under strict memory budgets. • From EI sign constraints to spectra: NSE diagnostics and spectrum shaping yield more interpretable and stable RNNs across time‑series/sequence tasks (including MNIST‑scale benchmarks). • From SL/RL to UL for combinatorics: surrogate losses and expressive GNNs (band‑pass) paired with local search deliver strong scaling and data efficiency on TSP. These shifts collectively emphasize scalability (larger graphs and models, more parts without exploding representation), data efficiency (self‑supervision and UL), and practical training trade‑offs (depth, spectra, quantization design, and anchor-free heads) that improve robustness and resource use over time.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the papers matching each topic:
> 
> **(i) Self-distillation / feature embeddings**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): analyzes JEPA self-distillation, showing latent-space (MSE-style) prediction biases networks toward high-influence, low-variance features vs. MAE's pixel reconstruction.
> - **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"**: analyzes cosine-similarity embedding objectives (InfoNCE family), showing mini-batch training raises negative-pair similarity variance; adds a variance-reduction auxiliary loss (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, ImageNet).
> - **LDReg**: local dimensionality regularization against dimensional collapse in SSL (ImageNet, with COCO detection transfer).
> 
> *Caveat:* I did not find an explicit CE-vs-MSE comparison paper; the closest is JEPA (MSE latent prediction) contrasted with reconstruction/classification objectives.
> 
> **(ii) Anchor-free detection, COCO, Precision/F1**
> - **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free part-body association detector (YOLOv5/v7 based). Reports Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO-val vs. ED-Pose (e.g., hands F1 ~46–47 vs ~22–24) and AP on COCO-HumanParts (e.g., 42.7–43.0 AP). *Caveat:* it is anchor-free but not truly attention-based (uses TOOD task-alignment).
> - **HASSOD**: self-supervised object detection trained on MS-COCO images; argues AP is misleading for class-agnostic detection and uses Average Recall instead.
> 
> **(iii) Memory-efficient AdamW / sub-byte states + LoRA**
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023): pushes Adam/AdamW optimizer states from 8-bit to 4-bit ("sub-byte") via block-size B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, and factorization. Achieves ~57.7% memory savings, enables LLaMA-7B fine-tuning on one 80GB GPU, and is discussed alongside/compatible with LoRA fine-tuning.
> 
> **(iv) Spectral / Dale's Law for recurrent modeling**
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023): spectral (singular-value) analysis of EI RNNs (ColEI vs DANN) on sequential MNIST, adding problem, PTB; shows initial weight spectrum (not sign constraints) drives learning/stability; proposes normalized SVD entropy as an interpretability/performance diagnostic.
> 
> **(v) Unsupervised TSP**
> - **UTSP** (NeurIPS 2023): fully unsupervised GNN (Scattering Attention GNN) trained with a surrogate loss (Hamiltonian-cycle constraint + shortest path) and heatmap-guided local search; near-optimal on TSP20–100 and outperforms RL/SL baselines on TSP200–1000 using only ~10% of parameters and ~0.2% of training samples.
> 
> **Development trend:** Across all five lines, the methods converge on *removing supervision and hand-crafted inductive bias while improving data/memory efficiency*: labels are replaced by self-distillation/unsupervised surrogate objectives (JEPA, UTSP), anchors by dense anchor-free prediction (PBADet), full-precision optimizer states by sub-byte quantized states for cheap fine-tuning (4-bit AdamW), and black-box RNN behavior by spectral analysis for stability/interpretability (Dale's Law). Underlying this is a shift from "how well it performs" to *understanding why*—implicit-bias/spectral/Hessian analyses explain learning dynamics—and a trend toward theoretically-grounded, efficient components validated on MNIST/sequential-MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, and COCO-scale benchmarks.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the available collection, here are the best-matching papers for each theme:
> 
> **(i) Self-supervised/self-distillation objectives (MSE vs CE, cosine similarity):**
> - *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features* (40fde037): analyzes JEPA self-distillation vs MAE, showing an implicit bias toward high-influence features via deep linear network dynamics (NeurIPS 2024).
> - *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (160e1407): unified framework of contrastive losses through cosine similarity (InfoNCE, SigLIP, DCL), showing mini-batch variance of negative-pair similarities and a variance-reduction auxiliary loss; tested on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet.
> - *LDReg* (51526068): local dimensionality regularization against (local) dimensional collapse for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE, validated on ImageNet and COCO detection.
> 
> **(ii) Anchor-free detection with Precision/F1 on COCO:**
> - *PBADet* (08b70bc3): one-stage, anchor-free part–body association detector built on TOOD-style task-alignment learning; evaluated on COCO validation and reports Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., ~48.52 F1 for all parts vs ED-Pose's ~31.51), plus AP on COCO-HumanParts.
> - Related: *HASSOD* (ef986d59) is self-supervised detection using frozen DINO ViT (attention) features, but it argues COCO AP is misleading for class-agnostic detection and reports AR rather than F1.
> 
> **(iii) Memory-efficient AdamW with sub-byte states:**
> - *4-bit Optimizers* (8d5e1455): quantizes AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128 block-wise, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, second-moment factorization), matching 32-bit accuracy with up to ~57.7% memory savings; enables LLaMA-7B fine-tuning (Alpaca) on a single 80GB GPU, and discusses LoRA fine-tuning as complementary.
> 
> **(iv) Spectral/regularization perspective for recurrent modeling (Dale's Law):**
> - *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (e63a94c4): shows spectral properties of the recurrent weight matrix at initialization (multimodal/dispersed singular values in ColEI) matter more than sign constraints; proposes normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as a diagnostic; gradient clipping stabilizes training.
> 
> **(v) Unsupervised combinatorial optimization (TSP):**
> - *UTSP* (1535109e): unsupervised learning for Euclidean TSP with a GNN (Scattering Attention GNN) and surrogate loss (Hamiltonian-cycle constraint + shortest path), heatmap-guided local search; near-optimal on TSP20–100, outperforms RL/SL baselines on TSP200–1000 using ~10% of parameters and ~0.2% of training samples.
> 
> **Development trend across these methods:**
> 1. **From supervision to label-free learning**: objectives move from supervised/RL (sparse rewards, expensive annotation) toward self-distillation, contrastive, and fully unsupervised surrogate-loss training (UTSP, JEPA, SSL), prioritizing data efficiency (e.g., 2,000 unlabelled samples vs 1M labeled/RL samples).
> 2. **From heuristic design to principled/theoretical understanding**: papers shift from architecture heuristics to analyses of implicit bias (JEPA), embedding-similarity geometry (contrastive learning), and spectral properties (Dale's Law, SVD entropy) as diagnostics for interpretability and stability.
> 3. **From anchor-based, multi-stage pipelines to streamlined anchor-free, attention/task-aligned designs**, with evaluation moving beyond AP to Precision/Recall/F1 or AR to reflect practical detection trade-offs.
> 4. **From full-precision to aggressively compressed training**: optimizer states go 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit via quantization + factorization, keeping accuracy while cutting memory/communication, and pairing with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA).
> 5. **Consistent emphasis on practical trade-offs**: memory vs accuracy, batch size vs embedding variance, spectral health vs trainability, and search-space reduction vs solution quality—each work reports explicit efficiency/quality trade-offs on MNIST/CIFAR/ImageNet/COCO-scale benchmarks.
> 
> Note: the collection does not contain a paper that explicitly compares CE vs MSE distillation objectives or one that is simultaneously anchor-free, attention-based, and reports F1 on COCO; PBADet (anchor-free, COCO, Precision/F1) and HASSOD (attention-based, self-supervised, COCO) are the closest matches.
