> {'answer': 'Cross-domain trend toward efficient, stable, and interpretable deep learning, 2023→2025\n\n1) From black-box training to structure, spectra, and compression (2023)\n- Memory/frugality: 4-bit optimizers (Adam/AdamW) compress both first/second moments to 4-bit with rank-1 normalization and zero-point–free linear mapping, retaining full-precision accuracy for Transformer fine-tuning (e.g., RoBERTa-L on GLUE, GPT-2 on E2E-NLG, LLaMA instruction tuning). This enables larger models/training on the same hardware and faster distributed fine-tuning (FSDP), aligning with fine-tuning/LoRA workflows.\n- Reliability via biological constraints: Recurrent EI (Dale’s law) networks are revisited through spectral analysis. Performance on sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and other tasks is linked to singular-value spectra (not just sign constraints). A simple scalar (normalized SVD entropy) predicts learnability and stability; DANN-style EI RNNs match standard RNNs and avoid the small-network pitfalls seen in ColEI.\n- Objectives/optimizers: squared-error (MSE) objectives analyzed in deep linear JEPA/MAE surrogates and used in experiments; Adam/AdamW standard, with state compression to 4-bit.\n\n2) From hand-designed heads to anchor-free, scalable vision detectors (2024)\n- One-stage, anchor-free PBADet replaces body→part offsets with a single part→body center offset per location, preserving a compact representation that scales to many parts without explosion in head size. On COCOHumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman it achieves strong AP and mMR−2, using CE-style classification plus IoU/DFL losses under SGD. This consolidates accuracy and efficiency in multi-part association while simplifying decoding (NMS + nearest-body center).\n\n3) From empirical success to principled bias in self-supervision (2024)\n- JEPA’s implicit bias is made explicit in deep linear analysis: predicting in latent space favors “influential” features (large regression coefficients), whereas MAE prioritizes highly covarying (possibly noisier) features. The JEPA bias strengthens with encoder depth, explaining faster emergence of semantic features and complementing reconstruction-based approaches. Both use MSE-type training objectives (squared errors), aligning with common optimizers.\n\n4) From generic function approximators to interpretable solvers for PDEs (2025)\n- INN-TD fuses finite-element-like, locally supported interpolation (C-HiDeNN) with tensor decomposition (CP) to build sparse, interpretable neural surrogates/solvers. Kronecker-delta and partition-of-unity properties give exact Dirichlet enforcement and Gaussian quadrature-based variational training; boosting and subspace iteration yield sparse linear solves. The tensor-product (mode-wise) structure reduces high-D S-P-T PDEs to 1D integrations, mitigating the curse of dimensionality. Demonstrated fast, accurate solutions (very low relative L2 errors) and inverse identification, with MSE loss for data-driven cases and Galerkin residuals for data-free solves.\n\nWhat this adds up to (integrated trend)\n- Efficiency at scale: anchor-free, one-stage perception heads (PBADet) and 4-bit optimizers reduce compute/memory; EI spectral diagnostics (NSE) and JEPA bias theory cut trial-and-error; INN-TD’s 1D integration plus tensor modes scales to 10+ dimensional PDEs.\n- Reliability/stability: spectra-aware EI RNN design improves sequential MNIST/Penn Tree Bank training; PBADet’s always-valid part→body offset simplifies supervision; zero-point–free second-moment quantization stabilizes 4-bit AdamW.\n- Interpretability/inductive bias: finite-element-like basis with exact boundary handling (INN-TD), biologically constrained RNNs with spectral guarantees, and JEPA’s depth-driven influential-feature bias provide explainable levers absent in black-box nets.\n- Unifying objectives/optimizers across domains: squared-error losses (JEPA/MAE, INN-TD) and CE/IoU (PBADet) under standard optimizers (SGD, Adam/AdamW, and their 4-bit variants) allow reliable training in vision, sequence modeling, and scientific computing.\n\nEvidence across tasks/metrics\n- Vision (COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman): PBADet reports AP (COCO-style), MR−2, and mMR−2, matching or surpassing prior joint detectors with simpler, scalable heads.\n- Sequence modeling: EI RNNs evaluated on sequential MNIST, the adding problem, Penn Tree Bank; spectra (eigen/singular) explain performance and size/E:I-ratio effects.\n- Scientific computing: INN-TD achieves very low relative L2 errors and high speed on high-D Poisson/Helmholtz and S-P-T parabolic PDEs; boundary conditions enforced exactly.\n\nOverall trajectory (2023→2025)\n- 2023: Practical reliability via compression (4-bit states for Adam/AdamW) and spectral principles for EI RNNs.\n- 2024: Scalable anchor-free part–body association with strong COCO metrics; theoretical grounding of JEPA’s implicit bias in deep linear settings.\n- 2025: Interpretable, FEM-like, tensor-decomposed neural solvers unify training/solving/inverse modeling for large-scale PDEs with high precision.\n\nTakeaway\nAcross modalities, methods converge on three pillars: (i) structural inductive bias (anchor-free offsets; EI constraints; FE-like interpolation), (ii) principled analysis (spectra for RNNs; JEPA bias), and (iii) resource efficiency (4-bit optimizers; sparse tensor decompositions). Together they deliver scalable, accurate, and explainable training/inference under standard MSE/CE losses and SGD/Adam-family optimizers, with validated metrics on COCO and sequential MNIST and precise PDE benchmarks.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here are the papers that collectively cover your six elements, followed by a synthesis of the development trend.
> 
> ## Papers matching each element
> 
> **(a) MSE/CE objectives under Adam/AdamW/SGD optimizers** — *"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"* (Tang et al., ICML 2025). Empirically studies the Hessian spectra of well-trained deep networks (LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, ResNet, GPT-2, TinyLlama) trained with SGD, Vanilla SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad, and AdamW (LLMs). It finds a power-law Hessian spectrum holds across all these optimizers once training succeeds, with the fitted slope correlating with minima sharpness and test error.
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit bias** — *"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"* (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes the training dynamics of deep linear self-distillation (JEPA) vs. MAE under MSE objectives, proving JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-ρ "influential" features and suppresses noise as depth increases, explaining the benefit of prediction in latent space. (Related context: contrastive learning on cosine similarity in latent space appears in *"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning,"* where positive pairs are aligned and negatives uniformly separated by cosine similarity.)
> 
> **(c) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association** — *"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"* (Gao et al., ICLR 2024). Introduces a single part-to-body center offset on top of anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones). On COCO-HumanParts it reaches ~42–43 AP (original) / ~41.8 (subordinate), and on BodyHands ~89 HandAP, ~92.6% conditional accuracy, ~86 JointAP; also leading AP on CrowdHuman face-body.
> 
> **(d) Recurrent models obeying Dale's law** — *"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"* (Li, Cornford, Ghosh, Richards, NeurIPS 2023). Studies ColEI (sign-constrained columns = E/I populations) vs. DANN and standard RNNs on sequential MNIST, adding, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. Shows via SVD analysis/spectrum transplants that initialization spectral properties (multimodal, dispersed singular values) matter more than sign constraints; normalized SVD entropy predicts performance.
> 
> **(e) Sub-byte (~4-bit) optimizer states** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (Li, Chen, Zhu, NeurIPS 2023). Quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller block size, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization). Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG, WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (incl. LoRA), saving up to 57.7% memory.
> 
> **(f) Interpretable tensor-decomposition PDE solvers** — *"Interpolating Neural Network-Tensor Decomposition (INN-TD)"* (Guo et al.). Combines C-HiDeNN locally supported finite-element-like interpolation with tensor decomposition; interpretable as a pruned MLP with FEM basis functions, partition-of-unity/Kronecker-delta properties. Beats CP-PINN and KAN on high-dimensional Poisson (rel. L2 ~1e-8–1e-6 vs ~1e-4–1e-2), solves Helmholtz, space-time heat transfer, and inverse problems.
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> 
> Across these works there is a clear convergence toward **efficiency, reliability, and interpretability of deep models**:
> 
> - **From empirical to principled understanding of training**: (a) moves from treating optimizers (SGD/Adam/AdamW) as black boxes to characterizing the universal power-law Hessian structure they all induce, linking it to sharpness and generalization — a spectral "diagnostic" of reliable training.
> - **From black-box SSL to mechanistic bias**: (b) explains *why* JEPA's latent-space prediction works by proving an implicit bias toward influential/low-noise features, replacing heuristic SSL design with analyzable dynamics.
> - **Toward simpler, more scalable one-stage designs**: (c) replaces multi-stage/anchor-based part–body pipelines with a single anchor-free part-to-body offset, gaining accuracy with fewer parameters.
> - **Biological constraint + spectral design**: (d) shows that obeying Dale's law succeeds only when initialization spectra mimic standard RNNs, shifting the focus from sign constraints to spectral conditioning and offering a pre-training diagnostic (NSE).
> - **Compression-driven efficiency**: (e) pushes optimizer states from 8-bit to 4-bit, showing lossless convergence for large-model fine-tuning, a push toward extreme memory frugality.
> - **Physics-aware interpretable architectures**: (f) blends FEM theory with neural nets and tensor decomposition, replacing opaque PINNs with interpretable, convergent solvers.
> 
> The overarching trajectory is: **from accurate but black-box, memory-hungry deep networks toward spectrally understood, compressed, biologically/physics-grounded, and interpretable models** — with shared emphasis on diagnostics (spectra/entropy/Hessian) for reliability and on efficiency (one-stage, 4-bit, tensor-decomposed) for scalability.
> 
> *Note on scope:* No single retrieved paper covers element (a) as a pure objective/optimizer convergence theory (e.g., MSE/CE guarantees under Adam/AdamW/SGD); the closest available evidence is the Hessian-structure study's optimizer experiments.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the context, here are the papers that collectively match the requested elements:
> 
> **(a) MSE/CE objectives under Adam/AdamW/SGD**: "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (ICML 2025) trains LeNet/ResNet/ViT/LLMs with cross-entropy under SGD, Adam, AdamW and many variants on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; "Learning a Neuron by a Shallow ReLU Network" (NeurIPS 2023) analyzes gradient flow with square (MSE) loss; "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" uses Adam/AdamW with CE objectives.
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit bias**: "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis" (NeurIPS 2024) — proves JEPA's implicit bias for predicting in latent space (prioritizing high-ρ "influential" features over noisy variance), unlike MAE; depth strengthens noise suppression.
> 
> **(c) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association on COCO**: PBADet (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset; reports AP on COCOHumanParts (AP 42.7–43.0), CrowdHuman (body MR-2 36.5, face AP 81.6), BodyHands (Hand AP 89.1, Joint AP 85.98).
> 
> **(d) Dale's-law RNNs via spectral properties on sequential MNIST**: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023) — compares ColEI and DANN EI-constrained RNNs on sequential MNIST, adding problem, PTB; shows initial singular-value spectrum (normalised SVD entropy) matters more than sign constraints; gradient clipping mitigates deficits.
> 
> **(e) Sub-byte (~4-bit) memory-saving optimizers for fine-tuning/LoRA on Transformers**: "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor via B128/rank-1 quantization with zero-point exclusion; lossless fine-tuning on RoBERTa-L (GLUE 89.1), GPT-2 Medium (BLEU 67.8), QA (F1 94.5), LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (Alpaca), up to 57.7% memory savings; used with LoRA-style tuning.
> 
> **(f) Interpretable tensor-decomposition PDE solvers with FE-like interpolation**: INN-TD ("Interpolating Neural Network-Tensor Decomposition") — integrates locally supported C-HiDeNN finite-element interpolation with tensor decomposition; interpretable (equivalent to a pruned MLP whose parameters are nodal values), solves high-dimensional Poisson (rel. L2 ~1e-8–1e-6, beating CP-PINN/KAN), Helmholtz, space-time, elasticity, inverse problems.
> 
> **Development trend**: The methods evolve from black-box, empirically tuned deep learning toward more *interpretable, efficient, and theoretically grounded* models: (1) optimization moves from full-precision SGD/Adam to principled loss-landscape analysis (Hessian power-law, spectral slope as generalization predictor) and to 4-bit compressed optimizer states enabling large-model/LoRA fine-tuning with no accuracy loss; (2) representation learning shifts from supervised/reconstruction objectives to JEPA latent-space prediction, with formal deep-linear analyses of its implicit bias toward semantic, low-variance features; (3) detection simplifies from multi-stage, anchor-based part–body pipelines to single-stage anchor-free part-to-body offset association with better AP/F1 on COCO; (4) recurrent modeling injects biological Dale's-law constraints and explains performance via spectral diagnostics (NSE) rather than sign constraints; (5) scientific computing replaces black-box PINNs with FEM-interpolation-based, tensor-decomposed solvers that guarantee convergence, interpretability, and dimensionality-robustness. Overall: a common push toward reliability (lossless compression, spectral/structural diagnostics, convergence guarantees) and interpretability across vision, sequence modeling, and scientific computing.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Across the five works, a clear trend emerges toward principled, scalable representation learning and safety calibration that replace heuristic choices with architectures, analyses, and guarantees tailored to the task and data regime.
> 
> 1) Detection: from anchors to scalable, one-stage anchor-free association
> - Shift: Anchor-based, multi-branch body–part association has given way to a one-stage, anchor-free formulation (PBADet) that injects a single part→body center-offset into dense detection heads over multi-scale CNN features (e.g., YOLOv7/v5). This reduces representation size from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2 (K=parts), improving scalability as part sets grow and simplifying post-processing. 
> - Outcomes: On COCOHumanParts and BodyHands, this design improves AP and joint AP while lowering miss-match (mMR-2). It generalizes across CNN backbones with SGD training and AMP, and offers stronger Precision/Recall/F1 than keypoint-based pose methods in head-to-head comparisons (the PBADet paper reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose). The trend is toward anchor-free, multi-scale, task-aligned heads with fewer hyperparameters and better large-scale behavior (COCO-scale) rather than anchor engineering.
> 
> 2) RNNs under Dale’s Law: from sign constraints to spectral control
> - Shift: Instead of viewing excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints as the core bottleneck, recent analysis shows spectral properties of recurrent weight matrices dominate learning quality. Column-wise EI partitioning induces multimodal, dispersed singular spectra and poor learning; DANN-style EI architectures converge to unimodal, clustered spectra similar to standard RNNs and train well.
> - Outcomes: Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance; spectrum “transplants” show spectrum matters more than sign constraints; small networks with realistic E/I ratios are most fragile. The field is moving from hard biological constraints alone to spectral initialization/monitoring as a scalable, architecture-agnostic principle for robust training (with gradient clipping when needed), across diverse tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and a naturalistic object classification task).
> 
> 3) Self-supervised vision: from reconstruction (MSE) to JEPA’s latent prediction bias
> - Shift: Deep linear analyses show a principled, time-resolved mechanism for the empirical finding that JEPA-style self-distillation learns semantic features faster than masked reconstruction. Predicting in latent space (vs. input-space MSE or CE) induces an implicit bias toward influential features (large regression coefficients), increasingly so with encoder depth; MAE prioritizes high-variance/covarying features.
> - Outcomes: This explains why JEPA-style vision encoders gravitate to bottom-PCA semantic subspaces more rapidly, and clarifies training choices: depth strengthens JEPA’s bias; both CNNs and Transformers (e.g., ViT) can benefit, but the dynamics—not the architecture—govern which features are learned when. The development is toward theory-backed training dynamics (ODEs, critical times) that link optimization, depth, and feature selection.
> 
> 4) Safety calibration: from batch calibration to active, anytime-valid RCPS
> - Shift: Risk-controlling prediction sets have moved from a one-shot, batch setting to sequential, anytime-valid guarantees coupled with active labeling. This replaces fixed thresholds with e-process (betting) martingales that control risk at all times, even under adaptive data collection, and uses model predictions to reduce variance and save labels.
> - Outcomes: With label budgets and predictors (from the same model being calibrated), the method achieves log-optimal growth rates and label-efficient calibration on large-class image tasks (e.g., ImageNet). The trend is toward online, risk-controlled deployment that co-designs labeling policy and predictor for scalable operations while maintaining formal guarantees on miscoverage.
> 
> 5) Video pretraining for RL: principled bounds clarify when it helps (and when it doesn’t)
> - Shift: A theory-first view shows forward modeling and temporal contrastive can recover latent state and enable polynomial-sample RL in Block MDPs (iid observation noise), but exogenous (temporally correlated) noise creates a statistical gap: purely video-based pretraining can become exponentially harder than trajectory-based pretraining.
> - Outcomes: Experiments on GridWorld and ViZDoom confirm: without exogenous noise, both methods support efficient downstream RL; with exogenous noise, contrastive often latches onto the noise, forward modeling is more robust but still degrades, while trajectory-based ACRO remains strong. The trend is toward matching method to environment assumptions (use video pretraining when exogenous noise is limited; prefer action-labeled trajectory methods or exogenous-noise-filtering objectives when it is not) and toward theoretically grounded choices over purely empirical heuristics.
> 
> Cross-cutting training and evaluation patterns
> - Architectures and optimizers: Detection leverages CNN backbones (YOLOv7/v5) with SGD and multi-scale heads; RNN work emphasizes spectral initialization and (when needed) gradient clipping; JEPA analyses isolate the role of depth; video→RL pipelines pretrain encoders and then use PPO for downstream control; RCPS uses online convex updates (e.g., COCOB) for label-budget tuning.
> - Benchmarks and metrics: COCO-scale human-part detection (AP, mMR-2, joint AP), ImageNet risk control and representation similarity (CCA) for JEPA vs MAE, vision tasks with Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., PBADet vs ED-Pose), and RL returns in GridWorld/ViZDoom under exogenous noise. These works collectively emphasize scalable evaluation (COCO, ImageNet) and principled risk/robustness metrics, not just accuracy.
> 
> Overall development trend
> - Replace heuristics with principled formulations that scale: anchor-free detection with concise association vectors; spectral control in EI RNNs; JEPA’s depth-driven latent prediction bias; e-process–based, active, anytime-valid risk guarantees; and explicit upper/lower bounds for video pretraining in RL. The unifying direction is to make representation learning and calibration robust-by-design across vision and control, with theory explaining when methods scale (datasets like COCO/ImageNet), how training choices (SGD vs spectrum control, depth) shape learned features, and where limits appear (exogenous noise in video-based RL).

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the context, the five papers you're describing are:
> 
> 1. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — extends anchor-free detectors (FCOS, YOLOv5/7/8) with a single part-to-body center offset for scalable part-body association; task-alignment learning; SOTA on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, with higher Precision/F1 than ED-Pose for hands/feet.
> 
> 2. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — shows that for E/I-constrained RNNs, the initial recurrent-weight *spectrum* (not sign constraints) drives learnability; ColEI yields multimodal/dispersed singular values, DANN matches standard RNNs; normalized SVD entropy predicts performance (sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition).
> 
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024) — proves that predicting in latent space (JEPA/self-distillation), versus reconstruction (MAE), biases toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients) and suppresses noisy features; depth strengthens this; I-JEPA aligns faster with low-variance perceptual subspace on ImageNet-1K.
> 
> 4. **Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets** (NeurIPS 2024) — extends RCPS to sequentially/adaptively collected data with anytime-valid guarantees (risk controlled at all times w.p. ≥ 1−α) via e-processes/betting, active labeling under a label budget, IPW, and predictor-based variance reduction; regret bounds; ImageNet experiments.
> 
> 5. **Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for Reinforcement Learning** (ICLR 2024) — analyzes autoencoding, temporal contrastive learning, and forward modeling in Block MDPs with iid vs. exogenous noise: polynomial sample-complexity upper bounds without exogenous noise; exponential lower bound with exogenous noise; forward modeling is more robust than contrastive learning; trajectory-based ACRO stays robust (GridWorld, ViZDoom).
> 
> **Development trend:** The methods move from heuristic, task-specific design toward principled/mechanistic understanding:
> - **Detection:** two-stage/anchor-based pipelines → one-stage anchor-free with a single unified offset representation (scalable, simpler post-processing, task-aligned supervision).
> - **Recurrent networks:** enforcing biological sign constraints → analyzing initialization spectral properties as the true determinant of learnability, with a diagnostic metric (NSE).
> - **Self-supervised learning:** reconstruction in input space (MSE/MAE) → latent-space prediction (JEPA), now theoretically explained as an implicit bias toward influential, low-noise features, amplified by depth.
> - **Safety/calibration:** batch, one-time RCPS → sequential, anytime-valid, active-labeling risk control with martingale/e-process guarantees and label-efficiency/regret analysis.
> - **Video RL:** empirical video pretraining → PAC-style guarantees distinguishing iid from exogenous noise, explaining failures and guiding objective choice (forward modeling over contrastive; trajectory data when exogenous noise dominates).
> 
> Overall, the arc is from "what works empirically" to "why it works" — spectral theory, implicit-bias analysis, anytime-valid statistics, and sample-complexity bounds — while grounding conclusions in practical backbones, objectives, and benchmarks (COCO-family, MNIST, ImageNet, GridWorld/ViZDoom).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the context, the papers that collectively cover your requested topics are:
> 
> **Core papers**
> 1. **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-WholeBody/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman; reports AP, Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose; YOLOv5/v7 backbones.
> 2. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — spectral (SVD/eigenvalue) analysis of RNNs under excitatory/inhibitory constraints; shows initialization spectrum, not sign constraints, explains poor learning; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as a pre-training diagnostic; tasks include sequential MNIST.
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** — joint-embedding self-distillation analysis proving predicting in latent space biases toward high-influence features (vs MAE reconstruction, which tracks variance); deep linear network dynamics; ImageNet CCA experiments.
> 4. **Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets (NeurIPS 2024)** — extends RCPS to sequential/adaptive data with e-processes and betting; active labeling with IPW and label budgets; optimal labeling policies/predictors with regret bounds; ImageNet experiments.
> 5. **Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL (ICLR 2024)** — video-based representation learning (autoencoding, forward modeling, temporal contrastive) for downstream RL in Block MDPs with iid and exogenous noise; PAC upper bounds and an exponential identifiability lower bound; GridWorld/ViZDoom experiments; ACRO (trajectory-based) as robust baseline.
> 
> **Supporting SSL/practical-training papers** (tie to SGD vs Adam, CNNs vs Transformers, ResNet-50, COCO, MNIST/CIFAR-100, precision/F1, embeddings, calibration)
> - **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** — optimal negative-pair similarity, variance-reduction loss; SGD, ResNet-18/50; CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100.
> - **LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularized SSL** — counters local dimensional collapse; ResNet-50 and ViT-B; ImageNet linear eval, COCO detection/segmentation (APbb/APmk), transfer to CIFAR.
> - **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure** — power-law Hessian spectra across SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, Yogi, etc.; LeNet/ResNet18/ViT on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; links spectrum to generalization.
> 
> **Development trend of their methods**
> - **From hand-designed, multi-stage pipelines to single-stage, unified designs**: PBADet collapses two-stage/anchor-based part-body association into one anchor-free framework with a single offset, improving scalability and robustness.
> - **From empirical performance to mechanistic/spectral explanations**: the RNN work replaces the "sign constraint" story with spectral properties at initialization (NSE as a predictive diagnostic); the Hessian work connects optimizer choice and architecture to spectral power laws and generalization.
> - **From objective choice by intuition to provable implicit biases**: JEPA analysis formalizes why latent-space prediction learns influential (low-noise, semantic) features over reconstruction (MSE) or classification-style objectives; SSL papers characterize embedding geometry (dimensional collapse, LID) and how to regularize it.
> - **From static guarantees to anytime-valid, label-efficient guarantees**: RCPS moves from batch calibration to sequential/adaptive settings with e-processes, betting, and active labeling — i.e., safety/calibration that holds at every time step under limited labeling budgets.
> - **From trajectory-dependent RL to provable video pretraining, with caveats**: video representation learning is shown to work (forward modeling and temporal contrastive) under iid noise with polynomial sample complexity, but exogenous noise creates an exponential barrier; trajectory-based methods (ACRO) remain more robust — motivating noise-aware representation design.
> 
> Overall, the trend is toward **principled, theoretically grounded representation learning**: simplifying architectures, diagnosing learning via spectra/embedding geometry, proving implicit biases of objectives, and extending safety guarantees to sequential/active settings — validated on standard backbones (ResNet/ViT/YOLO), optimizers (SGD/Adam), and benchmarks (COCO, MNIST, CIFAR-100, ImageNet).

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper development trends (2019–2024) across the five works converge on four themes: scaling-efficient perception, principled self-supervision under noise, safety-aware sequential calibration, and spectrum-aware training. Together they outline a path from accurate part–body association on COCO-like data, through robust pretraining from videos for RL, to anytime-valid, label-efficient deployment.
> 
> 1) Part–body association: from anchors and multi-stage to anchor-free, one-stage, and scalable
> - Earlier body–part joint detectors extended anchor-based one-stage detectors with multiple body-to-part offsets, which grow linearly with the number of parts and degrade performance as K increases (BPJDet, 2023). 
> - PBADet (ICLR 2024) flips the direction and removes anchors: a single part-to-body center offset per position on multi-scale feature maps encodes association, cutting the representation from 6+K+2K to 5+K+2. This reduces redundancy, scales to many parts without extra offsets, and simplifies decoding (one-to-one association preserved even with occlusions). 
> - Training moved from independent heads to task-aligned learning (TOOD-style) over classification, localization, and association, using SGD and standard detection losses, with top-K anchor assignment and NMS at inference.
> - Trend effect: accuracy improved and stayed robust as datasets and part vocabularies grew (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman). The anchor-free, single-offset design is the key scalability inflection.
> 
> 2) Self-supervision: from reconstruction to latent prediction, and coping with exogenous noise
> - JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024): in deep linear settings, both can learn similar spans, but their implicit biases differ. 
>   • With deeper encoders, JEPA/self-distillation prioritizes high-influence (predictive, low-variance) features; MAE prioritizes high-covariance (potentially noisy) features. This explains why latent prediction often yields faster, more semantic representations than pixel reconstruction.
>   • The JEPA advantage strengthens with depth (stepwise, greedy feature learning reorders by regression coefficients with L), clarifying why latent-space prediction transfers well to downstream perception.
> - Videos→RL (ICLR 2024): forward modeling and temporal contrastive both recover latent state and enable efficient downstream RL under iid observation noise (upper bounds). With temporally correlated exogenous noise, temporal contrastive is particularly vulnerable (optimizes by locking onto the exogenous signal), forward modeling is more robust but still degrades as noise increases, and video-only pretraining can be exponentially harder than trajectory-based pretraining (lower bound). 
> - Trend effect: the field has shifted from reconstructive objectives toward latent prediction (JEPA/forward modeling), complemented by explicit analysis of exogenous noise. Practical systems mix latent prediction for pretraining with exogenous-noise-aware designs or limited action-labeled traces when available.
> 
> 3) Safety at deployment: from batch guarantees to active, anytime-valid risk control
> - Batch RCPS (Bates et al., JACM 2024) provided one-shot guarantees. The 2024 extension introduces:
>   • Anytime-valid RCPS via e-processes (testing-by-betting) that maintain risk control simultaneously over all time, suitable for sequential updates.
>   • Active labeling under a budget: label only the most informative points using policies q(x) that prioritize large conditional variance σβ(x); integrate model-based risk predictors r̂(x,β) to reduce variance and labels further. 
>   • Optimality/regret: closed-form optimal q*(x) ∝ σβ(x) with growth-rate lower bounds; online updates (e.g., ONS) drive betting parameters toward log-optimal. 
> - Trend effect: calibration steps are moving from offline/batch to on-policy, sequential, budgeted operation with formal validity. This supports real-time gating of outputs (e.g., in detection or RL policies) while minimizing expert labels.
> 
> 4) Spectrum-aware design: from sign constraints to spectral regularity as the true bottleneck
> - Dale’s Law RNNs (NeurIPS 2023): poor learning in column EI (ColEI) networks stems more from spectral pathologies (multimodal, dispersed singular values with large modes) than from sign constraints per se. Recurrent Dale’s ANNs (DANNs) match standard RNN performance by restoring unimodal, clustered spectra akin to random-matrix predictions.
>   • Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) summarizes spectral “health” and predicts performance; small inhibitory fractions and small networks harm NSE and learning. 
>   • The insight generalizes beyond RNNs; spectrum-aware initialization/architectures should guide future EI designs in CNN/Transformer stacks.
> - Trend effect: the community is reframing biological and sign-constrained designs in terms of spectra (singular-value clustering, non-normality), yielding stable, scalable training without sacrificing constraints—an approach applicable to time-series modeling and sequential perception.
> 
> What this means for an end-to-end stack (detectors → video-pretrained RL → safe outputs)
> - Detection/association: adopt one-stage, anchor-free part-to-body offsets (PBADet) on multi-scale CNN/Transformer backbones with task-aligned training. This scales as parts are added (COCO-like settings) and preserves one-to-one pairings for hands/face.
> - Video pretraining for RL: prefer latent prediction (forward modeling/JEPA-style) over reconstruction; expect success under iid noise, and plan explicitly for exogenous noise (either via robust objectives, exogenous filtering, or selective action-labeled data). Temporal contrastive can be attractive in clean settings but is fragile under exogenous dynamics.
> - Safety and labeling: replace batch thresholds with anytime-valid RCPS; deploy active label policies that target high-variance regions and exploit risk predictors to cut labels while preserving guarantees.
> - Training stability: monitor spectra (e.g., NSE) when imposing architectural constraints (EI or adapters) in deep networks for time-series; target unimodal, compact singular-value distributions for reliable optimization.
> 
> Overall trajectory
> - Accuracy → scalability: part–body association moved from anchor-based and multi-stage to anchor-free one-stage with a single offset, improving utilization and scaling to many parts.
> - Heuristics → principles: self-supervision choices are now grounded in analyses of implicit bias (JEPA vs MAE) and noise models (iid vs exogenous) with sample-complexity bounds and lower bounds guiding method choice.
> - Static → online-safe: risk control progressed from batch to anytime-valid, label-efficient calibration with optimal active policies and predictor-augmented variance reduction.
> - Constraints → spectra: biological realism and stability are being recast in spectral terms (NSE), offering practical guidance across recurrent and feedforward deep networks.
> 
> These trends are consistent across CNNs and Transformers trained with SGD/Adam and standard losses (e.g., cross-entropy/IoU-type objectives), and they have already been validated on COCO-like datasets and sequential tasks (e.g., BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman; sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition). They provide transferable guidance for broader multimodal and adapter-based fine-tuning stacks: choose latent prediction for pretraining; design spectrum-healthy backbones; and wrap deployment with anytime-valid, active risk control.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is the development trend across the four areas, based only on the provided documents:
> 
> **1. Part–body association (PBADet).** Methods evolved from multi-stage, anchor-based, heuristic pipelines (e.g., BodyHands' separate hand/body detectors with learned association; BPJDet's body-to-part center offsets that grow with the number of parts) toward one-stage, anchor-free, end-to-end designs. PBADet's single part-to-body center offset is more compact, always valid, one-to-one, scales to any number of parts, and improves accuracy/efficiency on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, and CrowdHuman — the trend is simpler, unified representations replacing cumbersome two-stage/anchor machinery.
> 
> **2. Self-distillation biases (JEPA vs. MAE; LDReg).** The trend is from empirical SSL to theoretical understanding of implicit bias: MAE-style reconstruction prioritizes high-variance (often noisy) features, while JEPA self-distillation is biased toward "influential" (high-regression-coefficient, low-variance, semantic) features, with depth strengthening noise suppression — explaining JEPA's robustness to spurious/noisy features. Complementing this, LDReg moves collapse prevention from global dimensionality to local intrinsic dimensionality (Fisher–Rao metric), showing that local dimensional collapse hurts downstream tasks (including COCO detection), and that global variance/covariance regularizers alone are insufficient. Overall: latent-space prediction over pixel reconstruction, plus explicit local-spectral regularization.
> 
> **3. Spectral constraints in deep nets.** The trend moves from parameter/sign constraints to spectral analysis: Dale's-Law work shows singular-value spectra (measured by normalized SVD entropy) matter more than sign constraints for learning, with unimodal clustered spectra predicting good training. The Hessian power-law work extends spectral structure from CNNs to LLMs, links power-law spectra to generalization, and finds LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does — a key insight for adapter-based fine-tuning. Trend: from individual weight constraints to initialization/landscape spectra as diagnostics and design principles, scaling to foundation models.
> 
> **4. Active anytime-valid risk control.** The trend is from batch, fixed calibration (Bates et al.'s RCPS) to sequential and adaptive guarantees: anytime-valid risk control holds simultaneously at all times via e-processes/betting, then active labeling adds IPW label policies under a budget, ML-based predictors as control variates, optimal policy/predictor derivations, and regret bounds tying estimation error to wealth growth. Trend: from static one-time guarantees to time-uniform, label-efficient, covariate-adaptive guarantees (with LLMs as label oracles), reducing labeling cost while keeping risk violation below α.
> 
> **Overall trend:** moving from multi-stage/anchor-based and reconstruction-based systems toward unified, one-stage, latent-space, theory-driven designs (anchor-free association, JEPA with understood implicit biases, spectral diagnostics), and from batch heuristics toward rigorous, anytime-valid, label-efficient statistical guarantees — all increasingly applied at vision-language/foundation-model scale (I-JEPA/V-JEPA, LLM labelers, LoRA fine-tuning analysis).

**community 最终答案**

> ## Works that together cover your stack
> 
> 1. **Part–body association**: **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free detection of hands/face with a single part-to-body center offset; SOTA on BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman; also extends to quadruped part-body association. Complement: **HASSOD** — fully self-supervised object/part detection via hierarchical clustering on frozen DINO features + mean-teacher self-training (class-agnostic detection from unlabeled data).
> 
> 2. **Self-distillation biases / spurious features (JEPA vs MAE)**: **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — deep linear analysis showing JEPA self-distillation implicitly prioritizes high-influence ("slow") features and suppresses noisy/low-correlation ones, while MAE reconstruction prioritizes high-variance features (often noisy/spurious); depth strengthens noise suppression; a temporal flickering model quantifies the noise-vs-temporal-correlation trade-off. **LDReg** (ICLR 2024) — local dimensionality regularization against dimensional collapse in SSL (SimCLR/BYOL/MAE).
> 
> 3. **Spectral constraints in deep nets**: **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (ICML 2025) — well-trained CNNs *and* LLMs show power-law Hessian spectra (absent in random nets); power-law goodness predicts LLM generalization where sharpness fails; crucially, **LoRA fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure as full fine-tuning does**, and Hessian trace is a more reliable indicator for adapters — a direct insight for your adapter-based fine-tuning. Related: **Dale's-Law spectral study** — initialization singular-value spectra (NSE) predict trainability more than sign constraints.
> 
> 4. **Active, anytime-valid risk-controlled prediction sets**: **"Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"** (NeurIPS 2024) — extends RCPS to sequential, adaptively-collected data with simultaneous risk control at all times via e-processes/betting; active labeling with IPW, lower-bounded label policies, ML control variates; optimal labeling policy proportional to conditional-risk std; label-efficient convergence to the optimal threshold.
> 
> 5. **Exogenous noise in time series + video embeddings → RL**: **"Video-Based Representation Learning for RL in Exogenous Block MDPs"** (ICLR 2024) — proves forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning recover latent state under iid noise (polynomial sample complexity), but temporally-correlated, action-independent exogenous noise makes video pretraining **exponentially harder** than action-labeled trajectory data; temporal contrastive is most susceptible, forward modeling more robust, trajectory-based ACRO robust. **RaMP** (self-supervised RL) — pre-trains multi-step Q-functions on offline trajectories with random features as pseudo-rewards, then plans via MPC for fast task transfer — a recipe for using pretrained video embeddings to seed policies.
> 
> ## Development trend of these methods
> 
> - **Detection/association**: two-stage heuristic or learned association (Zhou 2018, BodyHands) → anchor-based body-to-part offsets (BPJDet) → **one-stage anchor-free part-to-body offsets** (PBADet) with task-alignment learning; and supervised detectors → **fully self-supervised detectors** trained on pseudo-labels from frozen SSL features (HASSOD).
> - **Self-supervised learning**: from reconstruction (MAE) and contrastive objectives → **theoretical characterization of self-distillation's implicit bias** (JEPA favors influential/slow, low-noise features; MAE favors variance) → explicit regularizers against dimensional collapse (LDReg, spectrum modulation).
> - **Spectral analysis**: from the coarse "two-component" Hessian picture → **power-law Hessian spectra** as a quantitative generalization diagnostic spanning CNNs → LLMs → **LoRA adapters**; and initialization-time singular-value spectra as a trainability predictor.
> - **Risk control**: from batch RCPS → **sequential, anytime-valid, active** variants built on e-processes/betting, with provably optimal labeling policies and predictor-based variance reduction for label efficiency.
> - **RL pretraining**: from action-labeled trajectory representation learning → **video-only pretraining with formal guarantees**, exposing exogenous noise as the key hardness barrier → self-supervised random-feature/implicit-model pretraining enabling reward transfer and policy initialization.
> 
> The common arc: **empirical recipes → formal analyses of implicit biases and spectral structure → scalable, label-efficient, provably safe designs**, with findings (e.g., LoRA vs full fine-tuning Hessian behavior, noise-suppression in JEPA-style embeddings) directly transferable to vision-language models and adapter fine-tuning.

Gold 1：

> The paper investigates what forward‑ and reverse‑mode automatic differentiation (AD) actually compute for neural networks containing non‑differentiable components such as ReLU and maxpool layers, focusing on the Clarke subdifferential as the reference notion of generalized derivative.
> 
> Key findings and trends:
> 
> - **Baseline guarantee**: For pointwise piecewise‑analytic activations with minibatch size 1 and *distinct* bias parameters, AD always returns an element of the Clarke (or Bouligand) subdifferential if its proxy derivatives lie in the corresponding subdifferential (Theorem 1). This generalizes earlier results to allow residual connections and more general proxy derivative choices.
> 
> - **Necessity of conditions**: If either distinct bias parameters are absent (Lemma 2) or the minibatch size is >1 (Lemma 3), AD can produce values outside the Clarke subdifferential.
> 
> - **Recovering correctness with proper proxies**: With distinct bias parameters, correctness can be restored for *any* minibatch size by using fixed convex combinations of left/right derivatives for each activation layer (Theorem 4).
> 
> - **Fully‑connected nets without distinct biases**: Theorem 5 gives a practical sufficient condition (linear independence of certain activation columns) that guarantees correctness; this often holds in practice.
> 
> - **Convolutional/shared‑bias cases**: For networks with shared biases and *no* maxpools, proper convex‑combination proxies again ensure correctness for all minibatches (Theorem 6). Having shared biases, no maxpools, and proper proxies are all necessary (incl. Lemmas 2, 3, 7).
> 
> - **Including maxpools**: Theorem 8 supplies a general sufficient condition, checkable via a linear program, for correctness even with nontrivial maxpools. This extends applicability to realistic CNNs.
> 
> - **Empirical validation**: On MLPs and CNNs (VGG, ResNet) trained in standard setups, these sufficient conditions held at all training steps, so AD's output matched a Clarke subderivative despite frequent hits on non‑differentiable points.
> 
> Overall trend: By characterizing architectural and proxy‑gradient conditions, the work maps out when AD’s chain rule computations align exactly with Clarke subdifferentials, extending theoretical guarantees from narrow special cases to broad classes of modern networks, and confirming empirically that these conditions are typically met in practice.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers matching the five topics
> 
> 1. **Part–body association on COCO** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/v7) with a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands, outperforming BPJDet/HierR-CNN (e.g., Hand AP 89.1, Joint AP 85.98).
> 
> 2. **Autodiff and generalized subgradients** — *What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?* (ICLR 2024). Proves forward/reverse AD returns a Clarke subdifferential element for pointwise ReLU networks (distinct biases, batch size 1), with milder sufficient conditions for maxpool/shared-bias networks; empirically verified on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet.
> 
> 3. **E–I networks under Dale's principle** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). Shows ColEI RNNs fail because of multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra, not sign constraints; introduces normalized SVD entropy (NSE) as a spectrum-pathology metric that anti-correlates with test error across EI ratios and network sizes (sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition).
> 
> 4. **Joint-embedding SSL biased to high-influence features** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). In deep linear models, JEPA/self-distillation is biased to learn high-influence (high-regression-coefficient) features while MAE reconstruction ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue; ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the perceptual PCA subspace (CCA) than MAE.
> 
> 5. **Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023). Pushes Adam/AdamW states from 8-bit to 4-bit via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, and optional second-moment factorization; matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet (Swin-T)/E2E-NLG/WMT14 and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (incl. LoRA-related instruction tuning), saving up to 57.7% memory.
> 
> Note: SVHN appears in no retrieved document; "Precision/AUROC vs CE vs MSE" comparisons appear only indirectly (e.g., DiffusionFake reports AUC; GEEA mixes BCE/MSE), and none of the five core papers above report those specific comparisons.
> 
> ## Development trend
> 
> - **From multi-stage to one-stage, end-to-end formulations**: part–body association moved from two-stage/anchor-based pipelines (BPJDet, HierR-CNN) to a single-stage anchor-free head with a universal part-to-body offset.
> - **From heuristic gradients to principled nonsmooth theory**: rather than assuming differentiability, work now formally characterizes what AD actually returns (Clarke subdifferentials) with checkable conditions and empirical verification.
> - **From "biological constraints hurt" to spectral interpretability**: Dale's-law failures are re-explained via initialization spectra (singular-value clustering, NSE), turning a performance puzzle into a measurable, architecture-driven analysis.
> - **From reconstruction to joint-embedding SSL, with theory**: the field is shifting from pixel-space reconstruction (MAE) to latent joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), backed by analyses of implicit bias toward high-influence features and noise suppression.
> - **From precision to efficiency**: optimizer-state memory has been driven from 32-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit through progressively finer quantization designs (smaller blocks, rank-1 norms, zero-point handling, factorization), enabling lossless fine-tuning of large Transformers at lower memory.
> 
> Overall, the trend is toward **unified/end-to-end formulations, theory-backed understanding of what methods actually compute and why they succeed, and aggressive memory/compute efficiency**, with empirical validation shifting to large-scale and fine-tuning settings.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers in this collection that map to each of your five topics, followed by the development trend.
> 
> ## Paper matches
> 
> **1. One-stage anchor-free part–body association on COCO**
> - **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`). Introduces a single part-to-body center offset on top of anchor-free YOLOv5/v7 multi-scale features, with classification/localization/displacement heads and TOOD task-alignment + DFL losses. Evaluated on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, and CrowdHuman, outperforming BPJDet, HierR-CNN, and ED-Pose (higher Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO). The paper argues part-to-body (one-to-one, always valid) beats BPJDet's body-to-part offsets.
> 
> **2. Reverse/forward autodiff returning generalized subgradients (ReLU/maxpool, MNIST/CIFAR)**
> - **What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?** (ICLR 2024, doc `c9b4b87f…`). Proves forward/reverse AD returns a Clarke subdifferential element for networks with pointwise piecewise-analytic activations when the minibatch size is 1 and non-differentiable neurons have distinct biases; extends to maxpool networks and shared biases under mild sufficient conditions (with failure cases). Empirically verified on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet, with an LP-checkable sufficient condition.
> 
> **3. Spectral/interpretability analyses of Dale's-law E/I nets**
> - **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`). Shows sign constraints are less important than the initial recurrent-weight spectrum: column-partitioned (ColEI) networks have multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent + random matrix structure), whereas standard RNNs and Dale's-ANN (DANN) match quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur clustering. Introduces **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** as a spectrum-pathology metric that anti-correlates with final test error across sizes and E/I ratios; gradient clipping helps ColEI.
> 
> **4. Self-supervised joint-embedding biased to high-influence features vs reconstruction**
> - **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`). JEPA-style latent prediction is biased to high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features, while MAE-style reconstruction prioritizes high-covariance (λ) features; the bias grows with encoder depth. ImageNet-1K I-JEPA-vs-MAE CCA experiments confirm JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features.
> - Related SSL papers in the collection: **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (doc `160e1407…`, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet top-1 accuracy, temperature/batch-size robustness) and **LDReg** (ICLR 2024, doc `51526068…`, local intrinsic dimensionality regularization improving SimCLR/BYOL/MAE on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and COCO detection/segmentation).
> 
> **5. Memory-efficient ~4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW fine-tuning**
> - **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`). 4-bit AdamW and 4-bit Factor for Transformers: smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear quantization for the second moment, plus Adafactor-style factorization; stochastic rounding and a convergence proof. Matches 32-bit AdamW on RoBERTa-L (GLUE, SQuAD), Swin-T (ImageNet), GPT-2 Medium, Transformer-Base (WMT14), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA), saving up to 57.7% memory and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. Practical guidance includes smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, and combining with LoRA/PEFT, FSDP, sharding, and offloading.
> 
> ## Caveats on requested metrics/datasets
> - **Precision/AUROC and SVHN**: these do not appear as reported metrics/datasets in the retrieved content; they could not be verified. The Precision/Recall/F1 reported is from PBADet on COCO, not AUROC.
> - **CE vs MSE**: the closest match is the JEPA-vs-MAE contrast (latent-space prediction vs input-space reconstruction) in topic 4; a BCE-vs-MSE choice appears only in GEEA (entity alignment, doc `c5ca0fc3…`), which is off-topic.
> - **COCO** appears via PBADet (detection AP/MR-2), LDReg (COCO detection/segmentation transfer), and HASSOD (AR on COCO/LVIS/SA-1B).
> 
> ## Development trend of the methods
> 1. **Detection**: two-stage/anchor-based and body-to-part association (BPJDet, HierR-CNN) → one-stage anchor-free part-to-body single center offset with task alignment (PBADet) — simpler representation, scalable to arbitrary part counts, better precision with less redundancy.
> 2. **AD theory**: from "AD may return arbitrary values" to formal guarantees that AD computes a Clarke subdifferential under mild conditions (distinct biases, single-example batches, proper proxies), with LP-verifiable conditions and large-scale empirical confirmation — a trend toward rigorous correctness plus practical verifiability.
> 3. **E/I networks**: from blaming sign constraints for poor learning to a spectral-initialization explanation — singular-value clustering and NSE, not signs, drive performance; biologically faithful architectures (DANN) that preserve healthy spectra train as well as standard RNNs.
> 4. **SSL**: reconstruction-based (MAE) → joint-embedding prediction (JEPA) with a provable implicit bias to high-influence features; theory (deep linear ODEs) validated empirically (CCA on ImageNet), complemented by geometric regularizers (variance reduction, LDReg) to prevent collapse and improve transfer.
> 5. **Optimizer memory**: 32-bit → 8-bit (Dettmers) → 4-bit states with outlier-aware quantization (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization) achieving lossless fine-tuning at scale, explicitly designed to combine with LoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning and offloading.

</details>

### paperscope:trend:447 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an HMI system that needs reliable hand/face–body association on COCO‑style data while also fine‑tuning a large Transformer with LoRA on limited GPUs. I need: a compact anchor‑free detector for part‑to‑body matching in crowded scenes; optimizer states compressed to very low precision (≈4‑bit) to run Adam/AdamW during instruction tuning; guidance on why my joint‑embedding self‑supervised pipeline outperforms masked reconstruction for downstream feedforward classifiers; and assurances that automatic differentiation returns meaningful gradients in deep nets with ReLU, BatchNorm, and maxpools. I also care about interpretability via spectral diagnostics under Dale’s Law, regularization choices (CE vs MSE), and robust metrics like Precision/AUROC on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet‑50. Are there works that cover these needs end‑to‑end?Please summarize the development trend of their methods.

Gold 1：

> The development trend of the methods discussed in these scientific literature papers shows an evolution toward broader applicability and robustness of automatic differentiation (AD) in neural networks containing non-differentiable functions (such as ReLU and maxpool). Early works established AD’s correctness with respect to standard derivatives under smooth conditions, but recent progress has focused on its behavior at non-differentiable points, characterizing outputs with respect to generalized derivatives like the Clarke subdifferential. The trend can be summarized as follows:
> 
> 1. **Expansion of Applicability** — Moving from strictly differentiable programs to realistic neural networks with common non-differentiable components, accommodating architectures with pointwise activations, shared bias parameters, convolutions, normalization layers, residual connections, and maxpools.
> 
> 2. **Refined Sufficient Conditions** — Development of precise sufficient conditions under which AD still returns an element of the Clarke subdifferential, even when minibatch sizes exceed one or bias parameters are shared. Conditions are increasingly designed to be checkable in practice.
> 
> 3. **Layer-wise Proxy Gradient Control** — Recognition that correctness depends on the choice of proxy derivatives AD uses at non-differentiable points; modern results formalize and generalize earlier ad-hoc choices, using convex combinations of one-sided derivatives or elements of the subdifferential.
> 
> 4. **From Theory to Practice** — Transition from purely theoretical guarantees toward empirical validation over practical architectures (e.g., fully-connected nets, CNNs like VGG and ResNet). Experimental results confirm that sufficient conditions often hold during real training.
> 
> Overall, the methods have shifted from narrow, idealized cases toward encompassing the architectures, components, and training setups found in modern deep learning, with verifiable and empirically confirmed conditions ensuring AD’s outputs align with established generalized derivatives.

**naive 最终答案**

> No single work covers all of your needs end-to-end, but the collection contains a paper for each major requirement, and their method trends line up coherently:
> 
> **1. Part–body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)**
> Trend: two-stage/heuristic/anchor-based methods (BodyHands association networks; BPJDet with per-part body-to-part offsets) → one-stage anchor-free detector using a *single part-to-body center offset* over multi-scale features, with task-alignment learning. It scales to any number of parts, guarantees one-to-one part–body correspondence, and beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts and CrowdHuman face–body association (and extends to quadrupeds). This directly matches your "compact anchor-free detector for part-to-body matching in crowded scenes."
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizer states (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Trend: 32-bit → 8-bit block-wise quantization (Dettmers) → 4-bit via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluded linear quantization of the second moment, optionally factorized. It runs Adam/AdamW at ~4-bit with lossless convergence across NLU, MT, image classification, and **LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning on Alpaca**, saving ~57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU) and combining with LoRA/FSDP/offloading.
> 
> **3. Why joint-embedding beats masked reconstruction (JEPA, NeurIPS 2024)**
> Trend: empirical folklore → theoretical analysis on deep linear self-distillation. JEPA's latent-space prediction has an implicit bias toward **high-influence features** (high regression coefficients) and suppresses noise, with depth strengthening the effect; MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue, is susceptible to dimensional collapse, and reconstructs uninformative/noisy pixels. LDReg (ICLR 2024) complements this by regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality (Fisher-Rao metric) to improve downstream linear classifiers/feedforward transfer.
> 
> **4. AD guarantees with ReLU/BatchNorm/maxpool (ICLR 2024)**
> Trend: correctness only for differentiable programs → guarantees for nonsmooth nets. With distinct bias parameters and minibatch size one, AD *always* returns a Clarke subdifferential element; with shared biases (conv/BatchNorm) and larger batches, correctness holds under mild sufficient conditions, empirically verified on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet with ReLU, BatchNorm, maxpools and residual connections. So your gradients are meaningful in practice.
> 
> **5. Spectral interpretability under Dale's Law (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Trend: sign-constraint explanations → spectral explanations. Column-constrained E/I networks (ColEI) fail not mainly because of sign constraints but because of multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra from a rank-one column-mean (nilpotent) structure; **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization is a diagnostic that anti-correlates with final error, while DANN/standard RNNs show unimodal random-matrix spectra.
> 
> **6. Metrics and regularization — only partially covered.**
> The Hessian-spectrum paper (ICML 2025) gives power-law spectral diagnostics on MNIST/CIFAR-10/ResNet (sharpness–generalization links, weight-decay pitfalls, LoRA not inducing the structure), and HASSOD argues AP can be misleading (advocating AR instead); the deepfake paper uses AUC/EER. However, **no work in the context directly compares CE vs MSE regularization, nor reports Precision/AUROC specifically on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50**, so those two points cannot be established from this collection.
> 
> **Overall development trend:** methods move from multi-stage, hand-crafted, high-precision designs toward (i) one-stage/end-to-end representations, (ii) aggressive low-precision memory compression for fine-tuning, (iii) theoretical and spectral explanations (implicit bias, power-law spectra, local dimensionality) that predict empirical success, and (iv) rigorous correctness guarantees for the practical building blocks (nonsmooth activations, normalization, pooling) used in real training.

**community 最终答案**

> Based only on the collection, **no single work covers all your needs end-to-end**, but each thread maps to a distinct paper, and together they show a clear methodological trend: replacing hand-crafted, multi-stage, high-precision designs with simpler, learned, low-memory, theoretically grounded counterparts.
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part-to-body detection → PBADet** (one-stage, anchor-free, ICLR 2024)
> - Trend: multi-stage/anchor-based pipelines (DA-RNN double-anchor RPN, JointDet, BFJDet, HierR-CNN, Detector-in-Detector; BPJDet's body-to-part center offsets) → **one-stage anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset** on multi-scale feature maps, plus task-alignment learning. This keeps a one-to-one part↔body correspondence, scales to any number of parts, and is validated on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, and CrowdHuman (face-body), where it beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN.
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW instruction tuning → "4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Trend: 32-bit → 16-bit → 8-bit block-wise quantization (Dettmers et al.) → **4-bit** via smaller block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizers for the second moment, optionally factorized (4-bit Factor). Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E-NLG and on LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca instruction tuning, with up to 57.7% memory savings and LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU (combinable with LoRA and FSDP).
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding vs masked reconstruction → JEPA deep-linear analysis**
> - Trend: contrastive SSL → non-contrastive/JEPA self-distillation; explanation moves from intuition to exact gradient-flow analysis of deep linear networks. JEPA has an implicit bias toward **high-influence features and noise suppression**, while MAE's feature ordering depends on eigenvalue magnitude; ImageNet experiments show I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace than MAE features—consistent with better downstream linear/feedforward classifiers. Related work (LDReg) shows MAE-type methods are prone to dimensional collapse, which hurts downstream evaluation.
> 
> **4. Meaningful gradients with ReLU/BatchNorm/maxpool → "What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks"** (ICLR 2024)
> - Trend: from "AD is correct only for differentiable programs" → **generalized derivatives (Bouligand/Clarke subdifferentials)** and LP-checkable sufficient conditions. The paper proves AD almost always returns an element of the Clarke subdifferential for practical nets (ReLU, BatchNorm, maxpools, residual connections, minibatches) and verifies this empirically on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet.
> 
> **5. Spectral diagnostics under Dale's Law → "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Trend: from blaming sign constraints (E/I partitioning) → **spectral properties at initialization** as the dominant factor. Simple EI partitioning (ColEI) yields multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and serves as a pre-training diagnostic. DANN/standard RNNs keep quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra and learn well.
> 
> **6–7. Gaps**: No work in the collection directly addresses **CE vs MSE regularization choice** or **Precision/AUROC evaluation on MNIST/CIFAR/ResNet-50**. The Hessian-spectrum paper (MNIST/CIFAR, ResNet/LeNet, LoRA) and HASSOD (arguing AP is misleading, advocating Average Recall) touch adjacent evaluation/regularization topics, but the specific comparisons you asked for are not covered.
> 
> Overall development trend: **from multi-stage/anchor-based detectors to one-stage anchor-free; from 8-bit to 4-bit lossless optimizer states; from contrastive to JEPA-style SSL with mechanistic (spectral/dynamical) theory; from "AD is undefined" to Clarke-subdifferential guarantees with practical verification; and from sign-constraint intuitions to spectral diagnostics**—each move toward simpler, more scalable, theoretically justified, and memory-efficient methods.

## 9. 核验与限制

所有 trace 副本 SHA-256 与服务器采集记录一致，所有模型轮次与 results.jsonl 的 rounds 一致。总体分数、token、耗时和题数已与原汇总交叉核对。没有新增 API 请求、重新评分、修改 gold 或调整实验配置。五组新实验共 532 对 QA；本报告只覆盖标题所示组。完整派生数据与提取脚本见 [summary.json](/Users/yunhaoz/Developer/MyProjects/community_wiki/data/analysis/trace_comparison_20260921/summary.json)、[analyze.py](/Users/yunhaoz/Developer/MyProjects/community_wiki/data/analysis/trace_comparison_20260921/analyze.py)。

本报告没有随机化重复试验或固定检索轨迹的消融，无法识别“社区算法单独造成的准确率变化”。特别是 query 已变、后续读取不同、judge 本身有尺度差异时，只能报告证据支持到的机制层级。
